item.title: 12 Smart Parenting Practices That Can Keep Your Child from Growing Into a Codependent Narcissist
item.description:
Every parent wants their child to grow up with a healthy sense of self. Although sometimes, without meaning to, we pass along habits that set them up for unhealthy patterns instead. One of those patterns is when a person turns out to be a codependent narcissist.

This is someone who struggles extremely with boundaries, craves approval, and at the same time tries to control others in a toxic way to feel secure.

The tricky part is that these traits don’t normally just start overnight. Typically, they are cultivated slowly, often starting in childhood. That’s why the everyday choices parents make matter.

We’ve put together a list of some smart practices that help kids grow into balanced adults who don’t fall into the trap of codependent narcissistic behaviors.

Teach kids that “no” is not a bad word

Children need to learn both sides of “no.” If they never hear it at all, they may grow up expecting the world to bend to their wishes. If they’re never taught how to say it, they may grow up afraid to stand their ground.

Both extremes feed unhealthy patterns.

As a parent, you can practice this by letting kids say no to small things, like not wanting another helping of food, and respecting it. At the same time, parents should use “no” themselves in a calm, firm way that shows limits are part of life. This teaches kids that boundaries are normal, not punishments.

Praise effort, not just results

Kids who only hear praise when they win or excel start tying their worth to their performance. That’s a fast track to narcissistic thinking. On the other hand, kids who never hear encouragement may grow into adults who constantly seek approval from others.

Instead of focusing only on outcomes, notice the effort. Say things like, “I appreciate how hard you worked on that project,” or “I saw you kept trying even when it was tough.” This builds resilience and teaches kids that their value isn’t tied to being perfect.

Let them solve small problems

It’s natural to want to protect kids from frustration, but stepping in too quickly robs them of the chance to learn problem-solving. Whether it’s a playground disagreement or a forgotten homework assignment, letting them figure things out teaches independence.

Over-rescuing feeds codependency, while over-controlling feeds narcissism. The balance is giving guidance without taking over. Ask questions like, “What do you think you could try next?” rather than rushing to fix things yourself.

Show them what healthy boundaries look like

Boundaries aren’t walls; they’re lines that protect relationships. Kids learn boundaries by watching how parents set them. If they see you respect your own limits – like saying you need quiet time after work – and honor others’ limits, they’ll grow up less likely to fall into codependent narcissist patterns.

Boundaries also mean teaching kids that it’s okay to disagree respectfully. This helps them understand that closeness doesn’t require sameness.

Encourage honest conversations

Kids sometimes hide their feelings because they fear disappointing their parents. Others exaggerate their feelings to get attention, which can all lead to unhealthy habits.

Create space for honest talk, without judgment, so they learn that truth is safe. Ask open questions like, “How did that make you feel?” and listen without rushing to correct or dismiss. When kids know their voice matters, they’re less likely to seek control or approval in unhealthy ways.

Teach the difference between confidence and control

Confidence says, “I believe in myself.” Control says, “I need to manage everyone else.” Helping kids understand the difference keeps them from confusing leadership with domination.

Parents can model this by showing confidence in their own choices without needing to control others. For example, saying, “I feel good about the decision I made,” is different from saying, “Everyone should do it my way.” This distinction helps kids grow into adults who lead without overpowering.

Model apologies that mean something

Parents who never apologize teach kids that admitting wrong is weakness. Parents who over-apologize teach kids that their worth depends on pleasing others. A balanced apology, clear, sincere, and not overdone, shows kids how to own their mistakes without losing dignity.

For example, “I was wrong to raise my voice. I’ll work on being calmer” is a healthy apology. It acknowledges the mistake without groveling. Kids who see this learn that accountability builds trust.

Give them chores that matter

Chores aren’t just about cleaning up. They’re about teaching responsibility and contribution. When kids see that their work benefits the family, they learn they’re part of something bigger than themselves.

Instead of assigning meaningless tasks, give them chores that have a visible impact. Assembling a new table, feeding a pet, or helping to choose curtains for the home shows them that their opinion matters. This is a direct antidote to narcissistic thinking, which thrives on entitlement.

Teach them to spot manipulation

Kids who don’t learn to recognize manipulation may grow into adults who either use it or fall victim to it. Talk openly about what manipulation looks like: guilt trips, silent treatment, or exaggerated flattery.

You can point out examples in everyday life, like a TV character who uses guilt to get their way. This helps kids see the difference between healthy influence and unhealthy control. It’s one of the smartest ways to stop codependent narcissist traits from forming.

Balance independence with connection

Too much independence without connection can breed self-centeredness. Too many connections without independence can breed dependency. The balance is teaching kids to enjoy being with others while also being comfortable alone.

Encourage solo play as well as family activities. Let them spend time with friends, but also value family meals. This balance teaches them that relationships are important, but so is self-reliance.

Show them that feelings are not weakness

Kids who learn to bury feelings may grow into adults who seek control instead of vulnerability. Kids who learn to dramatize feelings could grow into adults who manipulate others. Rather, teach a child that feelings are natural and manageable.

Say things like, “It’s okay to feel sad, and it’s okay to talk about it.” This normalizes emotions without making them the center of attention.

Teach gratitude, not just saying “thank you”

Gratitude isn’t just polite words. It’s noticing the good in everyday life. Encourage kids to name what they’re thankful for: friends, meals, opportunities. Gratitude shifts focus away from entitlement and prevents codependent narcissistic traits from taking root.

You can make gratitude part of daily routines, like sharing one thing you’re thankful for at dinner. This simple practice builds perspective and humility.

Balance in parenting comes from the small, repeated choices that shape how kids see themselves and others. Over time, these everyday habits protect them from falling into the unhealthy patterns of a codependent narcissist and instead nurture resilience, humility, and emotional strength.

Signs You’re Helping Kids Avoid Codependent Narcissist Traits

Parents often wonder if their efforts are making a difference. There are clear signs that show kids are learning balance instead of leaning toward unhealthy patterns. When children express feelings openly without fear of being dismissed, take responsibility without constantly fishing for praise, and enjoy independence while still valuing connection, it shows they’re learning that relationships and self-reliance can coexist.

These signs may seem small, but they reflect deep lessons about identity, respect, and emotional health. They are evidence that your parenting practices are steering your child away from the traps of becoming a codependent narcissist and toward becoming an adult who is confident, compassionate, and balanced in how they relate to themselves and others.

Why Professional Counseling Helps

Parenting is full of trial and error, and no one gets it perfect. But being intentional about these practices helps kids grow into adults who are confident without being controlling, connected without being dependent.

If you’re worried about whether your child is showing signs of becoming a codependent narcissist, or if you want guidance on building healthier family patterns, professional counseling is a wise step. Consider reaching out to one of the counselors listed on this site or calling the numbers on the screen.

item.title: Common Causes of Depression and Where to Find Support
item.description:
Introduction

This second article on depression is a look at our best understanding of what causes depression. There is no single cause, but a wide range of possible causes for an individual experiencing this troubling state. We can have many physical illnesses, such as an upset stomach, and there can be many causes, though the symptoms are quite similar.

Depression is real, and the impact on the person is great, affecting them emotionally, psychologically, and physically. The following is largely a survey of what some of the causes are for depression.

I was also curious as to examples of depression that there are in the Bible. One thing that has struck me is that God never shames anyone for feeling down, discouraged, or what we would call depressed. I believe it is because He knows well the emotions and the pain of that experience. We know this because of the life of Jesus. He was subjected to every temptation as us, but without sin (Hebrew 5:15). Jesus also showed great compassion for the downtrodden.

Elijah the prophet experienced such discouragement regarding those who were trying to kill him and asked God to take his life. He was so distressed that he couldn’t take life anymore (I Kings 19 and 20). King David expressed depression throughout the Psalms.

Job questioned why he was born and lamented his life in Job 3. For some of these examples, the conditions of life led to a sense of despair and we really don’t know for how long they were in this condition, but God’s response is not a “just snap out of it” but is patient and full of grace.

Negative Sense of Self

What I have found in my clients and research is that one key common thread to the causes of depression is when one takes an inward look and they conclude that, “I’m not good enough, I’m flawed, I’m self-indulgent, I’m evil” (McWilliams, p237) To carry this further, there is a general feeling that one believes that they are not worthy to be loved, riddled with self-doubt, feel out of place in social situations, feel incompetent, and many other self-condemning thoughts.

It’s a horrible feeling. Coming to this conclusion when deep in one’s soul there is the need for love, acceptance, and belonging, can be crushing. As one perceives themselves in this light and assume others concur that they find it difficult to combat these negative thoughts. This triggers a vicious internal thought loop of self-condemnation, fear of rejection by most around them and seemingly there is no way out.

These negative thoughts and feelings have a profound impact on the quality of life for the individual. These thoughts, often unconscious, are devastating to the individual and pull them ever further in a downward spiral. It only makes sense that such thoughts and feelings about oneself would be hard to bear and lead to suffering.

The influences of these thoughts and feelings are often the result of deprived nurturing and trauma in the form of abuse or neglect of a child. The child, as they seek to make sense of the world around them, begins to conclude that his/her care givers cannot be relied on to take care of their most basic needs. They conclude that adults cannot be trusted. Since the adults around them treat them harshly, they must not be worthy of their care or their love.

Children, including teens, will internalize these experiences as they build a schema to understand the world in which they live. The convictions they draw about themselves, like who they are, what they are about, are most often negative.

There are other influences besides families that can contribute to a negative sense of self. One author suggested that depression is a signature illness of our time. Meaning the complexities of modern life, intrusive technologies, and the push to find satisfaction in oneself and life through broadcasting everything that happens almost every day is ultimately harmful.

No doubt social media holds up standards of acceptability, favorability, and beauty by showcasing someone having more fun than you, being better than you, or having a better life, leading to a culture of comparison.

Another aspect of our time in the early 21st century is how “the enormous increase in individual choices of life’s perspectives lead to a loss of social security and makes one’s own identity a lifelong project of the individual.” (Leuzinger-Bohleber, p. 22).

Sociologist Alain Ehrenberg declares “the exhausted self to be the disease of contemporary society, whose norms of behavior are no longer based on guilt and discipline, but above all responsibility and initiative.” (Ibid.).

This is a bit of a turn from just blaming social media, by going deeper into how the new pressures of life, with a myriad of choices in identity, social grouping, education, career, are all geared to push one “to be all you can be.” And if you’re not, you’re a loser.

No doubt, some developing young adults might thrive in such an environment, but for many it is just too much. The mere number of choices creates anxiety and the potential for failure. Ehrenberg goes on to explain that depression is the “disease of the individual who is inhibited and exhausted by the tension between the possible and the impossible.” (Ibid.)

Meaning Making

 We are all locked inside our brains and experience everything in our own unique way. We also interpret what goes on around us based on our biases, experiences, notions, education, influential people, and many more. There is a saying: “perception is reality.” I still have a hard time wrapping my brain around this, but it does tend to play out for people. Our brains are designed to develop and see patterns in life.

When a person seeks to understand something, they automatically will piece together aspects of that thing and create a pattern. This is the meaning-making that can take several different roads. If, for example, a person tries to make meaning out of some tragedy or misfortune, whether it affects them or not, and thinks that they are the cause of this event, that is the kind of thinking that could lead to depressive thoughts and feelings.

This is common. It teeters on superstition. I have known Christians who have a version of this thinking who, when some difficulty has come upon them, believe it is a consequence of disobedience. If you start to string this out over time, it could lead to the conclusion that many other difficulties in the world around you are your fault.

That kind of thinking, without serious challenge, can lead to a serious negative sense of self. And that leads to depression. Our internal conversation is not the only thing that can lead to depression; life circumstances can often be a large contributing factor.

External Causes

There are also external causes that can lead to depression, depending on the situation. How one responds to these events can be critical to a healthy resolution or can lead to an unhealthy perspective, as mentioned above. A healthy way of looking at events such as an accident, a bad interaction with a person, a tragedy, or a natural disaster, as being a one-time thing or extraordinary (but that will pass), can help.

When you can look at these things and decide that they don’t have anything to do with you, it is easier to resolve them internally. But most unfortunate events can also deeply affect your mood because they represent a deep loss. When there is pain, suffering, or disillusionment, the pure weight of these circumstances can be too much to bear.

Surveys have consistently shown that one of the greatest external sources of depression is the death of a loved one (Murphy, et al., p. 599). Grieving manifests in different ways, but depression is often one of them. Most often determined by how close the person was in your life.

I have had several clients whose depression went on for several years due to their loss. Imagine the loss of a child, a parent, or a spouse. That grief can be overwhelming and difficult to process and thereby pull one down into a pit of depression.

Other things mentioned in these studies were conflict with friends, the breakup of family, or failed relationships. One of our basic needs is to belong, and when conflict with loved ones or a valued relationship goes south, it can leave us feeling alone, and our sense of security is dashed. I have worked with many couples, and the prospect of having their relationship end is almost always met with dread.

It often propels them to seek couples therapy and seek a path to healing their relationship. The pain, the loss of a dream, the loneliness, and the sense of failure of that relationship can add up to a major depressive episode or prolonged depression. It hurts badly, and the perseverating thoughts that come with it often contribute to and deepen depression.

There are other common stressors in life that can deeply affect one’s mood. The most common is financial stress. Unemployment by itself can defeat even the most optimistic personality. We tend to attach a lot of self-worth to the ability to support ourselves and our family if we have one. It can set in motion a downward spiral from which it is hard to recover.

Most kinds of stress that are prolonged will lead to a buildup of cortisol, a steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands, and that buildup can upset the bio-balance and, for some, lead to depression.

Chronic stress from situations like divorce, single-parenthood, dominant personalities at work or in the family, discrimination based on race, ethnic origin, sexual orientation, overwork, or a special needs child (and the list could go on) can lead to depression for some. Suffice it to say, these stressors, which are experienced daily, will take a toll.

Biological Causes

Some serious levels of depression are related to being pregnant and/or having given birth to a child. Most have heard of postpartum depression, but the more recent term is peripartum depression. The peri refers to the period surrounding the birth, in that it can be experienced shortly before giving birth as well as after. This is also a real thing and quite difficult to treat.

We have expectations that giving birth and the time after would be the greatest experience for a mother and often is. However, for many, it is not. Studies indicate that 13-19% of all women after giving birth meet the criteria for depression. For women who experience this, it is very distressing because they, too, think it should be the greatest thing ever to have a child.

There can be other biological causes of depression, such as seasonal affective disorder, common in the winter months when daylight is scarce. Folks in Alaska can attest to this. People with various debilitating injuries or conditions can become depressed due to the loss of mobility and related restrictions. Another biological cause is Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder, which can lead to a disruptive mood that reflects many of the criteria of major depressive disorder.

We know that the brain’s chemistry has a significant impact on us. The secretion of various hormones in our bodies can have a great impact on our moods and mental well-being. Introducing certain chemicals into our system can also lead some to experience depression, such as illicit drugs as well as prescription medications. The mechanism of how the brain works, with the connection of brain neurons to each other, is another area that can impact mood.

Neurotransmitters are the vehicle that helps the communication of one neuron to another, which leads to our thinking, memory, and emotions. The most common neurotransmitters are serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Serotonin regulates mood, sleep, and appetite. Norepinephrine affects the body’s stress response, and Dopamine controls pleasure and motivation. You can see that if any one of these is out of balance, it can affect one’s life. The biological causes can be inherently linked to someone’s genetics.

Genetics

Another source of depression is thought to be due to genetics. Studies have confirmed that people who have first-degree relatives (parent, sibling, or child) have a 2 to 3 times greater likelihood of having depression compared with those who don’t have a relative with that history.

Of course, this brings up the classic debate between the most influential impact on the development of personality and character: nature or nurture. Studies confirm that it’s most likely both, and it’s futile to try to separate them as one being the dominant cause. Identical twin studies have shown that if one twin has depression, the other has a much greater likelihood of having it as compared with the occurrence in fraternal twins.

Exposure to Adversity and Trauma

There have been many studies on the impact of trauma and abuse in early childhood, teens, and into adulthood. Not all lead to depression, but there is plenty of evidence that exposure to such dramatic experiences can lead to depression along with other disorders. Subjecting a child to physical, sexual, or emotional abuse can shatter their world.

The incomprehensible behavior of the abuser will inflict deep hurt, and the child cannot process the experience because they cannot do so. Those experiences will likely accumulate, and the child will internalize them and see themselves as being at fault.

There are other adversities where children can experience great stress and confusion, such as living in a home with an alcoholic. That experience is very disruptive to a child’s sense of security; the child will wonder what version of that parent might be coming home tonight: the drunk parent or the sober parent.

Family violence, with loud or destructive arguments, can be traumatic as well. Living with someone with a serious mental illness like depression, bipolar disorder, or a psychotic disorder like schizophrenia can lead to many traumatic experiences. Being able to know what is normal becomes impossible.

The Integrated Theory

I have set forth several possible causes of depression. I suggested at the beginning that there is no single cause but several ways to become clinically depressed. The integrated view is that each of us has certain vulnerabilities along with conditions in our lives that can send us down that road. For example, there are certain biological states that I mentioned that could be a vulnerability toward depression.

This could be combined with a psychological vulnerability such as low self-esteem, self-doubt, or fears of rejection that could tip one over the edge. Then combine that with the various stressors in life, such as personal loss, humiliation, and rejection, which can trigger the activation of stress hormones that can influence neurotransmitters.

These stressors can lead to interpersonal relationship problems and lack of needed support. When depressed, one can have negative beliefs about others and oneself, a sense of hopelessness, or dysfunctional attitudes. In essence, this describes the circling-down-the-drain experience that is so often the experience of depression.

If you identify with some of the causes and wonder if you might be depressed, first, don’t blame yourself. What you or perhaps someone you love is experiencing is a serious condition and can be treated. My next article will center on the treatment of depression.

If you are someone you know is experiencing depression or suspect they are, please feel free to contact me or someone else in our network at Spokane Christian Counseling. I can be reached at 509-569-7102 or martyr@spokanechristiancounseling.com.

References:
Barlow, D. H., & Durand, V. M. (n.d.). Abnormal psychology an integrated approach. Wadsworth/Thomson Learning.
Leuzinger-Bohleber, M. (2025a). Depression: A contemporary introduction. Routledge, Taylor & Francis Group.
McWilliams, N. (2012). Psychoanalytic diagnosis, second edition: Understanding personality structure in the clinical process. Guilford Publications.
National Research Council (US) and Institute of Medicine (US) Committee on Depression, Practices, P., & and the Healthy Development of Children. (1970, January 1). The etiology of depression. Depression in Parents, Parenting, and Children: Opportunities to Improve Identification, Treatment, and Prevention.
Westerbeek, J., & Mutsaers, K. (2008). Depression narratives: How the self became a problem. Literature and Medicine, 27(1), 25–55. https://doi.org/10.1353/lm.0.0017

Photos:

item.title: Economic Anxiety: Sacred Solutions and Biblical Tools
item.description:
Economic anxiety has no discrimination when it comes to faith. The reality is that money worries consume even the strongest believer’s mind. This creates tension between spiritual trust and earthly concern, resulting in an impossible situation in maintaining faith and battling the stress of financial uncertainty.

Financial anxiety affects many people in the Christian community and requires sacred solutions to address the financial struggle that runs rampant in today’s society.

This issue runs deeper than the simplicity of having enough money in the bank. It is a reflection of how we understand God’s provision, while simultaneously dealing with the practical concerns of everyday life.

The contradiction creates a feeling of spiritual failure due to persistent anxiety, despite prayer and faith. Managing anxiety around money becomes particularly complex for believers who feel they should just trust God while facing real financial issues.

Every person’s financial situation is unique, which means there are no clear-cut spiritual formulas to eliminate economic stress. Because of this, many Christians feel as though they are wearing clothes that don’t fit spiritually. They continually try to walk in a way of faith that seems disconnected from their daily financial reality.

The sacred solutions for managing anxiety need to acknowledge the spiritual and practical aspects of economic stress. Biblical tools that address real-world concerns are available through Christian Counseling.

For this reason I say to you, do not be worried about your life, as to what you will eat or what you will drink; nor for your body, as to what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air, that they do not sow, nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they? – Matthew 6:25-26, NASB

Biblical Tools for Understanding Economic Anxiety’s Impact

Economic anxiety creates a complex web of challenges, mentally and spiritually. These challenges extend beyond the bank account balances and affect faith and lifestyle. Financial stress is known to lead to anxiety, depression, sleep disturbances, and behavioral changes.

Each of these can present itself in psychological symptoms that indicate persistent worry. Since financial stress is chronic, it often becomes a constant background noise in our minds. This leads to the inability to concentrate and make clear decisions.

The spiritual impact of economic anxiety brings another layer of complexity to the struggle. Many believers struggle with guilt when they worry about money. They often interpret this anxiety as a lack of faith rather than a normal human response to genuine stress.

The self-condemnation of this issue creates an additional burden that will increase anxiety. Adding spiritual shame to an already overwhelming situation makes managing anxiety more difficult.

When faith and financial worry intersect, it often reveals deeper questions about God’s character and our understanding of his provision. Many believers struggle with doubts about whether God truly cares about their practical means when they face economic uncertainty. The spiritual questions are normal and valid. They do not indicate weak faith, but rather an honest wrestle with how divine sovereignty intersects with human responsibility regarding financial matters.

Sacred Foundations for Financial Peace Through Scripture

The Bible provides numerous examples of God’s provision that serve as anchors during times of economic anxiety. Understanding these promises requires intentional and careful examination of the context and application to modern finances.

God’s provision doesn’t always look like what we think it should look like. His timing rarely matches our schedule. Both can create tension for believers who are trying to manage anxiety and maintain faith in God’s provision.

God’s provision principle is woven throughout Scripture. It is seen in the daily provision of manna in the wilderness to the feeding of 5000 by Jesus. These stories demonstrate that God knows human needs and has the power to meet them extraordinarily.

They also indicate that his provision often comes in unexpected forms and requires participation from those receiving it. The Israelites had to gather the manna, and the disciples had to distribute the fish and the loaves.

Having a sense of meaning and purpose can greatly reduce stress levels, which will improve mental health. For Christians, this sense of purpose often stems from understanding their role in God’s will and trusting in His character.

Managing anxiety is more achievable when believers remember that their worth and security come from their relationship with God and not their financial status. The need for practical financial planning isn’t eliminated by faith.

A perspective from faith can reduce the intensity of financial anxiety by placing money in its proper context as a tool, and not a source of security. Viewing finances through the lens of stewardship, rather than survival, creates a space for practical action and spiritual trust to coexist.

Divine Tools for Managing Economic Stress Daily

Spiritual practices and biblical tools must work together to address and manage anxiety regarding finances. Prayer and meditation can provide emotional and spiritual grounding, as well as budgeting and planning to address the practical and financial concerns behind the anxiety. Mindfulness practices will calm the nervous system and create clearer thinking in terms of financial decisions and challenges.

One practical tool and spiritual exercise, and stewardship, is creating a realistic budget. Tracking income and expenses honestly reveals that our actual financial situation is either better or more manageable than anxiety suggests.

The fear of the unknown that often drives financial anxiety is reduced in this process. The simple act of creating a budget demonstrates trusting God’s provision and taking responsible action with the resources He’s provided.

Social support in managing financial stress is important because isolation often makes anxiety worse. Christians can find support through church communities, small groups, and Christian financial counseling. Sharing financial struggles isn’t always easy, but in the appropriate settings, it can reduce shame and open opportunities for spiritual and practical encouragement. Several churches offer financial classes or counseling, combined with biblical principles and sound financial practices.

It is important to develop healthy coping mechanisms to help with managing anxiety when it reaches its peak during a financial crisis. Practices and essential tools for maintaining mental health during financial difficulties can be:

  • Regular exercise
  • Adequate sleep
  • And stress-reducing techniques

These tools can also be combined with spiritual disciplines, such as:

  • Scripture reading
  • Worship
  • Prayer time
  • Fellowship

It’s also important to avoid unhealthy coping mechanisms like:

  • Overspending
  • Substance abuse
  • Avoidance of financial responsibilities

Following these healthy mechanisms for managing anxiety can protect mental health and financial stability.

Biblical Solutions for Long-term Economic Resilience

The Christian perspective of long-term financial resilience involves building practical financial habits, using sacred solutions that will withstand economic storms. This will require shifting from crisis-type thinking to strategic planning using wisdom and faith. Creating a financial plan can significantly reduce anxiety and provide a sense of direction, even in uncertain situations.

Emergency funds can serve as a practical safety net and an expression of faith in God’s provision. Putting money aside for unexpected expenses indicates there’s a trust that God will provide the means to save while also taking responsible action to prepare for future hardships.

Having a balanced approach like this acknowledges that God often provides when there is wise planning and preparation. The peace of mind that comes from having financial reserves will dramatically reduce the intensity of economic anxiety.

Cultivating multiple income streams and building marketable skills can create financial flexibility that will help with adapting to changing financial conditions. This will reflect the biblical principle of working diligently while trusting God for the results.

The book of Proverbs repeatedly emphasizes the value of hard work, planning, and skill development to create sustainable income. Knowing there are options because of abilities that help navigate the financial challenges makes managing anxiety easier.

A long-term perspective requires intentional and regular evaluation of the financial goals with an understanding of biblical values and priorities. This entails considering how financial decisions will align with principles of generosity, stewardship, and trust in God’s provision. Financial plans that reflect spiritual values create greater internal peace and reduce the conflict between faith and practical financial management.

The goal is not perfect financial security, but developing skills and faith to navigate the challenges.

For I know the plans that I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for calamity to give you a future and a hope. – Jeremiah 29:11, NASB

For more information or help with economic anxiety, contact our representatives. They can connect you with a local Christian counselor and provide the help you need.

item.title: What Most Women Wish Someone Had Told Them About Menopause and Depression
item.description:
Menopause is one of those life stages that everyone knows is coming, yet few women feel truly prepared for. Conversation about it is often limited to hot flashes, night sweats, or the end of monthly cycles. What is rarely discussed in detail is the emotional impact, especially the connection between menopause and depression.

Many women discover this reality only once they are living through it. They may wake up one morning feeling unusually sad, irritable, or disconnected, and wonder why. Some describe it as a fog that settles over their daily life. Others notice that tasks they once handled with ease suddenly feel draining. Because the emotional side of menopause is not openly discussed, women often feel blindsided when depression becomes part of their experience.

The silence regarding menopause and depression is one of the biggest challenges. Women are told to expect physical changes, but the emotional toll is minimized. This lack of open conversation leaves many feeling isolated, unsure whether what they are experiencing is normal, and uncertain where to turn for help.

One of the biggest challenges is that younger women grow up with a lot of myths about menopause.

Myths Younger Women Believe About Menopause

  • Some believe it happens overnight, as if one day periods stop and everything changes instantly.
  • Others think menopause is only about hot flashes or that depression during this stage is simply moodiness.
  • There is also a myth that menopause is the same for everyone. Younger women may assume that all women experience the same symptoms in the same way. This belief can make it harder to accept the wide range of experiences that exist.
  • Another common myth is that menopause only affects women in their late fifties. Often, symptoms begin much earlier. Some women notice changes in their forties, and others even sooner.

Depression linked to hormonal shifts can appear long before the final menstrual cycle. These myths create confusion and make it harder for women to recognize what is really happening when the time comes.

When Menopause Really Begins

Menopause is not a single event. It is a process, and the first stage is called perimenopause. This transition can last several years. During perimenopause, hormone levels fluctuate, cycles become irregular, and emotional changes begin to surface.

Perimenopause is not very well known because women may still have their periods, leading them to believe menopause has not started. Yet this stage is when many symptoms of menopause and depression first appear. Sleep disturbances, sudden irritability, and unexplained sadness are common.

Awareness that perimenopause is part of the journey is a way to help women understand that depression during this time is not unusual.

Perimenopause also highlights how gradual the process can be. Some women experience subtle changes that build slowly, while others face sudden shifts that feel disruptive. Understanding this stage helps women prepare for what lies ahead rather than being caught off guard.

How Menopause Manifests Differently in Women

One of the least discussed realities is how differently menopause manifests in women. Some experience mostly physical symptoms, such as hot flashes, night sweats, or weight changes. Others find the emotional side more challenging, with depression, anxiety, or loss of motivation taking center stage.

There is no single pattern. A woman may feel fine physically but struggle emotionally. Another may have intense physical discomfort but little depression. This variation is why menopause and depression are hard to generalize. Each woman’s experience is unique, shaped by genetics, lifestyle, and personal history.

Even within families, experiences can differ. Mothers or sisters may go through menopause at different ages with very different symptoms. This diversity is rarely acknowledged, leaving women to wonder why their experience does not match what they have heard from others.

Why Menopause and Depression Are Not Well Understood

Menopause and depression remain poorly understood for several reasons. First, medical training often focuses more on reproductive health than on the emotional impact of menopause. Many doctors are not fully equipped to explain the mental health side of this transition.

Second, cultural silence plays a role. In many communities, menopause is treated as something private, not openly discussed. Women may feel embarrassed to talk about depression or mood changes, fearing judgment or dismissal.

Third, research into menopause and depression has historically been limited compared to other health issues. This lack of attention means fewer resources and less public awareness. As a result, women are left searching for answers on their own.

Finally, the overlap between menopause symptoms and other life stressors adds to the confusion. Women in midlife may be balancing careers, divorce, caring for children, or supporting aging parents. Depression during menopause may be dismissed as general stress, when in fact hormonal changes are playing a significant role.

The Everyday Struggles No One Talks About

Menopause and depression affect daily life in ways that are rarely acknowledged. Concentration at work may become harder. Tasks that once felt simple, like cooking dinner or managing schedules, may feel draining. In addition, relationships can be strained when mood changes are misunderstood.

Sleep problems are another everyday struggle. Night sweats and insomnia leave women exhausted, which worsens depression. Fatigue makes it harder to cope with stress, creating a cycle that feels difficult to break.

Social connections may also suffer. Women sometimes withdraw from friends or family because they feel misunderstood. This isolation deepens depression and makes the transition even harder.

While menopause and depression bring challenges, there are practical ways to find support. Women do not have to face this stage alone.

Practical Ways to Seek Real Day‑to‑Day Support

Steps to consider include:

  • Track symptoms. Keeping a journal of mood changes, sleep patterns, and physical symptoms can help identify triggers and patterns.
  • Focus on lifestyle habits. Regular exercise, balanced nutrition, and consistent sleep routines can ease both physical and emotional symptoms.
  • Communicate with family and friends. Explaining what menopause and depression feel like helps loved ones provide better support.
  • Join support groups. Many communities and online platforms offer spaces where women share experiences and advice. Hearing others’ stories can reduce feelings of isolation.
  • Talk to a healthcare professional who understands menopause and depression. Ask specific questions about emotional symptoms, not just physical ones.
  • Explore counseling or therapy. Mental health professionals can provide coping strategies and help women process the emotional side of menopause.

These practical steps make the journey more manageable and remind women that support is available.

Menopause and depression are realities many women wish someone had explained earlier. The silence around emotional symptoms leaves women unprepared, while myths and misunderstandings add confusion.

Acknowledging important precursory stages (like perimenopause), understanding the differences in how menopause manifests, and having some insight into why these issues are not well explained are all part of building awareness.

The everyday struggles of menopause and depression are real, but so are the ways to find help. Professionally guided support groups across the USA, as well as one‑on‑one counseling, offer safe spaces to learn, prepare, and cope.

Seeking guidance even before menopause or perimenopause begins can help women feel knowledgeable and ready for the unknown symptoms ahead. If you are considering support, know that help is available. Reach out to a professional today to begin preparing for this stage of life with confidence and care.

On this platform, you can find listed professionals who have been helping countless women of all ages learn more about the real ways to prepare for and cope with this transitional stage in every woman’s life. If you need more information or would like to get started with pre-menopause counseling, there are numbers on this site you can call. Contact us today to learn more.

item.title: Can Emotionally-Focused Couples Therapy Save Your Marriage After an Affair?
item.description:
Everything you thought you knew about your marriage changes when there has been an affair. The questions are tougher to answer, and the closeness becomes an afterthought. It is a rawness that asks if it can be survived.

For some couples, the answer is an honest and painful no. But for others, there is another route to take. It is the route where the yes leads to emotionally focused couples therapy (EFCT). This type of therapy leads to understanding of what happened, identifying the needs of each spouse, and rebuilding a marriage after honest evaluation from both spouses.

What Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Is — and What It Isn’t

Emotionally focused couples therapy was developed in the 80s and grounded in attachment theory. Science emphasizes how people bond and what repair requires. The idea is that humans are wired for close bonds, and when those bonds break down, people act out. Anger and withdrawal aren’t indications of bad behavior. They are misguided attempts at connection that have gone wrong. When you and your spouse recognize this distinction, it changes everything about how healing begins.

The conversation then shifts from how this happens towards something that is more useful but harder. This conversation revolves around what was really happening between you and what each of you will need to do going forward. Emotionally focused couples therapy is effective at preventing relapse only when both spouses engage with genuine honesty. There has to be a mutual willingness to go through the process in order to reach the desired results.

Some Christian counselors are trained to assist Christian couples in finding a connection of faith and a therapeutic process to heal and move forward after an affair. The counselor can help couples understand the positive intent underneath even the most negative behavior.

Why It Feels Like More Than Heartbreak?

The affair breaks trust, and underneath that lies an emotional bond that was already becoming frayed. Through EFCT, the Christian counselor and both spouses pursue the bond and not just the behavior. If you are the betrayed spouse, then what you feel goes beyond hurt and rejection.

Infidelity produces trauma-like symptoms, such as insomnia, flashbacks, intrusive thoughts, and hypervigilance about feeling safe. These symptoms are not an overreaction. This is the response of your nervous system to a profound wound. Emotionally focused couples therapy treats this for what it is without rushing you toward forgiveness until the injury has been fully acknowledged.

Infidelity will also produce symptoms in the individual who initiated the affair. Shame, regret, and disconnection become the weight that a spouse will carry after they have been unfaithful. EFCT will also help with this.

Regardless of which side you are on, there is no justifying what happened, but both experiences need to be understood before healing can take place. Scripture teaches us to bear one another’s burdens not because it is easy, but because that is what genuine love and commitment look like when they are tested.

When a couple can engage honestly with the process, they will find improvements in intimacy and forgiveness over time. EFCT allows the couple to sit in the hard moments of this engagement. By sitting in these moments, the couple starts to reach for each other again instead of defending themselves. It is this shift in the relationship that EFCT builds toward.

What Makes Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Different?

Not every form of therapy is built to handle the damage that an affair causes. An affair is an attachment injury, and not just a communication problem. Attachment injury requires care that reaches deeper than communication, coaching, or conflict resolution strategies.

This distinction is important in choosing the correct approach that will help a couple who has faced infidelity. Emotionally focused couples therapy focuses on a different premise entirely.

Even the most successful therapy model for highly distressed couples is not as effective as EFCT. Couples whose trust had been destroyed by an affair were able to heal through this process. Christian counselors trained in EFCT are able to bring clinical expertise together with a faith-based understanding of the covenant and focus on the genuine human capacity for change.

Infidelity healing requires that both partners open up and talk about the pain honestly. It means they have to have the hard conversation about what led to the affair without assigning blame. The conversation leads the way to understanding so that an effective apology can be given. It is also vital to have an effective acknowledgment of the apology. Each person in the relationship is part of this conversation.

What Does the Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Look Like?

Infidelity healing through emotionally focused couples therapy is slow, challenging, and rarely in a straight line. In the beginning, the sessions focus on building enough safety for both spouses to be honest about the emotional patterns that existed prior to infidelity. Conversation about the affair is not part of these early sessions, but rather it is about the patterns that were underneath it.

Typically, the therapist will help you and your spouse identify and interrupt negative cycles that the marriage has been locked into. The cycles of pursuing and withdrawing, and shutting down and blaming, are replaced by patterns that are more sustainable. The unfaithful spouse takes accountability without defensiveness, and the injured spouse is required to stay present with the pain and not use it as a permanent wall.

Not every marriage will make it; sometimes, one or both spouses decide the damage is too much. But even then, therapy can make it possible to end things without heavy fallout. For those couples who choose to stay with the process, they will build something more honest than what they had before. The old relationship will be gone, and something new will be built.

What does Scripture say about this kind of bearing with each other? Colossians emphasizes patience, compassion, and bearing with one another even when it costs something. Christian counselors who specialize in this field understand that the goal isn’t just restoring things to their original state, but rather achieving something even better.

What Does the Process Ask of Each Spouse?

There is no straight line to healing through emotionally focused couples therapy, and the early sessions don’t focus on the affair. Through honesty about the emotional patterns that existed before infidelity, safety can be built to ensure healing conversations. Christian counselors are able to help identify and interrupt the negative cycles that once consumed the relationship.

Navigating this process means honesty and accountability from both sides. EFCT requires that each spouse move out of the mindset of pointing blame, becoming defensive, or shutting down. It will require that you and your spouse navigate the process with compassion and patience, regardless of what it will cost in the moment.

Christian counselors are able to help with infidelity recovery by emphasizing that the goal is to build something more honest and more resilient, rather than trying to restore what was lost. Sometimes, couples find that the damage is too serious, and the marriage doesn’t survive. For the couples who choose to work hard and stay with it, they will find that they can rebuild with purpose.

Could EFCT Help Your Relationship?

It is important that you and your spouse reach out for help as soon as possible. The reality is that by waiting for the pain to fade or for an honest conversation to be enough, the negative cycles become stronger. By choosing emotionally focused couples therapy, you are choosing a proactive investment in your future with your spouse. However, it only works if both of you are willing to engage honestly.

It doesn’t matter when the affair came to light; what matters is that there’s no wrong time to begin EFCT. For more information or to schedule an appointment with a counselor, contact our office today and speak with our reception team. They will be happy to answer questions and provide you with information to choose to rebuild the marriage that infidelity damaged.

The work ahead won’t be easy, but when you and your spouse are willing, the investment can pay off with a stronger marriage.

item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

References
1. Dolfi, A., & Tudose, C. (2025). Diagnostic challenges of autism spectrum disorder in women without intellectual or language impairments: a narrative review. Journal of Medicine and Life, 18(8), 710.
2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.

Photos:
“Walton Lighthouse,” courtesy of Paulius Dragunas, Unsplash.com, CCO License
“Lighthouse on Rock,” courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, CCO License

The post Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication appeared first on Mill Creek Christian Counseling.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

References
1. Dolfi, A., & Tudose, C. (2025). Diagnostic challenges of autism spectrum disorder in women without intellectual or language impairments: a narrative review. Journal of Medicine and Life, 18(8), 710.
2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.Photos:

2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.
