item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

References
1. Dolfi, A., & Tudose, C. (2025). Diagnostic challenges of autism spectrum disorder in women without intellectual or language impairments: a narrative review. Journal of Medicine and Life, 18(8), 710.
2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.

item.title: Treatment and Recovery Options for Different Types of Eating Disorders
item.description:
Eating disorders are a reality many Americans have to deal with, affecting people of all walks of life, age, race, or gender. Every year in the US, around 10,000 precious lives are lost as a direct result of an eating disorder. Nearly thirty million people in the US will struggle with an eating disorder during their lifetime. Eating disorders are becoming even more prevalent among young adults and adolescents.

With disordered eating affecting so many people, not just in the US, but across the world, knowing what they are and how to best support a loved one with an eating disorder is that much more important. For those struggling with eating disorders, understanding what they’re going through can help them process the experience. It can also help them find ways to move toward wholeness and feeling healthy.

Eating Disorders: Understanding What They Are

There are many ideas out there about what eating disorders are, how they affect a person, and who is affected. It may be helpful, by way of naming the myths surrounding eating disorders, to clarify what eating disorders are. One myth about them is that having an eating disorder is a choice that a person makes. The reality is that eating disorders are serious mental health conditions that are the result of complex causes.

Another myth that is abroad about eating disorders is that you can tell if someone has an eating disorder just by looking at them. There is, supposedly, a ‘look’ that a person with an eating disorder has, but this is based on some truth and the power of popular media. The reality is that many people who are struggling with an eating disorder will fall within the average or typical weight range, or they may appear healthy. It isn’t always easy to tell.

The other myth that is out there is that only or mainly teenage girls are the ones who get eating disorders. However, the truth is that people of all walks of life, genders, ages, and cultural backgrounds are affected by eating disorders.

These myths can make it harder to recognize problems, and people may delay seeking appropriate treatment. If you have an eating disorder, but one or more of these myths affect your perception or the perception of the people around you, your struggles may get dismissed or minimized. That can lead to a worsening of the problem.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions that go beyond any social or class divide. To address them, they need to be recognized for what they are, and professional help sought. A counselor can nurture the physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual well-being of the individual affected by them.

The Different Types of Eating Disorders

There are several types of eating disorders that have been identified and categorized over the years. They each have particular defining features that differentiate them, and their symptoms will also look different.

  • Bulimia Nervosa: This eating disorder involves a person getting caught up in cycles of binge eating that are followed by compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, fasting, using laxatives, or doing excessive exercise to deal with the excess consumption and get rid of extra calories. A person who suffers from bulimia will often feel that they have a lack of control during their episodes of binging.
  • Typically, after binge-eating, the episode is accompanied by feelings of shame and guilt.
  • Anorexia Nervosa: Often simply referred to as anorexia, this eating disorder is characterized by a person adhering to an extreme restriction on their food intake. Likewise, they have an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image. Even if they have lost weight and are underweight or malnourished, they might continue to consider themselves overweight and carry on restricting what they eat.An individual with anorexia may also exhibit excessive exercise habits and be in denial of the severity of their condition.
  • Binge-Eating Disorder: This disorder is characterized by recurring episodes of eating large quantities of food, often rapidly and to the point of discomfort, without regular use of compensatory behaviors. This can lead to significant emotional distress and various health complications. Binge-eating may be triggered by stress or other emotional states such as sadness or feeling overwhelmed.One of the differences between binge-eating disorder and bulimia is that with binge-eating disorder, instead of taking the extreme measures one does with bulimia, one may use compensatory behaviors such as eating less food at mealtimes or dieting.
  • Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID): This eating disorder, which has been recently identified, is a feeding or eating disorder that is more common in children and young adolescents than older people. With ARFID, the individual significantly limits the quantity or variety of the food they consume. One impact of this is that it can cause malnutrition, significant weight loss, or psychosocial problems.
  • Other Specified Feeding and Eating Disorders (OSFED): This category of eating disorders includes patterns of disordered eating that do not meet the exact criteria of the above disorders, but are nonetheless serious enough to impact emotional, mental, and physical wellbeing.

Key Signs of Eating Disorders

Eating disorders don’t all look or operate in the same way. The symptoms of each will be different. Each individual will have symptoms that are present in particular ways. Look out for a preoccupation with one’s body image or with food and dieting. This may be excessive, taking over a person’s life and attention.

Eating disorders can be signaled by a dramatic and noticeable weight loss or gain. Similarly, be concerned with conspicuous changes in eating habits such as eating secretively or skipping meals. If a person withdraws socially, especially from activities that involve food, take note. Gastrointestinal issues, irregular heart rhythms, or dizziness are linked to eating too much or too little.

You can also be on the lookout for hypersensitivity to food textures or taste, an aversion toward eating, and a fear of trying new foods. Should you encounter these concerns, it’s important to speak with a health professional for appropriate assessments and diagnosis. Some of the behaviors and symptoms associated with eating disorders may be linked to hormonal imbalances or life stressors, and a professional can help you discern this.

Treatment and Recovery Options for Eating Disorders

If you have a loved one with an eating disorder, how can you best support them? Educating yourself about the disorder they struggle with can help you to reduce your misconceptions and possible frustrations with your loved one. Being a present, non-judgmental presence makes a difference, as does creating a safe environment for your loved one to wrestle with and address the issues.

You can also offer your loved one acceptance and unconditional love. This doesn’t mean being blind to the issues but rather loving them in spite of it all. Choose to show up for them. Support them by encouraging them to seek and continue treatment from a professional. You can also pray for your loved ones, for comfort and strength.

Eating disorders indicate that a person may have an unhealthy relationship with food and their body. With the right support and effective treatment, it’s possible to attain goals such as rebuilding self-esteem, getting to a healthy body weight, and nurturing a healthy body image. It’s possible to begin noticing circumstances or situations that function as triggers for the eating disorder.

For effective treatment, several approaches may be necessary to achieve healing. A counselor will help by tailoring an approach that suits their client’s needs and addresses the situation effectively. A multidisciplinary approach may be necessary to effectively address an eating disorder. Immediate medical care may be necessary to see to physical health concerns from the eating disorder, for instance.

Apart from medical attention, guidance from dietitians and nutritionists is required to develop healthy eating patterns. There are support groups that can provide a sense of community and accountability as one struggles. Therapy may be helpful in pinpointing and addressing any underlying spiritual, emotional, and mental concerns that may be worsening the eating disorder.

When you are ready, you should reach out to a health professional to begin addressing any concerns you may have about eating disorders. Our office is available to receive your call and make an appointment with one of the Christian therapists in our practice. Begin your healing journey today!

item.title: Help for Single Moms (Older Mom Edition)
item.description:
When people hear about the struggles of the single mom, most think of the young mother juggling her new responsibilities of parenthood with the naivety of youth and maybe even the financial hardships most people face in their young adult lives. But not many people think of or acknowledge the unique struggles that some older moms face.

Perhaps society thinks that women, moms in particular, have life all figured out when they reach a certain age. Maybe they think that they don’t need the practical help they once did because their children are likely older and more self-sufficient.

But the reality that many people don’t understand is the hardship that can come from being an older single mother. Though, as an older mom, you aren’t as likely to be hand-feeding your children or having to hold their hands just to cross the street, you are facing some real and challenging obstacles.

Those Teenage Years

While the “terrible twos” get a lot of press in popular culture, parents of teens might argue that they are a piece of cake compared to the drama of a teenager. Hormones rage, bringing on physical changes in your child’s body and hot tempers you never knew lurked behind those innocent eyes.

Even two-parent households can struggle when their children reach their teens. Children at that age want to push their limits, explore independence, and learn what their true identity is apart from their parents. While there is nothing intrinsically wrong with this normal behavior, the “growing pains” can affect the single mom more than she is likely to admit.

Seeing your child grow into maturity is a beautiful experience, but seeing the comforts, security, and hopes of their childhood fade away is an emotionally daunting experience for parents. When a woman is alone during this time, she might feel particularly isolated, as her once-faithful little companion has grown into their own personhood and is often spending their time with friends or at activities rather than snuggling with mom.

In addition to potential loneliness, the weight of being the sole decision-maker in the household can be excruciating. “What time is curfew?” “When should I let them start dating?” “How do I talk to them about sex?”

These and a million other questions swirl through the single mother’s brain constantly, and without a partner to discuss them with, it can be overwhelming. With sole power also comes sole responsibility. A single mom knows that if she makes the wrong decisions for her child, she will feel responsible for the outcome.

Practical Help

As we age, our bodies no longer function quite the same way as they did in our youth. Mobility issues may intrude on performing everyday activities such as keeping the house clean or mowing the lawn. Without a partner in the house, a single mom might feel the effects of aging a little more harshly than someone who has a partner to take up the slack.

Some people think that mothers who have older children don’t have to worry about getting help with chores. They assume that the children will help fill in the gap where a father should stand. While it’s true that older children can more effectively clean up after themselves, do chores, and don’t need as much supervision, the reality is that the household workload still weighs mainly on mom’s shoulders.

Having children who, theoretically, can help and getting that practical help are two entirely different issues. Some older children have rigorous schedules of their own. Some play sports, participate in school activities such as theater or music, and have to keep up with their schoolwork. So even if the child is willing to help mom with household chores, the reality is that they often get left undone.

Some mothers try to deliberately limit the help they request from their older children. Typical age-appropriate chores are healthy for a child, but when the older child becomes a substitute parent for younger siblings, the weight of responsibility can be too much, and frankly unfair.

Assuming a mother of older children has fewer responsibilities than a mom of littles is unfair and probably untrue. As children get older, their needs shift, but don’t disappear.

Those busy schedules we just talked about? Mom is often the chauffeur of those events, particularly for kids who don’t have their own driver’s licenses. And any parent of active teens knows that they, too, will have a busy schedule.

There are games to cheer at, performances to attend, and other events that require a mother’s attendance. Children’s busy lives equal busy lives for parents, especially those doing it solo.

Facing Reality Alone

Along with all the practical responsibilities of single parenting comes the reality of doing life alone. When the kids are in bed, and mom is left to her own thoughts, it can be overwhelming to think about the reality of navigating life alone. Not just in this season, but in the next. And the next.

Loneliness is one thing, but the harsh reality of facing an empty nest that is truly empty, void of a partner or children, can be saddening and overwhelming.

The idea of growing old is daunting, too. It’s overwhelming for most people, even those with a partner, but growing old alone is a whole other world. “Will I be alone forever?” “Who will take care of me in my old age?”

These types of questions will haunt a single mom in still hours and create stress. Dreams of “growing old” with a partner may seem out of reach, and the reality that it might never actually happen can cause not only grief for unrealized dreams but anxiety about the future.

Therapy

One of the most helpful tools in a single mom’s toolbox is therapy. Therapy can help the older single mom on so many different levels. A therapist can step in to be that adult listening ear that is lacking in many single moms’ lives.

While it won’t replace the intimacy of a lifelong partner, a therapist can fulfill a similar, yet different, vital role. Your therapist can get to know you deeply and well and can help you make the decisions for yourself, your future, and your children that are weighing on your mind.

Most importantly, a Christian counselor can point you back to your loving Heavenly Father who has promised to be a father to the fatherless (By the way, that includes your children.) He also promises to be close to the widow (that includes you, no matter the reason you’re single).

Going to therapy, particularly with a Christian therapist, can also help you work through any trauma that might have happened that caused you to become a single mom in the first place. For some, it might be the trauma following the death of a spouse, for others, it’s the result of a divorce. There are many reasons a woman might find herself single-parenting, and a Christian therapist can help sort through the trauma and obstacles that got her there.

No One Said It Would Be Easy

No one ever said that single parenting would be easy, but for some reason, society thinks older moms need less help. As a single “older” mom, it’s your duty to inform those who hold this point of view.

Graciously share your heart with others who want to help. Accept any assistance you can from those in your ‘village’, whether that comes in the form of transportation for your child or the gift of a home-cooked meal.

And remember, when the going gets tough, the tough fall to their knees and pray for the wisdom and guidance of God. When you feel overwhelmed and alone, know that even though there isn’t a ring on your finger, you’re not parenting solo. You have God and professional therapists on your side.

To schedule an appointment with a professional Christian therapist, contact our office today.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

References

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568
  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568
  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735

item.title: Getting Old: Loving Your Spouse Through Retirement
item.description:
When you hear about couples having marital trouble, you usually think of people in the prime years of their lives. Maybe they’re newly married and trying to adjust to living life as a couple, or perhaps they’ve hit their “seven-year itch” and are starting to drift apart. These times are often stressful for married couples, but marital trouble can hit at any stage and at any age.

Getting older and hitting retirement can be trying for married couples. If you’re married and you or your spouse is approaching retirement, it’s best to be emotionally prepared for the inevitable changes you will be facing.

So Much Togetherness!

You love each other, so spending more time together will be blissful, right? That’s the ideal, but in practical terms, that’s not always the case.

Even if your relationship is rock solid, too much togetherness can put a strain on it. Maybe you get along great now because your time together is limited, and therefore peaceful and purposeful. When you don’t have a lot of time together, which is often the case for couples who work full-time and have families, you are more intentional in the little time you do have.

Where did all this time come from?

When the busyness of work and family obligations fades, you have a lot more time to spend with your spouse. That’s a good thing, but it can also change the way you interact with each other. When your time is limited, you might be more purposeful in your conversations or intentional with your plans. You might schedule intimacy so it fits into both of your calendars, and you may not nitpick your partner’s behaviors because you don’t have time.

When time is no longer an issue, and you abandon your established schedule, things change. You might find that the same rules of conduct that have worked for years no longer shield you from arguments.

Maybe you allow yourself to discuss topics that were previously off-limits because you didn’t want to ruin your limited time together. Or you stop planning intimacy because you assume it will come naturally now that you don’t have a rigid schedule. But without this intentionally blocked-out time, that intimacy may never happen.

Have you always been like this?

When you’ve spent decades working toward the common goals of building a career or raising children, you develop a system, a rhythm of sorts, that works. But retirement can disrupt that. In this new stage, the small habits or preferences that went unnoticed are front and center, 24/7.

You might find yourself wondering if they’ve always chewed so loudly or why they decided that retirement is the perfect time to reorganize the spice rack that you’ve successfully managed for thirty years.

Maybe your spouse wants to sleep in, which never happened except on weekends because they were obligated to a work schedule. But if you’re an early riser, this sudden shift in your partner’s sleep pattern can be off-putting. While they might seem insignificant, these little discoveries can become full-blown resentment.

Who am I? Who are you?

Retirement requires an emotional adjustment. There’s the feeling of finality and the feeling of grief. You’re leaving a career and stepping away from a role. The transitional period from what was to what is and what is to come can be lonely and full of uncertainty and tension.

Even though you are still the same person you were when you were working, you’re no longer defined the same way. And maybe your spouse isn’t either. Having your identity change can affect you deeply. Maybe you no longer feel like the family provider or the nurturer. Maybe you no longer feel needed.

Having a personal identity crisis can magnify the stress of a new schedule and can put a strain on the people who are going through this transition with you.

But I’m still working!

Retirement doesn’t usually happen for both spouses at the same time. If one of you is still working while the other is enjoying a leisurely game of golf, resentment can grow quickly! The working spouse might feel envious of the other’s freedom. The retired spouse might feel guilty for their time off or become demanding of the working spouse’s limited free time.

Intentional Steps

To make your retirement a time of peace and relational growth, you can implement some practical strategies.

Plan “me” time It might sound counterintuitive, but the secret to a happy retirement with your spouse is often spending some time apart. Just because you’re both home for most of the day doesn’t obligate you to be joined at the hip. Some of the healthiest marriages are often the ones where couples maintain separate hobbies or socialize independently of each other.

God made you as an individual before He ever brought you together. Honoring your individuality and personal relationship with God can strengthen your marriage. Keep your book club and standing lunch date with a friend. These independent activities give you both the space you need to maintain your individuality and give you something new to talk about when you do spend time together.

Negotiate domestic duties For years, your household roles were likely dictated by your individual work schedules. Now that these outside obligations are gone, the division of household labor needs to be adjusted. If one spouse stayed home while the other worked, it doesn’t automatically obligate them to continue in that role now that you’re both home.

It’s also important not to treat your spouse like an employee when you do work together on household chores. If you’re used to being the boss, it can be easy to bark out orders and try to manage a spouse. Keep in mind, you’re not managing a department anymore, but being a loving partner.

Create something new Since your old routine is no longer in place, it’s important to create some structure in your life. Without a calendar and routine, days can blend, and a feeling of aimlessness can take root.

To prevent this from happening, create a consistent morning routine that involves prayer or going for a walk with your partner. And to keep the love alive, schedule intentional date nights that don’t include anything from a to-do list.

It’s also wise to find new ways to serve others together. Many couples struggle with finding a purpose after retirement since their primary purpose has always been to take care of a family. Try mentoring a young couple at church or volunteering for a ministry project to help give you a joint purpose.

Talk about difficult topics While it might feel like retirement is a long vacation, it’s more of a major identity shift. Many people feel a sense of loss when they leave their career or their children leave their house, two major events that often happen within a short period of time.

These life shifts can cause an emotional upheaval, and it’s important to understand how these things have impacted each other. Talk with your partner and ask them how they’re handling the transition to retirement. Be quick to listen, and slow to speak. You can also use this season to talk about goals such as traveling or moving closer to grandchildren.

Finances are another sometimes touchy subject. You might want to live it up while your spouse is paralyzed by the fear of running out of money. This spender versus saver conflict can manifest as nitpicking over the grocery bill or the thermostat. To mitigate this, talk with your spouse about your finances in an open and transparent way.

While practicing these ideas with your spouse is a wonderful way to grow closer, it can also be difficult. It’s helpful to discuss them with a licensed, professional therapist, too. A therapist can help you and your spouse grow closer through couples counseling or can help you individually as you manage life’s transitions.

If you’re getting older or are planning for your future retirement, call our office to make an appointment today to help make the most of your golden years.

item.title: When to Seek Help for Family Problems
item.description:
Family problems can be a weight pulling you down. It can feel like taking two steps forward and three steps backward. Trying to get everyone on the same page seems fruitless at times. Whether you have babies, toddlers, grade school children, teens, or everyone in between, you want a home full of love, forgiveness, and peace. Why can’t everyone get along?

This is a fallen world, and the enemy knows where to hit the hardest to make a lasting impact: the family. Seeking help for family problems can help you get ahead and prepare you for future issues by equipping you with psychological methods and techniques, as well as faith-based principles.

Common Family Problems

Families have squabbles. Life happens, and sometimes lines are drawn in the household, but it doesn’t have to stay that way. Family problems are inevitable as personalities clash, hormones can take over, and circumstances can change on a dime. The wisdom is to get ahead of it by building a rock-solid foundation with shared beliefs and values, and open communication.

Before reading through the list of common family problems below, consider whether your family has Jesus as the cornerstone. Do you need to speak His name in normal daily conversation? Do you make decisions through a biblical lens, or do you make rash decisions that affect the entire family?

Search your heart for the answers. If you need Jesus to work on your heart and mind, ask for His forgiveness, repent, and lean on God to guide your family as the Head of the Household.

Marital Issues

Marital issues affect everyone in the family, although parents may feel that the problems lie with just the two of them. Children and teens are perceptive, and their moods and behaviors can change in response to growing fears or worries about stability. Marital issues can include emotional distance, betrayal, infidelity, financial concerns, chronic illness, procrastination, unequal household duties, and sexual intimacy problems, among others.

Marriage and family counseling are available for couples who need extra help in navigating life together. If you feel like you are alone in your marriage or that the two of you have become roommates instead of partners, seek help from a counselor.

Communications Within the Family

A communication breakdown can lead to feelings of resentment, anger, bitterness, shame, and regret. One person may push others, trying to get to the bottom of a conflict and trying to bully others to get their own way. Other family members may withdraw, becoming quiet and distant. Miscommunication leads to sibling rivalry and fights, parent-child disputes, and relationship drama between parents.

Family counseling teaches family members how to resolve conflict without insults and blaming. They learn how to manage anger and actively listen to each other. Counseling can also help spark confidence as each family member learns how to advocate for themselves.

Parenting Issues

Parenting issues include disagreements regarding discipline, sibling rivalry and fusses, and children who feel rejected, ignored, or isolated. One parent may feel that the other one contradicts them in front of the children or undermines them. Overwhelmed and stressed parents may feel like they are out of patience as they struggle to find five minutes just to think.

Problems can emerge between the two parents, divorced parents trying to co-parent, stepparents, and between parent and child. Counseling can help if every conversation feels like a struggle, or if you are only talking about surface-level topics with your teens or tweens.

Step-Parenting Adjustments

Blended families tend to have their own issues. An adjustment period is required when a parent remarries, and a new person begins living in the household. The new step-parent may have different rules or a different discipline philosophy. Parents and step-parents need to agree on how to raise the children they share.

Blended families may also include new step-siblings that change the dynamic. Children can feel neglected or ignored when other children are around. Personality clashes can also cause drama and angst in the home. Counseling equips children and parents with skills and techniques to defuse tough situations and express thoughts and emotions without resorting to insults or physical altercations.

Major Life Changes

Major life changes can turn your world upside down, sometimes for good and sometimes not. Life events can include a graduation, wedding, big move, new job, career change, pregnancy, birth of a new baby or adoption, or financial improvement. It can also include illness, death, loss of home or job, natural disaster, bankruptcy, divorce, and estrangement.

Emotional resilience builds as we face obstacles in this fallen world, but at times we may be unable to manage overwhelming blessings on our own. Counseling can help you prioritize your beliefs and values during major shifts.

Addiction

Addiction comes in many forms. You or someone in your home may struggle with addiction to alcohol, illegal drugs, prescription drugs, substances like glue or paint, pornography, sex, food, excessive shopping, or gambling. Anything that you use to fulfill a deeper need can become an addiction.

God created humans to desire Him, but because we have free will, we can reject His love or become confused. We feel an emptiness or numbness, and when we give in to an urge or impulse, we experience a temporary relief, a cascade of feel-good chemicals.

Unfortunately, unless we fill that empty hole with God, we will continue to indulge in addictions that can destroy relationships, jobs, homes, and physical and mental health. Christian counseling helps break the cycle and lean into the very One who created the heart.

Mental Health Disorders

Mental health disorders affect more than just the person experiencing them. Whether you or a family member struggles with any of the following mental health disorders, help is available.

  • Anxiety
  • Depression
  • Bipolar disorder
  • Eating disorders
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder
  • Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
  • Grief
  • Cognitive disorders
  • Behavioral disorders
  • Abuse and trauma

Christian counseling centers treat families for more than just squabbles. They dive deep into mental health issues and help the family heal as a whole, while addressing their emotional and spiritual health as well.

Poor mental health affects the physical body with unexplained body aches, headaches, digestive issues, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, rapid heart rate, chronic inflammation, and increased risks of heart disease, obesity, Type II diabetes, heart attack, or stroke. Treating mental health disorders while teaching the family how to manage symptoms and work with their family member creates unity and better health.

Why Now is the Time to Seek Christian Counseling

Family problems can rob your home of peace. Now is the time to seek Christian counseling. Even if your family is not experiencing major conflict, counseling can prepare you for the inevitable. When multiple people live at home, personality clashes can arise. Teach your family how to resolve conflict and manage anger before it becomes an issue.

Sometimes families wait to seek professional help due to fear or shame. There was a time when seeking help from a counselor was ridiculed, but psychology and culture have come a long way. More people understand that it’s okay to seek help for family problems, instead of hiding them. When we try to keep problems in the dark, they seem to grow, and in families, this can create emotional distance and estrangement.

If you live in a home with abuse, self-harm, or if someone is having suicidal ideation, seek help immediately. Don’t wait. A home should be a safe haven, and we want to help you in the hard seasons.

Counseling for Family Problems

If you are leaning toward counseling for family problems, you are not alone. Our families are precious to us and deserve the best version of ourselves and to learn about how they can follow Christ while also loving one another. Contact this Christian counseling center today to schedule a session. The counselors want to help you through tough seasons with the grace and mercy of Christ.
