item.title: What is Grief? What to Expect in Each of the Stages of Grief and Loss
item.description:
We all have many different life experiences that make us unique. However, if we live long enough, grief is a shared experience many of us carry. Grief can be described as a response to loss. This usually involves the death of someone, but it can also include other losses such as divorce, loss of a home or job, or loss of health or independence.

Grief is normal and healthy

Grief is a normal and healthy response to loss. We might have grown up with the idea that grieving is abnormal and unhealthy (real men don’t cry), but this just isn’t true. God designed us to love and care deeply, and the response to losing those we love is grief.

Not only is it normal, but it’s also healthy. When we refuse to grieve, we actually cause ourselves harm. It’s like a balloon. We can only stuff so much air into a balloon before it pops. We are like that with our emotions. We can only “stuff” our feelings so much before we pop, too.

We might explode in anger, experience depression, or even experience physical symptoms such as stomach problems or headaches. Also, unresolved grief can build upon itself when we experience the next grief. When we choose to sweep things under the rug, we are just causing ourselves more work and agony the next time we experience loss.

When we grieve, we not only grieve the loss of the person, but we mourn the loss of the roles, dreams, nuances, and routines that went along with our relationship with them. These are called secondary losses. Roles include parts the loved one played that will possibly need to be passed on to others. Some examples of this are the “fun one”, tech guy, party planner, banker, cook, etc.

We experience a loss of dreams and expectations, such as the deceased person not being able to be there when grandchildren are born. More subtle things include the way a person smells, physical touch such as sleeping in the same bed, etc. There are also many changes in routine when we lose someone. This might include having Thanksgiving at someone else’s house or changing from a couple’s Sunday school class to a women’s or men’s class.

Everyone grieves differently. This is based on many factors such as personality, type of death, our relationship with them, support systems, etc. For instance, an individual would normally grieve the peaceful passing of their ninety-year-old grandmother differently than their child suddenly being killed in a car accident.

The type of death and circumstances surrounding it often have a major impact. Sometimes a good relationship with the deceased makes their death harder, but a rocky, estranged relationship can also make grieving difficult.

The Five Stages Grieving Model

One common grief model puts typical grieving into five stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. Let’s look at what we might expect from each stage.

Denial

Denial usually happens when we first learn about the loss. It can include shock, numbness, confusion, and fear. Our bodies and minds cannot process the news we have just received, and it is hard to believe what has happened. It can be a protective coping mechanism that helps us get through those first few weeks. It helps us be able to plan funerals and make lots of hard decisions.

Often people will wake up from sleep and wonder if the loss really happened or if it was just a dream. It might cause us to walk into that person’s house and briefly look for them or call them, forgetting that they aren’t there to answer. Sometimes people are concerned that they don’t have much emotion in the beginning. All of these are common in the first stage.

Anger

Anger is common in the grieving process and can be directed at many different people. We might be angry with ourselves for not doing something differently or spending enough time with them. We might be angry with a doctor or the driver who caused a car accident. We might be angry with God for allowing this terrible thing to happen. We might even be angry with the deceased for not taking better care of themself or for how they treated us.

Sometimes we’re angry because we had such a good relationship with them, and sometimes we’re angry because it was a traumatic or difficult relationship. Anger is often described as a secondary emotion, meaning we’re never “just angry.” We experience anger because of some other emotion such as pain, embarrassment, or guilt. We experience many varied emotions when we grieve, and they often come out as anger.

Bargaining

This takes place when we have “if only” thinking. “If only we didn’t go on vacation.” “If only we had seen the doctor sooner.” We use magical thinking to try to undo something that happened. We often experience guilt in this phase. We blame ourselves for the death, thinking somehow we could have prevented it.

We wish we had spent more time or said certain things. We spend lots of time longing for the person to come back and grasp at anything to try to undo what has happened. We know logically this is futile, but it is a natural part of grief.

Depression

This can take many forms. Of course we feel sad, but it usually goes deeper than that. We might experience physical symptoms such as headaches, pain, or stomach problems. We might not be able to sleep or sleep too much. We might not enjoy doing things that used to bring us joy. Difficulty concentrating and making decisions is also difficult during this phase. We can feel like we’re in a fog, or our brain just won’t work right.

Isolation from others is often common. Part of us knows we should and need to get out and be around friends, but we just don’t want to. Sometimes it’s because we feel sad, and sometimes it’s how we perceive others at this time. We might be angry that people didn’t reach out to us in the way or as frequently as we wanted. Sometimes we are aggravated that people won’t leave us alone.

People often don’t know how to act around the grieving person or what to say to them. They often say foolish and unintentionally hurtful things. “They’re in a better place.” “You should be thankful your dad lived that long.” Others are uncomfortable and feel the need to fill the silence with ill-thought-out words.

This hurts and frustrates us and makes us feel like others just don’t understand. Sometimes they avoid the grieving person or avoid the elephant in the room because they don’t know what to say or do. All of these can cause isolation and hurt. It’s also easy to have irrational thinking and be oversensitive during this time.

Acceptance

Acceptance is the final stage of grief. It is the opposite of bargaining or longing for what was lost. We finally accept the reality that our loved one is no longer here. While we never truly get over the loss, we learn to live with it. It becomes our new normal and is a sense of finality.

Often, those who have moved on to the acceptance phase of grief desire to give back to others. It helps them make sense of the loss by turning it into something good. This can include giving money in the person’s name for a cause, leading a grief group, or bringing a meal to a person who has just experienced loss.

Often people want to know how long the grieving process lasts. Unfortunately, there is no time limit or date on the calendar when it will be over. Some experts say grief lasts about two years, but that can depend on a lot of factors. The first year will be hard because we have to experience all the “firsts”: first Christmas, first birthday, and the anniversary of their death. These are often hard days for several years.

Next Steps

Grieving is one of the hardest events we can experience in life. There isn’t a pill to take or a procedure to hurry it up. We have to give ourselves time and permission to grieve. Grief takes time, but it also takes work.

If you feel you are struggling with your grief, don’t go it alone. Talk to a counselor or grief group to walk with you through this difficult time. They can give you a safe place to express your thoughts, memories, and emotions and help you work through this painful process.

Photo:
“Sunflowers”, Courtesy of Lachlan Gowen, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post What is Grief? What to Expect in Each of the Stages of Grief and Loss appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: The Roles of Mind, Self, and Brain in Healing Depression: Learning to Stay Out of the River of Our Negative Cognitions
item.description:
Depression occurs when stressful life events influence the brain. These events create more negative thoughts and feelings and more distortion in the way the brain processes information. To understand this process is it is important to realize that the human brain consists of three distinct components which have a role in the management of depression.

Three Components of Depression Management

The first component, which we will identify, is the mind, located in the anterior cingulate gyrus. The mind is the stream or river of consciousness through which flow thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. It is not the source of the content of the river; it is a conduit for processing the content.

The second component is the Self, located in the prefrontal cortex, on the bank of the mind or river of consciousness. This component is our sense of “I”, the internal executor of the brain, and in a real sense, this is where our soul resides, called our “heart” in the Scriptures.

The Self could observe the thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations which flow through the mind and process them. The Self observes the contents of the river, but they are not the same as the mind.

Just because a thought enters the river, it doesn’t mean you have to believe it – the Self determines the validity of the contents of the river. The limbic system of the brain is the source of the contents of the river – thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. Remember, the brain is not the same component as the mind.

How the Brain Processes Information

The brain produces the stream of thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations by processing information from:

  • The real world
  • Your body and senses, including your gut
  • By recalling past packages of thoughts, feelings, beliefs, and motor/action plans or schemas that make sense of our experiences

For example, you see a plant while on a hike, and you’ve never seen one like it before. It might be a green leafy plant, but you’ve never seen this kind before. What is it? The automatic systems in your brain take over and process this real-world information with the anxiety you are feeling in your body and gut, as you are concerned this might actually be poison ivy, because you have heard there might be some around.

The brain then starts recalling things from your past. This plant has three leaves like the one you touched when you were a kid, so it sends anxiety and danger signals down the river. But these automatic functions only control 80% of your brain. The other 5-20 % come from the Self. So, you have some executor options. You can become overwhelmed by what the brain is sending, believe it, and jump in the river, or you can analyze and appraise.

You can say things like, yes, there might be poison ivy plants around, but they do not have leaves like the one I saw as a kid. Yes, poison ivy can cause problems, but didn’t that plant hurt me when I was a kid because I plucked it up? Have any of my friends had a problem with poison ivy on this trail?

The Brain and the Self

The brain is an organ, just like the gut or the heart. Sometimes it cooperates fully with the rest of the body, and sometimes it doesn’t. If you allow negative things into your brain, i.e., pornography, violent video games or movies, abuse, it will react negatively. You are not your brain, but you can change your brain.

Negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations sent into the river by the brain are observed by the Self, which is safely located on the bank in the real world, where it can reappraise after stepping back and seeing the situation clearly.

The problem develops when the Self becomes entangled in the river by ruminating on the thoughts and feelings it encounters there. You (Self) become the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations. This rumination results in a new reality. The Self, who is stuck in the river, creates a new thought: “My brain is telling me this, so it must be true!”

The result of this new reality is an overwhelming sense of sadness, lack of motivation, and loss of interest in things we formerly enjoyed. The Self is stuck in negative thoughts. One of the consequences of the Self being stuck in the river is that the prefrontal cortex is turned off and is not working as designed. The solution to the problem lies in learning to redirect attention to the real world through mindfulness techniques and cognitive restructuring.

Mindfulness

Mindfulness is keeping our thoughts in the present, where it is safe, and not in the past, which is dominated by “If onlys”, or the future, which is dominated by “What ifs.” Cognitive restructuring is challenging the validity and logic of the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, using the logical prefrontal cortex where the Self resides.

The safest place to direct attention is to the real world, not the river. If we fall into the river, we drown in depression. So, the question you need to ask yourself is, “Is there anything happening right here, right now in this room with which you cannot deal or handle?”

Healing depression focuses on climbing out of the river by remembering the scriptural admonition to claim the promise of Philippians 4:7, and receive the peace of God, which the Apostle Paul states, “…Surpasses all understanding, and will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Phil. 4:7 ESV).

If we can learn not to live in the past or worry about the future, but instead to learn from the past and apply the lessons learned, we can face the future assured of the strength of the Lord to guide us. And in the process, we allow the Self to resume the executor role of the brain as God designed it, and we stay grounded in the present in the real world.

Research has shown that the Brain has the capacity to stay in the present for 4-7 seconds before it starts to wander to the past or future. Consequently, we need to empower the Self, steal that attention away from the brain, and mindfully bring it back to the present.

We accomplish this with in-the-moment coping skills, such as diaphragmatic breathing, mindfulness techniques that activate prefrontal cortex activity, and challenging the validity and logic of negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations.

Challenging Negative Thoughts

We can systematically challenge each negative thought, each negative feeling, each troubling image, and each sensation by identifying what percentage they are true. At first, we might think they are 90-100% true, and that’s what keeps us in the river. But the Self, which is watching from the riverbank, can see that the reality is that the percentage is much, much lower. A common example is “I can never do anything right!” and it is believed 100%.

But hearing the Self challenge the statement with the logic that no one is always wrong, and everyone does some things right, lowers the percentage substantially and starts on the path to healing. Allowing the Self to put the negatives on trial, and asking, “What is the evidence that I should believe this?”, is another effective way to climb out of the river.

In conclusion, don’t forget that living in the “If onlys” of the past and the “What ifs” of the future will cause the brain to convince us that there is no hope. When we get the Self and the prefrontal cortex involved in the challenging process, we can claim the promise that healing and peace are only a prayer away!

So, if you feel you are drowning in the river of your negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, please know there is hope through a therapist who understands the healing process. Please check our website and make an appointment today. Peace awaits.

Reference:
Gary A. Sibcy II, P. (2021). Clinical Depression: Evidence-based Counseling Treatment and Strategies. CounselTalk Webinar. Lynchburg, VA: Liberty University.

Photo:
“River”, Courtesy of Mark McGregor, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post The Roles of Mind, Self, and Brain in Healing Depression: Learning to Stay Out of the River of Our Negative Cognitions appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: What is Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?
item.description:
We have all seen it before – a social media friend posts a picture of their perfectly color-coded closet. Their pantry is organized into matching containers. Every towel is folded exactly the same way. The caption reads: “#OCD.”

Or maybe you’ve seen someone look at a crooked picture frame or a stack of papers that isn’t perfectly straight and joke, “My OCD is going so crazy right now.” Most of us have laughed, nodded, or kept scrolling without thinking much about it.

But what if OCD is actually something completely different? What if the person silently battling Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder has a messy closet, an overflowing laundry basket, and a mind that never gives them a moment of peace?

The truth is that OCD has little to do with being neat, organized, or particular. It is a disorder driven by fear. It is a disorder built on uncertainty. And for those living with it, it can feel like you are battling a monster on steroids every single day.

Why OCD Thoughts Cause So Much Distress

One of the most difficult parts of OCD is that people often mistake intrusive thoughts for who they are.

An intrusive thought is exactly what it sounds like: an unwanted thought, image, or urge that repeatedly barges into your mind without your permission. These thoughts are distressing because they are the exact thoughts you do not want to have. If you could snap your fingers and make them disappear forever, you would.

Ironically, the harder you try to force them away, argue with them, or prove they are not true, the longer they tend to stick around. This is one of the reasons OCD is so exhausting. These types of thoughts are often referred to as “sticky thoughts” (also referred to as obsessions).

Everyone experiences random intrusive thoughts from time to time. A person who isn’t battling OCD may briefly notice the thought and move on with their day. Their brain simply lets it pass.

But someone dealing with OCD tends to get stuck. The thought lingers, replaying over and over. It may stay for hours or even days, demanding attention and creating tremendous anxiety. The brain becomes convinced that the thought must mean something important simply because it won’t leave.

People might think:

“What if I secretly want this?”
“What if this thought means something about me?”
“What if God is trying to tell me something?”
“What if everyone else is safe except me?”

However, the opposite is usually true. OCD likes to attack what matters most to us. A loving mother may develop terrifying thoughts about accidentally harming her child. A devoted Christian might become consumed with fears that they have committed an unforgivable sin or will in the future.

A compassionate person may become terrified that they could harm someone else, or even themselves, despite desperately not wanting to. Someone who deeply values honesty becomes trapped wondering if they lied without realizing it.

Deep down, people battling with OCD might even recognize that these thoughts are attacking the values they hold most dear. If a thought fills you with fear because it goes completely against who you are and what you believe, that is often evidence that it is not something you actually want to do. OCD doesn’t reveal your character. Instead, it attacks your values.

Could I be dealing with OCD?

If you’ve been reading this article and wondering whether this could apply to you, here are some common symptoms of OCD.

OCD may be the culprit if you:

  • Experience recurring intrusive thoughts, images, or urges that feel unwanted and distressing.
  • Spend a significant amount of time trying to figure out what your thoughts mean.
  • Constantly seek reassurance from others that everything is okay.
  • Feel driven to check, repeat, confess, avoid, or perform mental rituals to reduce anxiety.
  • Feel temporary relief after completing a compulsion, only to have the fear return later.
  • Find yourself avoiding people, places, objects, or situations that trigger intrusive thoughts.
  • Spend an hour or more each day consumed by obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors.
  • Notice that the anxiety is interfering with your work, relationships, parenting, school, or ability to enjoy life.

It is important to remember that everyone experiences intrusive thoughts from time to time. Having an intrusive thought does not necessarily mean you are dealing with OCD. The difference is how your brain responds to the thought. For someone who isn’t fighting OCD, the thought usually comes and goes without much attention.

For someone who is facing OCD, the thought can become “sticky.” The brain treats it like an emergency that must be solved immediately. This is where compulsions may develop. But, the more you try to make the thought go away, the stronger it often becomes. This only makes the cycles stronger.

If this cycle sounds familiar, know that you are not alone. OCD affects millions of people, and many go years before receiving an accurate diagnosis because they don’t realize what they’re experiencing has a name.

There is hope

If you recognized yourself in this article, know that OCD is highly treatable. You do not have to stay trapped in the exhausting cycle of obsessions (sticky thoughts) and/or compulsions (behaviors you adopt to relieve the anxiety you feel).

Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a specialized form of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), is the gold-standard treatment for OCD. Rather than trying to eliminate intrusive thoughts, ERP helps you change your response to them so they gradually lose their power.

Recovery doesn’t mean you’ll never have another intrusive thought. It means those thoughts no longer control your life.

If you’re struggling with OCD or intrusive thoughts, I’d love to help. Reach out today to schedule an appointment and learn how evidence-based treatment can help you break free from OCD and regain peace.

Photo:
“OCD”, Courtesy of Annie Spratt, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post What is Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD)? appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: Confronting and Letting Go of Toxic Shame
item.description:
Some of us grew up in families where we felt invisible and unimportant, regardless of what we tried to do to get attention and affection. Some of us had terrible experiences with people who should have loved and protected us, but instead hurt us and exploited us. Some of us were bullied, rejected, and ridiculed for things that we couldn’t help, by peers or by people old enough to know better. The painful memories from these experiences stayed with us in the form of toxic shame.

Toxic shame hides in our hearts. It tells us that we’re not good enough, that there is something wrong with us, that we’ll never amount to anything more than what we are now. It may even tell us that we are fundamentally unlovable.

These are sentences that we don’t necessarily hear. They are ideas and beliefs that we probably don’t repeat out loud, but they still affect our self-image. These are the beliefs that lie at our foundation, brought into being by the shame surrounding our most painful experiences.

At some point, though, we will encounter the opposite of what we’re used to. We will meet someone who wants to accept us, to cherish us, to love us, and to enjoy our company. When this happens, we will have no choice but to confront the toxic shame that shields us from accepting this love, and to heal it from the inside out. There is a long life ahead of us, filled with wonderful opportunities, but to advance, we must heal the hurt that lies beneath toxic shame.

We Accept the Love We Think We Deserve

Everyone has a baseline of the kind of treatment they think they deserve, and this is called our norm. It is our past experiences, both painful and positive, that determine our norms. When we get less than what we are used to, or when we are treated below our level of norm, our default emotion is anger. Imagine receiving your monthly paycheck, and it is significantly less than you are used to receiving each month. You will feel disbelief, you will want an explanation, and you will be outraged at the injustice of getting less than what you are used to.

When we get more than our norm, and when we have toxic shame, our response is guilt.

If someone else looked at their monthly paycheck and noticed significantly more money there than they are used to, they might also respond with disbelief. When they followed up about it and discovered that the amount was not a mistake, they would be delighted and grateful.

The person with toxic shame in this same scenario, however, would feel guilty and unworthy. They would reflect on their failures and human moments, and they would think of these moments as the reasons why they are disqualified from getting a pay raise.

Everyone evaluates their self-worth based on the way they were treated in their earliest memories, to the way they were treated through their childhood and teen years. The way others treated them dictates their value and sets the baseline norm of how they expect to be treated.

If they were neglected, abused, mistreated, or bullied, they will carry toxic shame as if they were to blame for those experiences. Their baseline norm for receiving love is low, and they feel guilty or ashamed each time they receive more love or when they are treated kinder than they are used to. This is what the phrase “We accept the love we think we deserve” truly means.

People who carry toxic shame purposely make it difficult for others to love them. In the Bible, we are told that Adam and Eve had a close friendship with their Creator, and the author even tells us that they were naked and had no shame. As soon as they do what they were told not to do, they become aware of their nakedness, they cover themselves, and they withdraw from God, hiding from Him as He comes to look for them. (Genesis 3)

Adam and Eve covering up, withdrawing, and hiding is a perfect picture of what toxic shame does to us. We put up emotional barriers and create distance from those looking to connect with us because we feel unworthy, exposed, or broken beyond repair.

Letting Go of Toxic Shame

Many of us spend our lives oblivious to our emotions and the thoughts behind them. Similar to the physical foundations of a building, we all have unseen thoughts and beliefs that form the foundation of our identity; it is the essence of how we feel about ourselves. A teacher might have scolded us in front of the class, telling us that we’re hopeless because we never listen to instructions. That simple sentence might go on to form the foundation of our identity, magnifying one of our struggles to the point that it becomes a defining feature.

Some of us were never told anything in our young lives, positive or negative. We were left alone for vast stretches of time, our achievements unnoticed, our needs unmet, and our painful emotions ignored. Neglected children grow up believing that they are unlovable and unworthy of praise, based on the affection that they never received.

This is toxic shame because it causes someone to feel guilty even when they were a victim. The same goes for children who were mistreated and abused. They carry toxic shame as if they caused bad things to happen to them.

It’s not simple, but it is possible to heal and release toxic shame. We are spiritual beings in a physical body, with minds and emotions. We must learn to reach and speak to every part of ourselves, leaving no broken area unaddressed. There are physical exercises that heal our nervous system, and there are affirmations to speak to our damaged mind and emotions. God has spoken loving truths to our spirits, and we must hear them and accept them to be healed within.

The further we go into dealing with our past and toxic shame, the more we will realize that some things are impossible to do alone. Many of us were hurt by others, and those same hurts can only be healed by others, as uncomfortable and scary as that idea might be.

One of the central parts of healing toxic shame lies in learning to become vulnerable with others, in the way God wanted Adam and Eve to be vulnerable with Him. Not everyone can be trusted, but we must find the ones who can. Healing will only come when we allow others to see our shame and love us anyway.

You might look at yourself in the mirror now and struggle to comprehend how anyone could love you. You have never needed to earn love, and you have never needed to make yourself lovable. Toxic shame has had you believing all kinds of things about yourself that have never been true.

It can be scary and deeply uncomfortable to confront your past and to let go of the beliefs you have been clinging to. It is only when you can let go of the handfuls of shame that you have been holding that you can have a free hand to receive and accept the love that you have always been deserving of and that the people around you have been desperate for you to receive.

Perhaps you don’t have someone that you can trust with details of your past. When you speak with a counselor, you are in a safe place, with someone who will keep your confidence. You can meet with as many counselors as it takes for you to feel safe and comfortable enough to open up to the right person. To get started, please consult our online catalog of counselors or speak with our reception team. We trust that you will find someone and begin the healing process soon.

The post Confronting and Letting Go of Toxic Shame appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: How to Define OCD: Three Areas That Are Helped By Counseling
item.description:
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders defines obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) as:

“…the presence of obsessions and /or compulsions. Obsessions are recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, whereas compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that an individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly” – American Psychiatric Association, 2022

Although concise, this definition can be made more understandable by breaking down different elements of this disorder. The two main components of this disorder are obsessions and compulsions.

Obsessions/Intrusive Thoughts

Obsessions are consistent thoughts, impulsive feelings or mental pictures that take place repeatedly in one’s mind. They take place without the person causing them and without the person wanting them to be there; this is where the term intrusive comes from. The thought, image, or urge intrudes on a person.

There are all sorts of obsessions that one might have, and they are as varied as people are. One person might experience an obsession as an intrusive thought that they have committed a sin, but that is only the beginning for someone with OCD. The thought of possibly committing a sin won’t leave their mind, and they find themself thinking about it over and over again, even when they don’t want to. This category would be called religious OCD or scrupulosity.

Another example of an obsession might be someone who feels an intrusive impulse (urge) to harm someone in some way and they are horrified by the realization. They continue to experience it over and over again, feeling more horror and more shame with each experience of it. This category is called harm OCD.

Yet another example might be someone who has intrusive mental images of sexual acts. This person does not want these images and is disgusted and horrified by them but cannot seem to get them out of their head. This would fall under the category of sexual OCD.

Because clinicians have noticed patterns among those who are diagnosed with OCD, obsessions have been grouped into particular categories, such as the ones used in the examples above. Other categories include but are not limited to hoarding/saving, symmetry/order, contamination, somatic (having to do with the body), and relationships.

Compulsions

It is often the case that both obsessions and compulsions are present in an individual who is diagnosed with OCD; however, only one of these needs to be present to meet the criteria for an OCD diagnosis.

The other component to a diagnosis of OCD is compulsions. Compulsions are physical or mental actions repeated over and over. These actions are characterized by an urge to complete them or by a particular and precise way of completing them. Compulsions are sometimes called “safety behaviors.” They are called this because one forms a belief that if they complete the behavior, they will be or feel safe.

For example, think of someone who has a contamination obsession. This person might obsess about the spread of germs. Their compulsion might be to clean everything that might have come in contact with germs. The compulsion might make them feel “safe” from germs, but only temporarily.

The trouble is that as the person uses the compulsion (cleaning) to temporarily feel safe, they are inadvertently training their mind that cleaning must happen to relieve the fear of germs spreading. The more one completes the compulsion, the stronger their belief that the compulsion will keep them safe from spreading germs.

You may see where this is going. The compulsions require more and more from the sufferer because it is not possible to be safe from all germs, and somewhere in their mind, they are aware of that. This awareness drives them to continue to try to fix the problem of germs being a danger. The solution to this is not to be or feel entirely safe from the effects of germs, as this is impossible. However, the OCD sufferer believes that this is the solution.

The Goal of OCD Treatment

In reality, the solution to symptoms of OCD is to build up the capacity to tolerate the discomfort and fear that comes with the thought of germs. The more this tolerance is built up, the less the compulsion will feel needed.

The same is true for any category of OCD: the OCD sufferer has convinced himself that the compulsion brings safety, but the reality is that it does not bring safety but demands continued engagement in the compulsions and mounting fear that drives the obsession. There are specific fears behind every obsession, and the goal for treatment of OCD is to build up a tolerance and a capacity to live with those fears.

Ways That Counseling Can Help

Sharing Obsessions and Intrusive Thoughts

Many people with OCD find the intrusive thoughts, obsessions, and compulsions they experience as frightening or shameful. This often leads to suffering in silence and fear, without knowing these are symptoms of OCD and without knowing that there are people who can offer help and support.

In particular, those who suffer from harm and sexual OCD symptoms often believe that they are bad people for having these unwanted and intrusive thoughts or compulsions. The word intrusive means that the thought is unwanted, uninvited, and unexpected. As you may be able to imagine, having sexual images suddenly come into your mind or unexpectedly thinking about harming another person would be quite disturbing!

This is common in those who suffer from OCD. The truth is that all people experience thoughts that are unwanted. Those who do not have OCD move past these thoughts without forming any judgments about themselves or the thoughts. Those with OCD have thoughts about these thoughts, which often lead to compulsions to get rid of these disturbances.

Meeting with a counselor and sharing these thoughts, obsessions, or compulsions with them can offer great relief from shame. Counseling can offer a place where someone can share these things that disturb them, and they will not be met with judgment but with compassion and help.

This is an important step for those who suffer from OCD. Being able to share this part of their life with another person who does not believe that they are “bad” for any of these things can bring a profound sense of relief and a starting point for continued treatment of OCD.

Tolerating Discomfort and Fear with Support

Once a person has been able to share these disturbing obsessions and compulsions with a caring counselor who does not respond with judgment, support and treatment can be discussed. The most common and efficacious treatment for OCD is called Exposure Response Prevention (ERP).

The first step is exposing the person to the fear behind the obsession. There are many ways to do this. Some people can use real-world exposures, and some can use imagining different scenarios as an exposure. This is done in the presence of a counselor, and the individual will share their emotional experience with the counselor.

It is important to note that the process of exposure causes great anxiety and fear to emerge in the individual. The purpose of this is to reform the brain processes to allow the person to not engage in a compulsion when they normally would and to teach themself that they do have the ability to tolerate the fear and discomfort they are attempting to avoid.

Response prevention involves the individual refraining from engaging in the compulsion or safety behavior, whatever that might look like. The point of refraining from the safety behavior is to train the brain and body to tolerate the discomfort of the fear or anxiety experienced when not engaging in the compulsion.

Eventually, the intensity of discomfort will subside, and the exposure will be over. This can be an overwhelming and scary experience, and this is why it is important to do it with a trained and caring counselor. The goal is for the individual to grow skilled at doing this so that they can practice it outside of their treatment with a counselor and eventually be able to do it on their own.

Identifying Unhelpful Thinking Patterns

An important part of treatment for OCD is identifying different thinking patterns that are not helpful. All of us experience what we might call automatic thoughts. These are generally based on different beliefs that we have about the world or ourselves.

For example, one person might experience an urge to floor the gas pedal as they are stopped in rush hour traffic. An automatic thought from someone who does not suffer from OCD might be “Wow, that’s a weird urge to have” or “That’s kind of funny that urge just showed up in my mind.” Someone who suffers from OCD might have the thought of “I’m a terrible person who cannot be trusted to operate a vehicle!”

The automatic thought of the person who suffers from OCD could bring up feelings of guilt, fear, shame, etc. If one can identify this automatic thought, one can then decide if they truly believe that thought. More often than not, these automatic thoughts contain errors in logic.

In this example, one of the errors in logic might be that the person is confusing feelings with facts. The person feels terrible for having that image come into their head, but that doesn’t mean that they are terrible for having that image come into their head. Slowly, with time and support from a trained counselor, these automatic thoughts can be identified and examined for alignment with the truth.

In summary, obsessions and/or compulsions are the components that are the diagnostic makeup of obsessive-compulsive disorder. As with all mental disorders, for one to be diagnosed, the symptoms must cause significant difficulty in functioning. In other words, the mere presence of obsessions or compulsions in one’s life does not mean that one meets the criteria for an OCD diagnosis. It is when it gets in the way of functioning that it becomes a mental disorder.

There are three significant ways that counseling can help one who suffers from OCD: sharing obsessions, intrusive thoughts, or compulsions with a non-judgmental and skilled counselor; engaging in ERP treatment; and learning to identify and slowly change unhelpful thought patterns.

There are many other ways that counseling can help those who suffer from OCD; this list is not exhaustive. Those with OCD need not suffer in silence nor continue to be bound by OCD; there is hope and people who want to support you in healing!

References:
American Psychiatric Association: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision. Washington, DC, American Psychiatric Association, 2022.Photo:
“Vacuuming”, Courtesy of Giorgio Trovato, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post How to Define OCD: Three Areas That Are Helped By Counseling appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.

item.title: Overwhelming Anxiety: Why the Anxious Mind Replays the Past
item.description:
Anxiety is multifaceted, complex, and yes, a relentless machine. If you live with overwhelming anxiety, you know that it often feels more powerful than you. Not only does it give you racing thoughts, tight muscles, and the need for hypervigilance, but it is also more annoying than the worst playground bully.

Anxiety, the aggressive historian that it is, has the exhausting superpower of dragging you back in time. Overwhelming anxiety feels like it is forcing you to sit in a theater of your own making and watch replays of your most painful and embarrassing moments.

Why does overwhelming anxiety dwell in the past?

Someone without anxiety might look to the past for the sake of nostalgia or maybe even to look for meaning or lessons in their most painful moments. The anxious brain, however, relentlessly scans history for a different reason. It loops through painful memories and uncertain moments because it’s terrified of the future.

Deep down, overwhelming anxiety operates on a core belief. It fully believes that if it can figure out exactly what went wrong in past painful experiences, it can keep those and other bad things from happening in the future.

Anxiety is an authoritarian that forces you into the role of a detective who’s tasked with examining a crime scene. You must analyze data, searching for hidden clues you missed or rewriting conversation scripts as if this new dialogue can also rewrite history.

This is called rumination and is vastly different from healthy self-analysis or reflection on the past. While acknowledging a mistake and learning from a lesson is healthy, an anxious mind refuses to move on from it, even after the lesson is learned.

On a conscious level, you might recognize that no amount of dwelling can edit an already existing past or change an outcome. Subconsciously, the anxious brain treats these memories as a present or future threat that must be dealt with.

How Your Body Handles Overwhelming Anxiety

As if ruminating thoughts aren’t enough of a debt to pay for past missteps or pain, the anxious mind drags the body into the punishment, too. When a memory surfaces, it’s no longer just a historical record, but your body views it as a physical threat. Your stomach might tighten as your jaw clenches. Your heart rate may increase as your body sensations experience the past as if it is playing out again in real time.

Unfortunately, the human body can’t always distinguish between an emotionally charged memory from the past and an authentic present threat. While your rational brain may know that the embarrassing conversation ended long ago or the aggressive confrontation is already over, the nervous system still responds as if the danger is imminent.

God of the Past and the Future

When the anxious mind fixates on the past, it almost always does so through a lens of harsh accusation and criticism. The instant replays it insists you view aren’t objective but are heavily edited to show your flaws and perceived inadequacies.

The Enemy loves to use the anxious mind’s natural tendency toward rumination to convince you that your current worth is directly linked to your past mistakes and negative circumstances.

Thankfully, God is more powerful than Satan. He is more powerful than you or your anxiety, too. In Isaiah 43, God speaks directly to the people of Israel during a period of exile. They were a people who felt burdened by their history, much like you might. “Forget the former things; do not dwell on the past. See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it?” (Isaiah 43:18-19, NIV)

Notice that God doesn’t tell them “Don’t look back,” or that they should ignore their past trauma entirely. Instead, He is telling them not to dwell there. And then He asks them a question. Maybe this is the question He is asking you. He asks if they have perceived the new thing that He’s doing in their lives.

When you get so wrapped up in deciphering and rescripting the past, you often lose sight of the goodness of God. If you make that memory the idol in which you are fixated, you might miss the new thing that God is doing as a result of that past trauma or mistake.

Forgiveness and Anxiety

Was your past painful? Did you make mistakes? Even if the answer is yes to this and all the other accusatory questions your brain asks you, it doesn’t matter in God’s eyes.

While your anxious brain might want you to pay penance for your past, God wants you to live abundantly. He forgives your mistakes, even when you can’t forgive yourself. Numerous Scriptures reinforce the concept of God’s forgiveness and redemption. Psalm 103 says, “…as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” (Psalm 103:12, NIV)

When your anxious brain replays your past through a lens of condemnation or shame, you can remind yourself of that Scripture. Once you’ve asked God to forgive you through Jesus Christ, He removes your sins and casts them into an infinite, unreachable place. And you have no business trying to drag those memories back into the present.

God Is Doing a New Thing

God’s forgiveness is a life-giving reality, but His love doesn’t stop there. When you’re a child of God, even your past can’t haunt you forever. Will you have consequences for your actions? Yes, of course, there are natural consequences. God is also able to intervene and protect you from your own missteps and from those who might have hurt you in the past.

“And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love Him, who have been called according to His purpose.” (Romans 8:28, NIV) The beauty of this verse is that it doesn’t try to gaslight you into believing that everything is good, but it shows you that those painful situations that you keep replaying can be used to build something purposeful in God’s Hands.

In Genesis, Joseph says to his brothers, “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.” (Genesis 50:20, NIV) Joseph could have allowed the pain of his brothers’ betrayal to define him or keep him stuck in the past.

Joseph acknowledges the reality that his brothers intended to harm him by selling him into slavery. Yet he recognized that God’s supreme authority and unrelenting love for him took those ill intentions and turned them into massive blessings.

He can do that for you, too. He can take your past traumas, awkward conversations, and all those mistakes you’ve been replaying. They don’t have to continue to condemn or define you. God wants you to break free from those ties that bind you to the past trauma.

Breaking Free

While God can instantly deliver you from anxiety, sometimes healing is a process. If your brain is caught in a loop of memories and rumination, a Christian counselor can help you break free from the relentlessness.

Therapy provides the opportunity to dig into your past to determine where your anxiety comes from. A therapist can help you understand your options for dealing with past trauma, learned responses, and biological predispositions.

Through a variety of techniques, a therapist can help you redirect those automatic replays the moment they start. They can help you learn how to challenge the lies that your brain is telling you and help you realize that analyzing and replaying a situation does not offer you protection.

If you or a loved one feels exhausted from constantly reliving the past, reach out to our office today. Let us help you process your past so it doesn’t negatively impact your future.

Photos:

The post Overwhelming Anxiety: Why the Anxious Mind Replays the Past appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.

item.title: Self-Care for Depression: Small Changes that Can Help Improve Your Mood
item.description:
Self-care involves taking proper care of your daily needs, such as eating, sleeping, and personal hygiene. However, depression can drain your energy and make it hard to find the strength or motivation to do so. Just thinking about taking care of yourself may feel like an unattainable challenge. The result is a vicious cycle where the worse you feel, the less you do, and the less you do, the worse you feel.

This is because depression is more than a mindset problem. It is a mood disorder that involves changes in brain chemistry and nervous system regulation, zaps energy and motivation, distorts thinking, makes everything feel harder than it should, and makes activities that would lift your mood, such as self-care, feel pointless.

As a result, self-care for depression tends to be a difficult, counterintuitive process of doing the things that help even when you do not feel like doing them.

Habits that Fuel Depression

Small automatic daily habits you may not even be consciously aware of tend to add up over time, shaping your moods, leading you to feel mentally and emotionally overwhelmed, and fueling the symptoms of depression. The good news, however, is that if you learn to recognize these habits, you can take steps to unlearn them.

Discounting the positive Constantly discounting positivity, expecting the worst, dismissing wins, and rejecting compliments trains your brain to ignore the good and focus only on the negative.

Self-criticism Judging and berating yourself for the way you feel instead of accepting your emotions and criticizing yourself for all the things you do not do fuels shame and inaction.

Numbing behaviors Trying not to feel bad by numbing your feelings through distracting yourself or turning to food or alcohol may provide temporary relief from emotional pain, but tends to make your depression worse in the long run.

Rumination Ruminating on the past and replaying mistakes, perceived failures, injustices, or what could have been only keeps you stuck and deepens your depression.

Cognitive distortions Using emotional reasoning and allowing cognitive distortions such as all-or-nothing thinking to convince you that nothing you do will help or work creates unreasonable standards and reinforces feelings of worthlessness and hopelessness.

Self-neglect Using fatigue as an excuse to avoid self-care or engaging with others causes your energy to drop even lower and makes it even harder to do the things that can help you feel better.

Isolating Withdrawing from life to avoid difficult situations and isolating from others to avoid being hurt reinforces false beliefs of worthlessness and deprives you of the positive interactions and emotional support needed to help regulate your mood.

Waiting to feel motivated Waiting to feel motivated before taking action can become an easy trap to get stuck in that keeps you from taking any action at all.

Small Daily Practices that Can Help Improve Your Mood

The following are some simple evidence-based self-care practices that can help you break the inertia caused by depression and improve your mood. Strive for consistency rather than perfection.

Prioritize quality sleep Not getting enough sleep worsens symptoms of depression, whereas healthy sleep habits can lift your mood, improve brain function, and increase your level of energy.

To help facilitate good sleep, create and stick to a consistent sleep schedule, going to bed and getting up at the same time each day; have a calming bedtime routine; keep your bedroom cool, quiet, and dark; avoid caffeine late in the day; and limit screen time for a couple of hours before bed.

Create structure in your day Creating structure in your day by establishing a simple daily routine with small, realistic, achievable goals such as getting up at a certain time; eating three balanced meals; and completing simple tasks like making your bed, taking out the trash, or loading the dishwasher can add shape and direction to the day, provide a sense of control and predictability, and help combat lack of motivation.

Pay attention to your thoughts Depression changes the way your brain processes information, and thoughts like “nothing will ever change” or “I can’t do anything right” can feel like facts that, over time, reinforce feelings such as hopelessness.

When you notice yourself having these thoughts, stop and question them rather than accepting them as reality. Ask yourself whether there is any evidence to support that conclusion, or if there is an alternate, more balanced, realistic way of looking at it.

Journal Journaling can help you release painful emotions and overwhelming feelings by getting them out of your head and onto paper, where you can process them without trying to fix them. It can also help you track mood patterns and what seems to influence them, as well as identify, challenge, and reframe habitual negative thoughts.

Practice gratitude Write down three things you are grateful for when you get up in the morning, or before you go to bed at night. Making a habit of looking for small joys and positives as you go about your day can help boost your mood, as well as retrain your brain by redirecting its focus to small daily accomplishments and things you are thankful for.

Move your body Studies have shown that regular physical activity can significantly reduce symptoms of depression by lowering levels of the stress hormone cortisol and boosting the release of feel-good chemicals such as endorphins.

You don’t have to engage in an intense workout or anything strenuous. Even light physical activity such as walking, stretching, or gardening can give your mood and energy a boost. Small amounts add up. Find something you enjoy, make it part of your daily routine, and aim for consistency and regularity.

Spend time in nature Spending time outdoors in the fresh air and sunlight can have a positive impact on your mood. 30 minutes daily not only has a mood-lifting effect; it also supports vitamin D synthesis and circadian regulation.

Set screen time boundaries How you engage online matters. Active engagement, such as creating content or connecting with others in a meaningful way, can be positive, whereas passive engagement like endless scrolling tends to worsen symptoms of depression. Set boundaries for yourself, such as limiting the time you spend on social media, not bringing your phone to the table at mealtime, and avoiding screen time for at least an hour before bedtime.

Practice grounding techniques Grounding techniques, such as deep breathing or mindfulness exercises that use your five senses to center you in the present moment, help reduce the physical symptoms of depression and interrupt the process of rehashing the past or worrying about the future

Eat a healthy diet What you eat affects your mood. Eating a healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, healthy fats, leafy greens, whole grains, and lean protein, and staying hydrated, can help lift and stabilize your mood.

Connect with others Depression makes you want to withdraw from social contact, but lack of social contact worsens the symptoms of depression. Reach out to someone you trust and tell them how you are feeling, or join a support group where you can connect with others facing similar struggles and who can relate to what you are going through,

Do one thing you enjoy every day Make a habit of doing one thing every day that you used to enjoy, even if you don’t feel like doing it.

Be kind to yourself Be kind to yourself, and treat yourself with the same compassion you would extend to a friend. Instead of berating yourself for things you could not do, acknowledge the efforts you made and the things you accomplished – however small.

If you have questions about this article on self-care for depression or need more help than it could provide, please do not hesitate to give us a call.

References:
Kimberly Holland. “22 Ways to Cope With Your Depression.” Healthline. Updated May 9, 2025. healthline.com/health/depression/how-to-fight-depression.

Photo:
“Enjoying the View”, Courtesy of Brooke Cagle, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Self-Care for Depression: Small Changes that Can Help Improve Your Mood appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Why Is it Called Codependency if Only One Person is Dependent?
item.description:
At first glance, the term codependency can feel a little confusing, especially when it seems like only one person is doing all the giving, over-functioning, and people-pleasing. You might ask yourself, How is this co-anything when I’m the only one carrying the emotional load?

That’s a fair question. And it’s one that many people ask when they start to see just how one-sided their relationships have become. Codependency is more than just who gives more and who needs more. Codependency is a dynamic that puts two people into roles that seem opposite but are actually deeply connected.

What’s the “Co” in Codependency

The “co” in codependency describes a dysfunctional relationship dynamic that involves two people caught in different but connected roles. The term codependency came from the addiction recovery movement in the 1970s and 1980s. It was used to describe spouses and family members of alcoholics and drug addicts.

While one person had the addiction, the other was often trying desperately to hold everything and everyone together. Eventually, the helper, or enabler, gets as emotionally entangled in the situation as the person with the addiction. That’s where the “co” part of codependency comes in. Both parties have a pattern or addiction, albeit not the same thing, but both can get stuck.

While the two parties involved aren’t necessarily dependent on each other in the same way, they are co-participants in the same drama, trauma, or addiction. One avoids responsibility and the other one picks it up. One creates chaos while the other manages it. One is emotionally unavailable or toxic, while the other stays busy trying to win love by proving their value. The roles may be different, but they are both a part of the same issue.

What It’s Like Being in a Codependent Relationship

Being in a codependent relationship causes you to lose your emotional independence. Someone else’s mood, choices, or chaos starts dictating your own sense of peace and even your goals. Your identity gets blurred and put on the back burner. Your needs are buried as you manage and tend to others.

Real, genuine love involves freedom, not control. It doesn’t make you feel like it’s your sole responsibility to hold everything and everyone together just to keep the peace. Love does not necessitate that you always rescue someone or constantly manage their emotions so they don’t fall apart.

Instead, real love allows both people to live authentically and honestly. It doesn’t require you to walk on eggshells so you don’t trigger someone. Real love is two people being fully themselves, the people God created them to be, learning to carry their own weight and growing side-by-side in Christ.

One of the most difficult parts of being in a codependent relationship is that you might not even recognize it. It might not feel dysfunctional because you have always looked at it as loyalty and commitment. This type of implied devotion can make you feel good in the moment.

If you’re the one who is managing the emotions of others, it can make you feel stronger and more capable than they are. And maybe that’s even true, but deep down, there is also a price for this ego boost. The price is wondering what would happen if you just stopped being there for everyone. That trap, the shackles that are imposed upon you, keep you in the cycle.

How Does it Happen?

No one enters a relationship thinking, “I’d like to lose myself for the sake of someone else’s emotional survival.” Codependency creeps in slowly and methodically like a calculated predator. You make one small concession or adjustment to accommodate someone and then another. Before you know it, your whole life is off kilter. Instead of orbiting around God or even your own responsibilities, it orbits around them and their needs.

Even in this, you praise yourself for your loyalty and devotion. Maybe even other people notice it too. But inside, you feel exhaustion and even stress due to the overbearing weight of carrying not only your own responsibilities but someone else’s.

Why Stay?

If a codependent relationship is so exhausting, why do people stay in them? Walking away isn’t always so easy. There’s usually a complicated and compelling reason that people hang on so tightly to relationships that no longer serve them.

For some, they grew up in a codependent family, so this dynamic feels familiar and comforting. For others, they struggle with guilt, fear, or the belief that letting go of the relationship would make them a failure.

If you grew up in the church, you might have been taught that never giving up on people, no matter how much it costs you, is the right thing to do. So you stay and give and pour out your life, again and again. And instead of calling it one-sided or toxic, you convince yourself that it is love and grace.

Breaking Free from Codependency

Changing the routine of a relationship can be unnerving and disorienting, even if you’re the one who’s doing it. The process can lead to feelings of selfishness and doubt. You’ll worry about what people will think or what other consequences lie just on the other side of the upheaval.

Those are valid feelings to consider. Some who break free from or redefine codependent relationships are accused of being selfish or self-serving. They are told that they are not showing the love of Christ or that they aren’t meeting expectations. But in reality, in most codependent cases, these accusations come from a place of selfishness, not by the accused but the accuser.

The person who is no longer getting their needs met doesn’t necessarily or automatically see their need for self-motivation or individual responsibility. They are so accustomed to having their needs and wants met by someone else that they no longer know how to do it on their own.

Even if you’ve made it your habit to care for someone else, is it your responsibility? Just because you’ve always done something one way doesn’t mean that you have now taken on a lifetime commitment. It might make you feel uneasy at first. Soon you will realize that you are not abandoning them, you’re just establishing healthy boundaries and reestablishing your own sanity instead of constantly running triage in someone else’s life.

God and Therapy

God has never asked you to sacrifice yourself for someone else. Loving people is a biblical mandate and part of your calling, but you are to love in a way that reflects His character, not your fear, obligation, or guilt. Sometimes the most Christ-like thing you can do is to step aside and let someone face the consequences of their own choices.

“Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:2, NIV) This verse compels us to be there for each other when life gets too heavy to carry alone. But just a few verses later, Paul adds something else that matters just as much: “For each one should carry their own load.” (Galatians 6:5, NIV)

The second verse doesn’t cancel out the first. It just puts things into perspective. There’s a big difference between helping someone carry a heavy burden and dragging around their entire life on your back while ignoring your own.

At some point, you will have to decide if you’re being loving or if you’re avoiding conflict. Consider whether you’re being helpful or you’re enabling. That clarity often comes through prayer and sometimes therapy.

A Christian therapist can give you the permission you need to step out of the roles of codependency. Therapy can give you the confidence to establish and communicate boundaries, helping you learn to love people well without losing yourself in the process. Begin to find freedom from codependency today. Connect with a therapist in our office.

The post Why Is it Called Codependency if Only One Person is Dependent? appeared first on Los Angeles Christian Counseling.

item.title: Family Rifts in the Age of Social Media
item.description:
Remember the good old days when your family drama was played out exclusively within the comfortable confines of your house? Sure, there may have been the occasional phone call between family members to hash out the drama or retell some family gossip. Still, for the most part, the majority of your family skeletons were safely and securely trapped behind closed doors. Family rifts were kept private. But that isn’t how things are today.

Social Media and Family Rifts

Enter the age of social media. Now the he saids and she saids are often shared on social media for all the friends, followers, and lurkers to see. The private conversations that used to take days or weeks to circulate social circles now have an instant platform.

Additionally, people who should have no role in the argument suddenly have a seamless way to share their opinions. Because they can do it safely behind the protection of a screen, the delivery of these opinions is often harsher than they would be in a face-to-face interaction.

Family drama is inevitable, but it should also be private. Airing the details of your family dynamics and dramas on social media is not the way to resolve relationship issues. Even vague posts like, “Some people really need to learn respect,” or a meme that passively aggressively pokes fun at a husband, wife, sibling, or parent, can stir the pot.

No names or details need to be given to spark a flood of comments. “You okay?” and “Who did that?” start filling the comments section. Before long, there’s a full-blown social media courtroom holding court as a jury of your often biased peers start taking sides and offering unsolicited advice.

Why Post Family Rifts on Social Media?

There are a number of reasons why someone might want to post about their latest family squabble on social media. If someone feels wronged and isn’t getting satisfaction through private conversation, they might post online. This can be their way to call someone out or be a self-help therapy exercise in trying to let their feelings out. Perhaps the most common is that the poster is looking for validation and emotional support.

When someone feels hurt, wronged, betrayed, or misunderstood, they often want to know that they’re not alone and want to be validated in their feelings. Social media provides a fast, visible way to get that assurance. It only takes a few “You’re right!” comments to get that rush of assurance that you’re being supported. And it works.

The problem is, social media validation may give quick comfort, but it doesn’t come free. In fact, the long-term effects of airing your dirty laundry online can be quite costly. After the initial surge of support, these emotionally charged social media posts can backfire.

Why You Shouldn’t Post on Social Media

While posting family drama on social media might give you an immediate high as the heart emojis start trickling in, this seemingly benign act can lead to some heavy consequences. When emotions settle and damages become clearer, those heated posts you made remain. They live forever, rent-free in the minds of your readers and in the recesses of the internet.

What are the consequences? The person you posted about is likely feeling betrayed and embarrassed after being publicly shamed. Even if your post is vague, they usually know it’s about them, as does anyone else who knows your situation. That might feel like a victory in the moment, but that kind of public exposure makes it a lot harder to repair trust.

A post may also change people’s opinion of you. Some may publicly show you support by clicking a thumbs-up icon, but they might also start to view you as someone who can’t be trusted with personal matters and someone who thrives on drama. They may view you as reactionary and desperate, and most certainly attention-seeking. That type of hit to your reputation may affect other friendships, your witness for the Lord, and even professional opportunities.

The validation may feel temporarily comforting, but the cost of it may trickle down to other people in your life. Friends, extended family, or even workmates may chime in with their opinions. This can not only deepen the conflict in the moment, but also cause social division long-term.

As more people are pulled into your drama, loyalty lines are drawn. Those you love may find themselves on the other side of the battle line from their spouse or their child, causing a fracture in their own relationships.

The real questions are: Why? And to what end? What did you accomplish by posting your drama on your social media account? Temporary validation and revenge? Social media doesn’t solve the conflict.

Once your emotions have cooled down, you may regret and delete your post, but you can’t delete the information that is in your followers’ minds. No matter how embarrassed or guilty you might feel, there is no way to unsend the message from their thoughts.

Posting Your Problems Doesn’t Work

Family wounds don’t heal in the comment section. No amount of likes, shares, or digital validation will mend a broken relationship or validate your side of the story. No amount of meme posting or emotional blasts will bring reconciliation or happiness.

The temporary satisfaction you feel when you see the number of thumbs and hearts being sent your way will fade. When your post gets buried under tomorrow’s gossip, you will be left with the same set of problems, the same broken relationship, and a reputation that may not be as flattering as you were hoping for.

Finding Help for Family Rifts

Are you looking for real healing? That takes work and surrender. It requires uncomfortable conversations, humility, and forgiveness. And sometimes, it takes a miracle. God understands family better than anyone. The Bible is filled with stories of messy and complicated families like Cain and Abel, Joseph and his brothers, and the prodigal son and his father. Yet, time and time again, we see God work miracles in the middle of dysfunction.

Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. – Colossians 3:13, NIV

God can restore your family and repair your fractured relationships. He can offer hope and peace that no amount of likes and hearts can equal. And God can forgive you. While you might not be the one who started it, you are likely a participant in the family drama. God’s forgiveness is all-encompassing and infinite.

As a Christian, you too are called to forgive others even when they show favoritism, owe you money, or exclude you. Forgiveness is the key to reconciliation, and giving it doesn’t mean you’re weak or that you weren’t wronged. It doesn’t even mean that you’ve forgotten the hurt.

Forgiveness is a sign of strength in character and emotional regulation. It is a way of choosing to let go of bitterness so that healing in your own spirit and in the relationship can begin. Even if you haven’t yet received an apology, you can take responsibility for your part and extend grace.

If the burden of the drama feels too much to bear and forgiveness still feels out of reach, seek the help of a trusted professional family therapist. They can offer you real help that social media can’t offer and guidance that the internet never will. Seeking counsel allows you to vent in a constructive environment and gives you the support you crave, which is much more fulfilling than the heart emoji.

Before hitting the post button, hit pause. Realize that these emotions you’re feeling are temporary, but internet posts are not. Are you posting because you are looking for revenge, validation, or do you simply not know how to resolve conflict in a healthy way?

Instead, bring your frustrations to God. Pray. Seek wisdom. Talk to the people involved instead of the entire internet. Talk with a family therapist and forgive as you have been forgiven. Your family is worth it.

A Christian counselor can help with family rifts. Reach out to the office to connect with a counselor.
