item.title: Understanding and Finding Help for Nighttime Anxiety from a Faith-Based Perspective
item.description:
To the outside eye, the scene looks tranquil. The lights are out, and the fan provides a steady harmony and the occasional soft breeze. There are no loud neighbors or barking dogs. In fact, there’s nothing that could derail the perfect night’s rest. Nothing except nighttime anxiety.

What Is Nighttime Anxiety?

Nighttime anxiety is the nervousness, worry, or panic that occurs just before bed or late in the evening. It’s not a distinct or separate medical diagnosis, but rather a common manifestation of generalized anxiety or stress that peaks when the distractions of the day fade away.

While daytime anxiety is often tied to immediate tasks and interactions, nighttime anxiety tends to be more introspective. It frequently causes you to focus on existential worries or get stuck replaying the day’s troubles, even if they are minor.

What Nighttime Anxiety Feels Like

Nighttime anxiety behaves the same as it does during the day but can be more obvious or intense because of several factors. Some of these are emotional or mentally internal while others are physical.

There are the characteristic racing thoughts and possibly a racing heart. There’s likely physical tension as muscles stiffen and breathing becomes irregular. It is common to feel dread or panic that feels overwhelming, too. The intensity of anxiety can vary from person to person. While some experience a sense of uneasiness, some people with more severe cases experience nocturnal panic attacks that can wake them from sleep.

It’s a feeling that’s hard to explain unless you’ve gone through it. And while most people can identify with feelings of anxiety, clinical anxiety disorders are different than normal, everyday stress. Anxiety at night can be more intense and recurring. It can feel terrifying and crippling when anxiety occurs at night.

Why Does it Happen at Night?

For many people, anxiety becomes more noticeable at night, simply because there are fewer distractions than during the day. During the daytime hours, there are many other distractions to draw your interest, which helps to quiet the voice of anxiety.

There are conversations to have, errands to run, work to be finished, and people to take care of. In these busiest of moments, the mind stays occupied by all the distractions. But when the world slows down, unresolved issues and familiar anxious thoughts can crawl their way back to the surface. While the silence of the night should be a source of comfort, for some people with anxiety disorders, this quietness can quickly turn into toxic overthinking and anxiety.

Anxiety triggers vary. For some people, conversations that didn’t land as well as intended start playing in a loop. Those embarrassing moments get magnified. For others, worries of the future suddenly become realistic outcomes rather than far-fetched possibilities. You might worry about your health, your loved ones, finances, parenting, or even the purpose of life, before you even get the alarm set for the next morning.

Fatigue and Nighttime Anxiety

Fatigue also plays a role in how you respond to anxiety. After a full day of work, stress, and responsibilities, your body and your mind can feel exhausted. This deep state of fatigue weakens your ability to reason calmly or to cope effectively with the problems your anxious brain presents to you.

Fewer Distractions

For some people, nighttime anxiety digs a little deeper into insecurities and deep-seated fears. Maybe the struggle of being alone or fear of a terminal illness are the most terrifying triggers you can imagine. These worries are not necessarily triggered by a nighttime routine, although that is sometimes a factor, but are present constantly.

Things like this might be more manageable during the day, when you have to be calm for others. However, these deeply rooted fears surface with a vengeance in the quiet of the night.

Anxiety Loves Isolation

Because anxiety loves isolation, it often does its most sinister work in the dark cover of night. When you are with others, there is often a social pressure to act calm. Sometimes, the act of appearing calm can actually help keep your anxiety in check temporarily.

As you pretend to be at peace, your body can be triggered to react peacefully. While pretending to be calm during the day might temporarily keep anxiety at bay, suppressing it all day often leaves you emotionally exhausted by bedtime.

Another reason anxiety feels more intense at night is that if it strikes during the day, you can sometimes quiet its voice immediately by talking with a trusted person. Even if you’re not with a person you feel comfortable talking to about your biggest fears, the simple act of being around others (assuming they are not part of what is causing the anxiety) can help calm anxious feelings because humans were created for community and social interaction.

At night, you are often alone. This can make it difficult to find support when you struggle with nighttime anxiety.

Habitual Triggers

One attribute of anxiety that is particularly pronounced in people who also have Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is the nighttime routine. If you have a set nighttime routine, you might be inadvertently contributing to your nighttime anxiety.

That’s not to say that you shouldn’t have a routine. In fact, routines can be part of a healthy and calming sleep. But the wrong type of routine can cause nighttime anxiety. If you are in the habit of scrolling through social media just before bed, you could be feeding your anxiety with more things to hyperfocus on, like triggering news stories or a new person to compare yourself to.

Maybe some part of your nighttime routine has become associated with a deep-seated worry. For example, your routine of checking and rechecking your door lock is a response to a prior burglary. While checking to make sure the house is secure is common sense, doing it repeatedly at night might be keeping the trauma of the burglary at the forefront of your mind when you’re at your most vulnerable.

What To Do About Nighttime Anxiety

Sleep is a vital part of overall health. If anxiety is preventing you from getting a good night’s rest, here are some ideas on how to calm those nighttime fears.

Change Your Routine

If your bedtime routine is triggering anxious thoughts, change it. Even a routine that looks healthy on the exterior and one that has served you well before might trigger anxiety now.

Sometimes routines become unintentionally tied to fear or stress. Your brain begins associating certain activities, sounds, or even certain times of night with anxiety itself. If that has been happening, introducing new and calming habits can help break that connection.

Be Responsible, Not Obsessive

If your habit of checking to make sure the house is secure reminds you of a traumatic experience, then find a safe workaround. If possible, pass the responsibility of checking door locks and other safety issues off on another responsible adult in the home. Or perform this routine earlier in the night, so it isn’t directly associated with your bedtime behavior.

Reassociate Bed with Joy

Anxious brains are often creative brains. When a creative brain suddenly has no external stimuli to focus on, it gets bored. Anxiety sometimes strikes through that vulnerability and forces you to turn inward. If you associate bedtime with worry and fear, it can become a habit that’s difficult to break. But you can break it when you flip the script on your anxiety.

Try going to bed a little bit earlier and indulge in an activity you will look forward to. Keep a good book on your nightstand and allow yourself a fifteen-minute window before bed to enjoy it, for example. Whatever brings you joy, whether that’s photos of loved ones, a new sudoku book, or even a beloved pet, make it part of your bedtime routine.

Invite God

Inviting the Prince of Peace into your night will not only usher in the sweet peace of the Holy Spirit but remind you of the goodness of God. Say a simple prayer, have an honest conversation with your Creator, read Scriptures, or play worship music softly in the background. Anything you can do to infuse God into your nightly routine is bound to bring comfort.

Therapy Can Help Nighttime Anxiety

There is something at the heart of your nighttime anxiety, even if the cause is unclear. Finding the root cause can help you better understand not only what your anxiety is doing but why it is showing up at night. Therapy can provide a structured place for you to explore those patterns with someone who’s trained to help you without judgment.

If you’re struggling with nighttime anxiety, call us today to make an appointment. Together with your trained counselor, you can start to reclaim your night and finally get peaceful sleep.

item.title: The Unquiet Mind: Finding Support for Nighttime Anxiety
item.description:
There’s something about the dark that strips away the distractions, and during the day, with a packed schedule, a phone full of notifications, and a relentless to-do list, the noise keeps moving fast enough that deeper worries stay in the background.

Nighttime anxiety has a way of surfacing everything that the daylight hours help push aside. The room is quiet, and the mind gets loud. Many individuals find that this is when the fear, dread, and rumination settle in like unwelcome guests. No amount of exhaustion seems to make the anxiety move out so that sleep can move in. This is an experience that goes deeper than a habit of overthinking, and it affects far more people than most would expect.

The psalmist wrote from that same place – needing rest and finding it not through effort, but through trusting God.

In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O Lord, make me dwell in safety. – Psalm 4:8, ESV

The Mind That Won’t Slow Down

The mind was not designed to simply switch off at bedtime. What unfolds during the night is often a continuation of what the brain has been processing all day, except now it is without buffers.

Societal expectations, unfinished conversations, and fears about the future compete for space in a mind that is depleted but not yet rested. This results in a cycle that feels impossible to break. The more an individual tries to force themselves to sleep, the more alert the brain becomes, and this alertness leaves more room for worry to expand.

Prevailing attitudes toward stress management often center on productivity and positive thinking, leaving little room for what happens in the dark. Individuals are told to decompress, meditate, and develop better routines as if anxiety simply responds to instruction.

The mind doesn’t follow a schedule, and nighttime hours are often when the body finally reckons with what has been set aside all day. For many, it is the first real moment of stillness in hours – and stillness, without the proper foundation, can feel more threatening than restful.

Christian counselors recognize this kind of internal reckoning – and they understand it is not a sign of weakness. It is, in many cases, the beginning of genuine healing.

Nighttime Anxiety and the Stories People Tell Themselves

One of the hardest things about lying awake with anxiety is the narrative that forms in the silence. It’s no surprise that the mind tends to reach for worst-case scenarios after dark – the health concern that becomes a diagnosis, the financial worry that becomes a catastrophe, the relational dilemma that becomes permanent loss.

These are stories built on fear, and the late-night hours provide a stage where they can feel entirely convincing. Without external input, they have room to grow and deepen well beyond what the waking hours would allow.

This kind of anxious thinking frequently follows a specific pattern: a thought enters, the body responds with a physical stress reaction, and the thought grows larger in response to that signal. Anxiety and sleep disruption are closely interconnected, feeding each other in a loop that becomes harder to interrupt the longer it continues.

Just because an individual understands this cycle doesn’t mean it will not automatically break – but it does begin to shift the relationship a person has with his or her own thoughts. This understanding introduces the possibility that what feels overwhelmingly true at two in the morning is not necessarily the full picture of reality.

Scripture offers an anchor that is more stabilizing than perspective:

You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. – Isaiah 26:3, ESV

Learning to return to that anchor in the middle of the night is a practice worth developing.

What the Body Carries Into the Night

Anxiety is not just a mental experience. It is also deeply physical. The body tends to hold the day’s stress in ways that are not visible until the demands of wakefulness are removed. Elevated cortisol levels and a heightened nervous system can cause nighttime symptoms, such as restlessness, muscle tightness, or an inability to settle into stillness.

It is for these reasons that an approach must address more than the mind; it must also include the body. Practices such as slow, intentional breathing, deliberate muscle relaxation, and grounding techniques can signal to an overactive nervous system that it is safe to settle.

These are not instant solutions, but over time, they offer a meaningful starting point for releasing what the body has been carrying throughout the day.

Chronic stress and sleep disruption can become embedded in the nervous system, which makes genuine relaxation difficult even in safe environments. This is a physiological response to sustained pressure and is one of the reasons why professional support will make a meaningful difference.

Christian counselors are trained to address both the emotional and physical dimensions of anxiety, recognizing that the person seeking help is not just a collection of thoughts. They are a body, a soul, and a spirit navigating something real. Jesus extended a direct invitation for this kind of exhaustion:

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, ESV

Navigating Nighttime Anxiety Through Faith and Support

Just because an individual has faith does not mean he or she will not experience anxiety. But faith offers a foundation that remains stable even when the mind is not. This allows the individual to bring fear into an honest conversation with God instead of trying to manage it alone in the dark.

Developing practices that return the nervous system to a place of safety through surrender is itself a form of healing. Prayer, Scripture, and intentional breathing serve as anchors in the late-night hours when the mind continues to spiral.

Professional support becomes essential when anxiety persists, deepens, and begins to affect daily functioning. When someone works with Christian counselors, they find a space where the clinical and the spiritual dimensions of anxiety are held together. It is in this space that they can examine the thoughts that surface in the night and understand the patterns beneath them. The result is the development of real tools for moving through nighttime anxiety.

Faith and professional care are not competing approaches. Together, they reinforce each other in powerful ways. Scripture reminds believers not to be anxious about anything, but to bring every request to God through prayer and thanksgiving – and the peace that follows surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:6–7, ESV).

The Night Does Not Have the Final Word

The hours after midnight can feel like the loneliest place to be – especially when the rest of the world is asleep, and the mind is running its own quiet marathon. In those hours, it becomes easy to believe that what an individual is experiencing is uniquely theirs and that no one else will grapple with these particular fears in these particular hours.

The reality is that this experience is shared among many, connecting more people than the silence would suggest. Those who carry their faith into the dark hours find something profound in the knowledge that God is not absent from the night. He knows what surfaces when everything else is still; He is present in it and steady when nothing else seems to be.

Healing from anxiety is a process that deserves real investment. It involves understanding how the mind works and giving the body what it needs to release accumulated stress. Sometimes it requires support from people who are equipped to walk alongside the fears that surface in the dark.

For many, simply naming what surfaces at night and bringing it into an honest counseling relationship is where real movement begins. This journey calls for patience – and the willingness to cast every anxiety at the feet of the One who already carries them.

If you or a loved one has found that nights have become a source of fear rather than rest, support is available. Reach out to our reception team to get connected with support that can help you navigate nighttime anxiety from a place of faith.

item.title: How To Overcome Depression After Breakup
item.description:
Breakups can be harsh. You may have loved the person and didn’t see the end of the relationship coming. Maybe it blindsided you. Or perhaps, due to circumstances, you had to initiate the breakup for your own peace of mind.

The aftermath of a breakup can leave you sad, lethargic, and turning to bad habits to cope with hurt, rejection, grief, and self-acceptance. If your sadness persists for more than a few weeks and interferes with your daily life, you may have developed depression.

Depression after a breakup is common, especially if you love the person. But there are ways to make yourself feel better and return to being you, albeit a newer and stronger version.

Ways to Feel Better from Depression After a Breakup

Depression after a breakup can feel like the death of a loved one. The grieving process (denial/shock, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance) can be the same.

The following is a list of common ways to overcome depression after a breakup. Try each one and keep moving forward. Your heart needs time to heal and adapting each lifestyle tip into your day keeps you focused on your personal development, helping you stand on your own two feet.

Set Boundaries

Creating clear boundaries sends a message to others that you value your time and peace of mind. Not everyone needs to have access to you all the time. If your ex still calls or messages you, it may be time to set a boundary. If you share children, plainly state when you are available to discuss the children or meet for custody exchanges. Your heart needs time to heal and avoiding the one who broke it is in your best interest for now.

Process Your Emotions

It may be tempting to keep yourself busy to avoid feeling the pain after a breakup. However, avoidance is a coping mechanism and is not always healthy. It is better to sit with the uncomfortable feelings and allow yourself to process those painful emotions.

No one likes pain. Our brains will do whatever it takes to protect us from pain. If you are struggling with facing these emotions, speak to a counselor. Unresolved emotions can display themselves in other ways.

Avoid the Social Media Trap

You might want to check on your ex, or worse, bash them on social media. Refrain from doing either. Social media makes it too easy to see what others are projecting to the world. Comparison is the thief of joy, and if you see your ex happy without you, this will only fuel your depression. Bashing them for all to see will only make you look bitter and resentful (even if they are in the wrong).

Confide in a Friend

Venting to a friend for support is healthy. A burden is lighter when you share it with someone you trust. Confide in a trusted friend about the breakup and your emotions about it. Your friend may suggest other perspectives you have not considered. Invite your friend for a movie and dinner to discuss the relationship. Talking and crying with a friend can make you feel better.

Socialize

You might want nothing more than to hide away from the world after a breakup. But socializing can lift your spirits. Ask a friend or a group of friends to join you on an outing. Get out of the house, whether that is a special event, a festival, a movie, or a comedy club. If you still do not feel up to going out, consider volunteering in your church or community. Serving others will shift your focus on someone in need while allowing you time to spend interacting with people.

Create a Soothing Nightly Routine

Sleep is your friend and yet, it may elude you after a breakup when your thoughts are running wild and free. Help your mind to shut down by sending it a signal that it is time to wind down for bed.

Create a nightly routine that you find soothing and comforting. For example, after tidying up from dinner, take a warm bath, put on your comfy pajamas, and settle into bed with a good book and a cup of tea. As you repeat this nighttime ritual, your body will relax, and sleep will follow.

Are You Processing Your Emotions After a Breakup?

If you are experiencing the grieving process after a breakup, a Christian counselor can help. Your self-esteem and confidence can take a hit after a breakup, but a counselor can help you realize your potential. You are so much stronger than you know. You are a son or daughter of the King. He knows your every hurt and every rejection.

Christian counseling can teach you the skills to move forward while drawing you closer to Christ. Contact our office today to schedule a session to manage depression after a breakup.

item.title: What to Ask Before Getting Married and How to Find Support for a Healthy Marriage
item.description:
Getting married is a huge life event, perhaps one of the largest leaps you will ever take. Spending the rest of your life with your best friend is a dream many people have, but to make it last, you need to be clear about expectations from both sides.

Questions to Ask Before Getting Married

You can save yourself from future arguments and heartache by clarifying your relationship before getting married. If you plan to marry your significant other, you must agree or discuss important matters.

The following is a list of questions to ask your love before getting married.

How do you manage stress?

Some people engage in harmful coping mechanisms to manage stress. Knowing up front if your loved one will lash out at you or throw things is critical for your mental and emotional health.

How do you manage conflict?

Does your loved one try to find a solution that ends in peace? If your loved one is confrontational over small matters, this may be a red flag to underlying anger.

What are your core values?

Core values are the things that matter the most to you. For example, your core values might be your faith, family, health, and creativity. His might be his faith, health, and ambition. Your loved one’s core values may combine well with yours, but if his core values conflict, such as being too ambitious to spend time with family, it may lead to problems.

Why do you want to get married?

What is the real reason behind wanting to get married? It cannot be because he is afraid of being alone or she wants children. A marriage will only last if the motive is a deeper relationship and partnership with the spouse.

Are you close to your family?

It is healthy to have close relationships with family. However, it is important to note that boundaries should be clear before marriage to allow the couple time to be alone and build their own family unit.

How do you feel about household chores?

Depending on how you were raised, you may have a different idea about household responsibilities than those of your significant other. Do you want to delegate household chores? Have whoever sees that they need to do them? Are you more of a traditional belief that women should do the housework while men do the yard work? If you disagree on these points, you may want to speak to a counselor to come to a compromise.

How do you manage finances?

How will you manage finances as a married couple? Are either one of you bringing debt into the marriage? Who will carry insurance, or will you both take it individually? Marriage combines finances, so make sure you are clear on what you have before and during the marriage (and what may happen in divorce).

Do you want children?

Be sure to ask this question before the last minute. You should know upfront how your significant other feels about children and how to raise them. If this is your second marriage and his first, you may be done with having children, but will your new spouse want one of his own?

What dreams do you have for the future?

Discuss your future dreams, what you see yourself doing, and where you will live. Find out what your significant other wants to do. Do these dreams meld well? Can you both pursue your dreams together?

How do you feel about divorce?

Many people only consider divorce in the case of adultery, while others may resort to divorce if they feel neglected, disrespected, or cannot agree on important matters. How you feel about divorce may have to do with your core values, upbringing, and experiences. It is important to know how your significant other feels about the topic. What are your non-negotiables?

Are you open to premarital counseling?

Is your significant other open to premarital counseling? If your marriage gets into trouble in the future, is counseling an option they are willing to consider? How do you both feel about receiving help and learning new skills to resolve conflict and communicate better in the marriage?

Seek Counseling Before Getting Married

If these questions feel intimidating to ask your significant other before getting married on your own, consider premarital counseling. A counselor can also help with any disagreements the two of you have about the topics.

For example, suppose your significant other is close to his family, but you want to set boundaries before getting married. In that case, a counselor can assist in creating limits that will not leave the in-laws feeling ostracized but allow you to have freedom as a couple.

Contact our office to schedule a session with a premarital counselor today.

item.title: How to Manage Depression with Connection
item.description:
The symptoms of depression are a paradox. The things that most help prevent and manage symptoms are often the very things that, for the person with depression, are the hardest to perform.

Symptoms of Depression

Imagine you and your friend are camping in the wild and rainfall starts. You look at your friend and provide them with a wet stick and soggy leaves for tinder and encourage them by saying, “Here, use these; that should get the fire started.” You might want to prepare to dodge the stick that will boomerang back in your direction as they walk toward the car to get away from you.

Isolation, disconnection, estrangement – these are not necessarily symptoms of depression but often outcomes of the symptoms of depression. Temporary or chronic fatigue, disinterest, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and intense emotions, often internally waged, can push a person to spend more time apart from others.

Others may have difficulty understanding the internal or external battle that is being waged and say or do things that drive the individual further inward. Friction occurs in the paradox where one of the greatest lines of defense for managing depression is connection, but often an aspect that takes the greatest hit.

Depression can show up in a number of ways. It could be the summary of grief after losing someone or something. It can come from the changing weather. It can come from changes in life that are hard to orient to. It can show up as part of somebody’s personality, kind of that Eeyore mood.

Depression, the Bible, and Relationships

Depression can ride the tailcoats of trauma or stress. It might show up as part of intense mood swings. It can be the result of a medical diagnosis. Regardless of how or why it shows up, the Bible gives directions on how to reduce or manage depressive symptoms. Altogether, it gives good directions on how to do all things and manage all emotions.

Consider that since God is the creator of the universe and knows the intricacies of all things, He is the ultimate source of truth for the best and most effective operations of all things created; it is no surprise that instructions given in the Bible are going to be the most clear-cut and direct methods for best outcomes in a practical sense.

God commands us to pursue relationships with great intentionality, because the outcomes that come from being challenged and encouraged in consistent connection with others are what initiate and develop feelings of hope, determination, strength, motivation, support, and love, which are emotional catalysts that combat depression, among other things.

Read from the Bible in Mark 12:28-31, where Jesus describes the most important commandments, “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength. The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no commandment greater than these.”

God is wholly relational. There is nothing we take out of this world, but we leave behind the relationships we have cultivated. The hard thing about relationships is that they don’t just simply appear. It takes measures of intentionality and connection to form a type of relationship.

Consider the most common reason people engage in therapy: wanting to restore, resolve, or repair how relationships have been impacted by their own circumstances or circumstances of others. Relationships are one of the greater things we are called to in life, and one of the harder things to work on, so when we are not in connection with others, we can lose much of our sense of purpose.

The Research

That is an existential commentary on connection and depression, but what does it mean in a practical sense? Humans, through research, are always working to find concrete, explainable causality between things, and research in the field of mental health is no exception. This is a good thing. God invites us to be curious and to explore. There have been numerous studies researching whether social connection helps manage depression.

First, most studies examine the language used to define connection. For example, in a study by Matthews et al. (2016), there is a discussion of the difference between social isolation, a form of voluntary or involuntary estrangement from others, and loneliness, “a subjective feeling of distress, arising when social connections are perceived to be inadequate or unfulfilling.”

Then there is usually exploration of why disconnection occurs, which varies between exploring themes of asking for help, support, barriers to connection, etc. For example, an article by Sørum S., Lockertsen V., and Rivenes Lafontan S. (2025) looked at barriers to asking for help with depression in engagement with medical practitioners.

Their findings explored themes of validation or dismissal, confusion or lack of guidance, experiences of powerlessness, frustration, and lack of resources matching the true nature of their needs.

Another article by Ziggi et al. (2015) reviewed multiple findings on the relationship between connection and depression and summarized findings that, in fact, there might not yet be concrete causality between whether social connection is related to depression, but that there is still an unexplainable relationship between support and engaging in diverse social networks and how it helps manage depression.

The Practical Side

So, humans have been asking why social connection helps manage depression for whatever reason that it appears. What people have discovered is that it feels good to be validated for our experiences. It meets a need both emotionally and physically. It most certainly helps when experiencing any type of suffering or sorrow, because there is someone there to confront the depth of those emotions with us.

What does staying connected look like in a practical sense? In essence, we can’t ignore or let the rhythms of relationships deplete, because that is probably where we find ourselves the most vulnerable and at risk for all sorts of harmful behaviors and thinking patterns. Do the “normals,” whether you feel like it or not, which include spending time with others because it is a good kind of irritant.

We need things to get us motivated, fired up, changed. Change is something we get to consider and choose (Hodges, 2012). Find a meet-up group and commit to attend whether you feel like it or not. There is no requirement to be the best member, just to be present. Commit to meeting regularly with people you can be real and vulnerable with through every season. Accept invitations from others and show up and just be present.

Eat, hydrate, and move physically by any measure as rhythms to combat fatigue and lethargy that pull us from relationships. Remember that there is also a difference between being alone and isolation or disconnection. The Bible has lots of examples of the importance of rhythms where we take time to ourselves but be intentional in relating with God. This means that even when we are not with others physically, God is with us.

We are never truly alone, even if we feel lonely, unless we are choosing separation from God, and even then, God is like the ever-watchful parent and ready for his children to turn to Him and hear His voice. Attending therapy can also be a great “normal” when feeling uncertain or unmotivated to connect. Therapists can offer compassionate and careful consideration of your needs and make powerful recommendations of how to begin.

Depression is a great paradox but not unknown to God. He is the author of our emotions and the guide that gives real direction on how to walk through a world that is full of hardship and suffering. He calls us to relationship with Him and relationship with others to offer us real help and a strategy against depression.

Next Steps

Though we might experience loneliness, we are never alone. If you struggle with connection, consider meeting with a therapist to explore how and where to begin moving in change to any degree.

References:
American Psychiatric Association. (2022). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., text rev.).
Hodges C. D., (2012). Good mood, bad mood. Wapwallopen, PA: Shepherd Press.
Matthews, T., Danese, A., Wertz, J. et al. Social isolation, loneliness and depression in young adulthood: a behavioural genetic analysis. Soc Psychiatry Psychiatr Epidemiol 51, 339–348 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00127-016-1178-7
Sørum S, Lockertsen V, Rivenes Lafontan S. Patient Experiences of Seeking Specialized Mental Health Care in Norway: A Qualitative Study. Journal of Primary Care & Community Health. 2025;16. doi:10.1177/21501319251350601
Ziggi Ivan Santini, Ai Koyanagi, Stefanos Tyrovolas, Catherine Mason, Josep Maria Haro, The association between social relationships and depression: A systematic review, Journal of Affective Disorders, Volume 175, 2015, Pages 53-65, ISSN 0165-0327, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2014.12.049. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165032714008350)

Photos:

The post How to Manage Depression with Connection appeared first on San Diego Christian Counseling.

item.title: Relaxation Techniques for Anxiety: Getting Momentary Relief and Developing Lasting Calm
item.description:
It’s no secret that life is stressful and that it can be a challenge making it through the month in one piece. You might be anxious because you are living from one paycheck to the next, because you have to deal with relationship or parenting issues, because you have a difficult work project, or a combination of all of these things. While it may be helpful to find ways to cope in the present moment, you can also benefit from learning relaxation techniques for future anxiety.

Build an Anxiety Coping Toolbox

When a house is falling apart, a repair person will come and inspect each problem and the extent of the damage. From here, they will gather the necessary tools and materials and fix one problem at a time until the house is repaired. Working on your mental health is similar to fixing up a house. Many issues are connected, but you will only make progress when you focus on one problem at a time. Additionally, the job goes faster when you have a full toolbox.

When you fill your self-help toolbox with relaxation techniques for anxiety, you can learn to cope in anxious moments. Practicing coping effectively today can also help to build a foundation for peace and calm in the future. To fix the damage caused by anxiety, you must learn to surrender certain parts of your life while taking control of others. It’s not easy to know how to do, but you can begin learning today.

Quick Relaxation Techniques for Anxiety

It is difficult, and often feels impossible, to learn anything new until you have learned to de-escalate your anxiety in the moment. Luckily, there are many relaxation and focus exercises you can acquire to place in your self-help toolbox. When you find the most effective ones, you can practice them both when feeling calm and whenever your anxiety spikes.

Anxiety is not always linked to overthinking. Sometimes a feeling of dread and panic feels like it comes out of nowhere, escalating until you are sweating, out of breath, and your heart is racing. You can reduce the physical effects of anxiety by practicing breathing techniques and by focusing your attention on the outside world. It might take many attempts to complete these techniques. If you practice them consistently, you will find them becoming an automatic reaction to sudden anxiety.

Start by focusing on your breathing. When your nervous system goes into panic mode, your body floods with adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prime your body to face a threat or run from it, even when there is no threat. When you control your breathing with deep, steady inhale-exhale rhythms, your brain begins to calm as it realizes you are not in immediate danger and brings your nervous system back to its rest-and-digest mode.

There are different inhale-exhale rhythms you can try, and some will be more effective than others. A simple one to start with is inhaling through your nostrils, imagining your breath going down to your belly, slowly filling up your lungs to their capacity, holding the breath for three seconds, then slowly emptying your lungs by blowing through your mouth. Try to make the exhale longer than your inhale.

One of the most common and effective relaxation tips for anxiety is the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding method. This exercise helps you focus on the outside world as a distraction from your anxiety and an effective mindfulness practice. After taking a few cleansing breaths, find five things that you can see, four things that you can feel, three things that you can hear, two things that you can smell, and one thing that you can taste. Check in with yourself before and after, noticing the severity of your emotions.

When you focus on your five senses in this way, your parasympathetic nervous system becomes activated. Your body will automatically start to calm and come out of panic mode. Relaxation exercises like these are simple and are most effective when repeated over and over again. You can practice them daily in any location. Most importantly, they are an effective way to impact your anxiety immediately.

Changing How You Worry

While you may find tools that will help you calm down immediately, your anxiety will likely return. Relaxation techniques for anxiety must help your physical response to anxiety. This is the short-term coping method. Next, you need to find techniques that will help you cope with anxiety in the mid-term future. This involves addressing your mental state. Later, you will look at the emotional reasons you are anxious as a long-term way to cope with anxiety.

You know from experience that there is no on/off switch when it comes to worry. You also know that worry escalates to panic unless you keep it in check. An effective way to cope with worry is to allow yourself some time each day to worry about things.

For example, you could choose 5 p.m. each afternoon as your designated “Worry Time.” During Worry Time, give yourself ten to twenty minutes to ruminate on a single issue. You can be as dramatic or understated as you wish. If the issue pops into your head at any other time through your day, tell yourself that you will worry about it during Worry Time later, or tomorrow if it is late at night. It can be helpful to have a list to jot worries down for later.

Practice logging information about your anxiety. Whether you use a physical book or a note app on your phone, keep track of things like:

  • Where were you when you began to overthink?
  • What was the issue?
  • What started the panic session?
  • How did you respond to it?
  • How long did it last?

Over time, this record will show you the patterns and your progress surrounding anxiety, panic, and overthinking. This gives you further tools, like knowing what you need to avoid, what you need to focus more on, and some ideas of what is effective for you when you begin worrying.

You can better deal with anxiety in the mid-term by doing one helpful action a day. Pick an action that directly reduces your anxiety and be intentional in performing it daily. It could be checking in with a certain friend, going for a walk in a certain spot, having quiet time with your Bible and prayer journal, or whatever activity makes you feel comforted. When you perform one calming activity daily, you will make better decisions about how you handle stress in the future.

Dealing with Anxiety in the Long-term

When you have filled your self-help toolbox with tools that help you deal with anxiety in the moment and cope over time, you can turn your attention to dealing with anxiety for the future. Relaxation techniques for anxiety are only a single aspect of dealing with the bigger issue. There is deeper work to be done if you are going to get a handle on anxiety for good.

When you have developed a daily routine for handling anxiety, and when you have been consistent with practicing the techniques that help you, you might find that the anxiety has not disappeared. You have not failed. As frustrating as it is, you might have something unresolved that you need to deal with. Alternatively, you might have a medical issue that can be aided with medication. Either way, this is where you must seek outside help.

If you have never had a vulnerable conversation with someone, now could be the time to do it. It’s natural to be guarded about certain things. Many people feel embarrassed about having anxiety at all, even though it is not their fault. Your best chance at handling anxiety long-term is to find someone you can trust, and to begin having some honest conversations with them. You might find that what you needed most was to share a few burdens with someone who cares.

People often find that it’s easier to open up to a stranger than it is to their close friends. This is part of the reason counseling is so effective; you can share whatever you want with a professional listener who will keep your confidence. If you would like to meet with a counselor, reach out to us or consult the online catalog of counselors we host.

item.title: Self-Care for Men Over 50 Is Essential to Your Wellbeing
item.description:
Most men find worth in their careers and jobs, physical appearance, stamina, or spouse. Christian men lead their families as the head of the household, guiding and protecting them. Maybe this is why more men have trouble caring for their own health, especially men over the age of 50. However, the pressure continues to build. Self-care for men is needed now more than ever.

Self-Care for Men Over 50 Tips

According to the CDC, only around 7% of men seek counseling, compared to twice as many women who seek counseling from a professional. Perhaps men view professional mental health help as a weakness, something they should be able to figure out on their own. But anxiety, depression, and other mental health conditions can be the result of several internal and external factors.

Taking care of yourself over the age of 50 increases the likelihood that you will be around for a long time to care for your family. Self-care for men is not an expensive spa day. It is the intentional care and mindfulness you give to your health.

The following are several self-care tips for men.

Keep Moving

Movement is life for the body, especially as we age. Strength training maintains muscle mass and bone density and decreases fat percentage. Cardio strengthens the heart and lungs and regulates heart rate and blood pressure. Flexibility training keeps you limber and decreases your risk of falls. Functional training includes movements you do daily, such as lifting a box over your head, that keep you independent.

See the Doctor

Illnesses can come on quickly, so keep all appointments with your physician. Your doctor will order routine lab work and screenings. These can potentially catch conditions early and increase your chances of effective treatment.

Get Stress Under Control

Chronic stress is a killer. If you are over the age of 50, consider your lifestyle. Keeping up with the Joneses will not matter much if you are too sick to enjoy anything. Instead, downsize on things you no longer need and prioritize what’s most important. Look at your schedule and cancel or delegate responsibilities that no longer serve you.

Keep Regular Connections

As we age, we lose social connections. Even if you were the most popular guy in school, you may notice now that you seem to have fewer “real” friends, if any at all, other than your family. Try to keep regular connections by joining a small group, volunteering in the community, or serving at church.

Sleep Well

Self-care for men includes going to bed early enough to sleep at least seven hours. It is true that as we get older, we seem to get by with less stress. But sleep deprivation can activate the fight-or-flight response and keep cortisol flowing, increasing your chances of problems later. Stick to a consistent bedtime even on the weekends.

Christian Counseling for the Christian Man

Christian counseling is available for men virtually or in-person. Admitting that you need help is a strength, not a weakness. Self-care for men includes caring for your mental, emotional, physical, and spiritual health. Although many Christians seek help from our center, we also encourage men who are not Christians or who have walked away from the faith to join our clientele. Your counselor is a licensed professional in psychology. We want to help you. Call us today to get started.

item.title: When You’re Getting Older and Still Haven’t Found Love
item.description:
Most of the love stories in Hollywood suggest that life doesn’t truly begin until you find the one. We are conditioned to believe that if we just wait long enough or stay attractive enough and thin enough, our own happily ever after will eventually arrive.

But when you’re sitting solo while your younger friends or relatives celebrate anniversaries or the birth of their children, that happily-ever-after narrative starts to feel less like a promise and more like a sucker punch. It can leave you feeling left out or unworthy. It can make you feel envious of people who are just living out their lives, unaware of your secret longing and hurt.

Dealing with your aloneness when you’ve asked God for a partner.

Grow where you’re planted

This isn’t the answer you’re hoping for, is it? When you’ve prayed so long, waited and hoped, and maybe even done all the “right” things to find a mate, being told to “grow where you’re planted” can feel dismissive. This advice isn’t meant to minimize your desire for love, but to redirect your focus to what God is doing in you, right now, redirecting your focus from the future or from whether you find a mate to your current life.

Perhaps one of the most limiting things you can do is to put your life on hold while you’re waiting for something to happen. Being in a waiting period can make you feel like you’re missing out or that God has forgotten you. That couldn’t be further from the truth. Just because your current reality doesn’t look like you hoped or planned doesn’t mean that it can’t be beautiful.

It’s hard to see the beauty when you’ve put a timeline on your life, thinking you have to meet a certain benchmark by a particular time. This can undermine the life God has given you. It’s tempting to look around at weddings, anniversaries, and baby announcements and feel like you’ve missed your window of opportunity, but your life is not – and should not – be defined by what you don’t have. What matters is how you choose to live with what you’ve been given.

Growing where you’re planted obligates you to invest in your life as it is today, not in the life that you’re hoping will eventually come. Build friendships, pursue dreams, serve others, and anchor your heart in God. Watch your life blossom, even without the mate you so desperately desire.

Build your own community

One of the most alluring parts of marriage for single people is often the desire for companionship and practical help. While it might feel ideal to fulfill all your needs for community in one person, you can still find your fulfillment in other ways.

God wants us to live in community and encourages us to find fellowship. Sometimes that is with a spouse, but sometimes it’s not. Just because you don’t have a spouse doesn’t mean you’re doomed to a life of solitude. You may need to be more strategic and intentional about building the kind of community that married people seem to fall into naturally, but it can be done.

Putting yourself out there might feel uncomfortable when you first initiate plans or invite people into your life. But there’s something incredibly empowering about creating your own curated support system, filled with chosen family that doesn’t hinge on one person being able to meet all your needs.

Friendships can fill in the gaps where you feel the absence of a spouse. Maybe the neighbor is handy with tools and can fix that leaky faucet like a husband would. Or maybe the nice lady at church who greets you every week can provide the occasional home-cooked meal. Maybe those kids of a single mom could use the mentoring of a chosen friend, parent or grandparent.

Being surrounded by a village of chosen relationships can fulfill you in ways that no one person ever could. Though you may not have a spouse, you have the opportunity to build many close relationships with people of diverse perspectives and varied talents.

Trust God with the timing and outcome

This may be the hardest part. Waiting for God requires that you loosen your grip on a deeply desired dream. Trusting God with faith requires that you trust God’s sovereignty, even when His timing is different than your own.

Waiting on God can sometimes feel like He is absent. There may be moments when you feel like God is ignoring your heart. But the truth is that God is not careless with your life. He isn’t distracted or playing favorites.

Remember, He’s not late. Ecclesiastes reminds you that God has “made everything beautiful in its time” (Ecclesiastes 3:11, NIV), even when that time doesn’t align with your desired schedule. Trusting Him with the timing is also trusting Him with the outcome.

The outcome is His, too. It’s particularly painful to admit that your frustration about when is often masking a deeper fear of if. What if it never happens? What if the life you’ve imagined, wanted, prayed for, envied, never actually comes to pass at all?

That can be a hard reality. Instead of blaming God for the fact that you’re single and may never be partnered or married, realize that it isn’t Him who is wrong. You may have established your own set of expectations and feel disappointed when they’re not met without ever consulting God. Did you prayerfully imagine your future, or did you simply follow after cultural norms or family expectations?

Maybe God has a beautiful life of singleness planned for you. There’s freedom in singleness. Freedom to explore who you are in Christ without having to fit into anyone else’s life or schedule. Freedom to deeply invest in friendship and family, and to be the Hands and Feet of Christ in your community. Freedom to pursue passions and callings that might have been put on hold if you were to have been married.

The Fear and Grief of Singleness as You Age

Getting older and being alone can be a scary combination. The mental load of managing a life entirely on your own, from car repairs to financial planning, is heavy, indeed. Having constant responsibilities can be both physically and mentally exhausting.

In your older years, you might be grieving. You may not be missing a specific person, like you would a departed spouse, but you might mourn a version of your life that you thought you’d be living by now. This is called disenfranchised grief, and it can manifest itself in sadness for a wedding that hasn’t happened or children you never had.

You might worry about who is going to take care of you in your old age. But the truth is, everyone goes through that fear, even those who are married. A marriage license isn’t a guaranteed insurance policy against loneliness or the future. Many married people feel incredibly alone, and many spouses find themselves trying to manage their old age alone after a partner passes away.

Navigating Your Future

You have a life to live, growing to do, and relationships to be made. God has a plan for you. Maybe it includes a love story between you and a spouse. Maybe that love story is just between you and a loving Heavenly Father.

If you’re struggling in your singleness and are feeling the strains of aging in singleness, talking with a therapist can help. A therapist can walk you through processing your emotions, teach you how to challenge negative thoughts, and give you tools to help you build your community. Best of all, Christian therapy can help you recognize that God is fully able and willing to help you live abundantly, even in singleness.

Call our office to make an appointment with one of our licensed therapists who can help you embrace your single life at any age.

item.title: Is Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Right for Me?
item.description:
Emotionally focused couples therapy, commonly referred to as EFT, is based on attachment theory going back to the 1980s. What makes this therapy so effective is that it does not focus as much on the arguments themselves as on the high-emotion responses and what they may mean.

How Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Works

Emotionally focused couples therapy addresses the underlying emotions behind behaviors. For example, you and your spouse may keep having the same arguments about money. Although the finances may be an issue, there may be a cycle, a pattern that emerges.

One spouse may be angry and resentful because they feel they work and always seem to be behind. The other spouse may feel insecure and afraid of losing everything, especially their spouse, and feel like it is all their fault. One spouse pushes harder while the other withdraws further away.

Emotionally focused couples therapy identifies these patterns and pulls them apart through slower sessions focusing on the words, actions, and emotions present. Once the couple is aware of the pattern, they can work together in a gentler approach to address these concerns.

One note: Abusive relationships may not improve with just counseling. If you are in an abusive relationship and are in danger, seek help immediately.

Identify the Cycles

Emotionally-fueled disagreements typically fall into a cycle. This cycle can start with one spouse pushing and prodding about a subject, becoming overbearing at times, and asking for an answer or a reason. This behavior then causes the other spouse to withdraw, remain quiet, and create emotional distance between them.

Recognize the Patterns

When these cycles persist, a pattern emerges that widens the gap between the couple. Learning to recognize the pattern will help you know when to seek help. Keeping a journal of disagreements may be helpful in this case, although the records will be created after the argument and you may not be able to recall the emotions as vividly.

Counseling Dissects Arguments and Conversations

Your counselor during emotionally focused couples therapy will slow the conversation down to dissect how each person felt during the conflict. There may be feelings of anger, resentment, bitterness, jealousy, insecurity, fear, shame, or guilt.

Next, the counselor will help you verbalize these feelings so that you can work through them together using attachment language. This may appear as a statement like, “I get upset when you are on your phone for hours because I’m afraid I’m losing you.” This type of statement reflects fear of emotional distance and insecurity in the relationship, although during the confrontation it may appear as anger or withdrawal.

How to Get Started with Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

For emotionally focused couples therapy to work, both people need to be on board. Get with your spouse and research EFT, discuss the problems in your marriage, and the emotionally charged conflict. Confirm that you both want to work on the marriage and conflict resolution, incorporating EFT.

If your spouse is hesitant about EFT, you can still attend marriage counseling. Eventually, your spouse may recognize the patterns emerging during therapy.

Who to Look For

You want a professional mental health practitioner who specializes in emotionally focused couples therapy. You can ask if they are certified in EFT or attachment theory. This will ensure you receive the highest level of counseling for your situation.

Find a counselor that both you and your spouse feel comfortable with. This may mean attending an initial session or assessment to get to know one another before the actual work begins.

What You Can Do Before the First Session

Before you attend your first session, it might be prudent to sit with your spouse and journal surface disagreements. Take note of the emotions from both sides during these conflicts. Your counselor will not be taking sides but will dissect the emotion-fueled arguments.

Also discuss your goals for counseling. Is it to get back to where you were, with a deeper knowledge of and sensitivity toward one another? You want to be able to get to the root of an issue in the future together and work through it constructively. Showing vulnerability can be difficult for some people. Try to practice kindness and grace during these upcoming sessions.

Virtual Christian Counseling Offering EFT

Our Christian counseling center offers both in-person and virtual sessions, making counseling more accessible to couples. When you call our office, you will reach a representative who will match you to a Christian counselor specializing in emotionally focused couples therapy. Complete the contact form or call us today to schedule an introductory session.

item.title: How to Give Effective Support to a Depressed Person
item.description:
It is never easy to witness the suffering of others. That is even more so when the person who is struggling is someone you care about. You sympathize with them and feel as if you have taken on some of their burden.

When it comes to giving effective support to a depressed person, it can be a challenging, emotional, and deeply meaningful goal. Not only do you need patience, empathy, and wisdom, but it is also important to be physically and emotionally present for them without losing yourself in the process.

How Best to Support a Depressed Loved One

As you consider how best to support a depressed loved one, it is important to consider how best to position yourself for that role. While it may be easy to jump in feet first to help a loved one, it is not wise to do so when you do not know what is going on or how best to help.

Some of the things to consider before you proceed to be a support to a depressed loved one include the following:

Wield your influence well One of the things to consider before providing support to a depressed loved one is that you have limits and/or boundaries. It is wise to know your boundaries and work well within them. It is good to encourage and model healthy routines like getting good rest, getting exercise, and eating well. You can reinforce hope and connection by reminding your loved one of their value and worth as an individual created and loved by God.

Part of wielding your influence also includes being a support for them to get professional care. You can help them research options for therapy and even take them to their appointments.

Avoid dysfunction or codependency You cannot cure your loved one’s depression. Your role is one of offering support. Set healthy boundaries and say “No” if you start feeling overwhelmed. You should maintain your own commitments, hobbies, and other friendships. Setting a boundary does not mean that you are withdrawing your love from your loved one.

You can also encourage your loved one’s independence by guiding them to manage their own wellness journey instead of doing everything for them. These activities or commitments need to be communicated honestly so that you prevent any miscommunications that might arise.

It is also wise to know how and when to step back. If it comes to a place where your support enables your loved one to avoid therapy or their responsibilities, it may be time to reevaluate your participation. Recognize the limits of your role, because you are not your loved one’s therapist or savior. While your support is valuable, it is not a cure-all. Depression is a serious mental health and psychological condition that requires professional help.

Care for yourself, too Supporting a loved one with depression is a challenge. In order to provide effective support, you also need to care for yourself. That includes setting emotional limits and knowing when you need a break to prevent burnout. Setting limits also helps you maintain balance in your own life and reduces the risk of becoming resentful.

Caring for yourself also includes seeking your own support. Find a trusted friend, family member, or therapist so that your needs are also met. Prioritize rest and good sleep, eating healthy, and activities that recharge your batteries. It is wise to educate yourself about depression. Understanding what depression is helps you to respond both compassionately and effectively on behalf of your loved one.

Giving Effective Support to a Depressed Person

As you consider how to give effective support to a loved one dealing with depression, it is important to consider how to position yourself so that you can be of effective help. Some of the ways you can support a loved one struggling with depression include the following:

Recognize the signs. Depression is a mood disorder that affects an individual’s thinking, how they feel, and the way they act. When you know the signs, you can urge your loved one to get the help they need sooner. The signs of depression include persistent sadness, irritability, excessive guilt and self-blame, hopelessness, and a loss of interest in hobbies and activities they once enjoyed.

Some behavioral signs to be alert to include your loved one’s neglect of their responsibilities, withdrawing from loved ones or social activities, immersing themselves in work, and significant changes in their eating and sleeping habits. Cognitively, they may struggle with indecisiveness and difficulty remembering things or concentrating.

Your loved one may also exhibit physical signs such as lethargy, slowed movements, unexplained aches and pains that do not go away with standard treatments, and fatigue. It is important to look out for red flags, such as talk about death, self-harm, or suicide. These red flags should not be ignored. They need immediate attention.

Practice listening Listen to your loved one without judgment. Allow them to talk without needing to jump in immediately to fix things. Acknowledge their pain and experiences, reassuring them that it is okay for them to feel as they do. Do not minimize their feelings by sharing sentiments such as “Others have it worse than you,” or “Just cheer up; it will be okay soon enough.”

Be present There are many ways for you to be present for your loved one, including checking in regularly, even if it is a simple text message or a call that helps them to feel loved and less alone. You can also offer practical support through gestures such as helping with errands, cooking them a meal, or accompanying them when they have an appointment with their doctor or therapist.

Don’t take things personally When you interact with a depressed person, their mood can affect you, particularly their irritability or withdrawal. This is not a reflection of what they think of you. The illness does strange things to people and how they respond to others. Remember that in those moments you are tempted to take their behavior personally.

Take a measured approach It is easy to become overly responsible for a depressed loved one’s well-being. Their depression can pull you away from your own life, and you can also feel guilty when you cannot always help them. Boundaries are important, as is the reminder that your love, presence, and support are a part of the puzzle, but they are not the whole solution.

Taking a measured approach means reminding yourself that by stepping back to allow them greater independence and not neglecting your own needs, you are also caring for yourself. This enables you to show up better for them as well. You do the most good for a depressed person when you are consistent and compassionate toward them, balancing that with taking adequate care of yourself.

Encourage them to seek help Depression requires the intervention of professionals, and you should not take the load on yourself. Do not pressure or nag them, whether it is to attempt to tell them to snap out of it, or to go see a therapist. This will only serve to increase their feelings of guilt and perhaps even resistance to the idea of getting help. Rather, you can gently guide your depressed loved one toward a therapist or counselor for the help they need.

Helping a Depressed Person

Depression is a significant challenge, but one that can be overcome. You can effectively come alongside a depressed loved one to help them as they face this challenge. Love and nurture them in a wise, healthy, and balanced way. This requires understanding what depression is and how it works, being present for them within healthy limits, and encouraging them to seek professional help.

Whether you are looking for support in this process or for a resource for someone who is depressed, a Christian counselor can help. Connect with a counselor today to get started.

item.title: Burnout Self-Care for High School Students Can Reduce Stress and Overwhelm
item.description:
High school is a time of reflection and looking forward. If you are a student, people are always asking about your plans after graduation, even if you are only a freshman. Parents of high schoolers try to help their student manage graduation requirements, extracurriculars, social events, and community service hours.

But high school students can get overwhelmed by pressing requirements, pressure to maintain a certain G.P.A., or the need to do well on standardized tests. Teens’ mental health can spiral if they are not taught how to incorporate burnout self-care.

Burnout Self-Care Tips

Burnout can happen to anyone when you push yourself past your limits with little to no rest to recharge your mind.

Signs of burnout include:

  • Waking up exhausted
  • Sleep issues
  • Appetite changes
  • Procrastinating
  • Brain fog/inability to concentrate
  • Forgetfulness
  • Losing interest in things you like to do
  • Withdrawing from friends and family
  • Drop in grades
  • Irritability
  • Unexplained body aches or headaches
  • Persistent sadness (depression)
  • Overwhelming worry or fear (anxiety)

Learning how to avoid burnout means balancing school and activities with rest. The saying “putting your nose to the grindstone” will only carry you so far before your body and mind force you to rest.

The following are several tips for adapting to burnout self-care.

Manage Time

Delayed gratification means working on something with a focused intensity now so that you can play later. For example, it is doing the Chemistry homework before watching the new movie streaming on TV. It is working on a project before playing video games.

If you struggle with concentration, try the Pomodoro Technique. Focus on a task for 25 minutes, followed by a 5-minute break. Repeat the cycle one or two times more, then take a longer break to do what you want, like watching half the movie or playing the game for 45 minutes.

Sleep Is a Must

Burnout self-care includes sleep. It’s tempting to stay up late, chatting with friends, playing games, or binging your favorite series. But your body and mind need time to recover and recharge, and that only happens while you are sleeping. Aim for 8 to 10 hours of sleep nightly.

Stay Active

Exercise provides the body with more than a healthier appearance. Exercise triggers the release of hormones such as serotonin and dopamine, as well as endorphins, which leave you feeling happy and confident.

Teens who exercise and make intentional movement (taking the stairs, walking more) part of their day stay healthier and are less likely to develop physical conditions such as obesity and Type 2 diabetes.

Eat Healthy Following the 80/20 Rule

Eating healthy as a teen doesn’t mean giving up all of your favorite foods or avoiding specific food groups. The 80/20 rule for healthy eating means eating 80% of your meals from whole foods, such as lean protein, fruits and vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats like nuts and seeds. Then, use the other 20% of your meals and snacks for treats like theater candy or a couple of slices at the pizza party. Balance and moderation are key.

Know When To Say No

Boundaries are important, and learning to set them as a teen is important. Know when to say no to avoid getting stretched too thin. You should have time for school, volunteering, pursuing hobbies and interests, working if you need to, and resting. FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) will pass, and you want to manage your physical and mental health with boundaries to maintain your peace.

Choose Your Friends Wisely

Jim Rohn was a wise motivational speaker who said, “You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with.” Choose your friends wisely. Walk in peace with everyone you can, especially if you are a Christian and follow Christ, but watch for influences that may pull you away from Jesus. If you are involved in a toxic relationship, seek help to learn how to move away from it without hurting yourself.

Practice Grounding Techniques

Grounding techniques help you focus on the present, bringing your mind forward and away from worries. They are helpful during anxiety attacks or feelings of burnout. One of the easiest includes digging your heels into the ground (barefoot, if possible, although not necessary). Another is the 5-4-3-2-1 method. Name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste.

Christian Counseling for Teens

Christian counseling for teens is available through virtual and in-person sessions. Whether you are looking for more burnout self-care tips, struggling with anxiety or depression, or need someone to talk with, contact our center today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor.
