item.title: Surviving Divorce: How to Thrive While Experiencing Loss
item.description:
Painful life experiences abound, and a good deal of them are connected with relationships. We are relational and social creatures, with the result that our relationships make up a large portion of what matters most in our lives.

When our relationships are healthy, that’s a good indicator that we’re flourishing. When things go awry in relationships, it affects overall well-being. Nonetheless, surviving divorce and flourishing when a marriage ends is possible.

The Complexities of Divorce

It would be a mistake to think that divorce is easy, especially when the marriage was marked by unhappiness and interminable struggles. Divorce can be and often is one of life’s most painful experiences, regardless of the circumstances.

When most people enter a marital union, they do so with hope and faith that they will be happy together for the rest of their lives. Ending such a relationship comes with layers of grief and confusion.

Working through divorce requires that you face the situation with honesty as well as healthy support that helps to anchor you through it all. There isn’t just one path that everyone who’s getting divorced takes. Every marriage is its own story, and the end of a marriage is also its own unique story.

When a divorce happens, it’s rarely the result of a single event. Often, there are many steps along the way that lead to the eventual breakdown of a marriage, to the point where a couple can’t see themselves together.

That process may take months or years, and it brings about many complex emotions like guilt, anger, grief, shame, and even relief. These emotions can appear at different times, and they touch nearly every part of a person’s life.

The most obvious change that a divorce brings is the change in relationship status, but that’s far from the only change. Divorce often brings other changes and concerns, such as needing to financially rearrange your life, adjusting your parenting responsibilities, and managing your living situation.

Another result of divorce is that it can stir up deep spiritual questions about forgiveness, your identity and sense of self in this new season, the Lord’s plan for your life, and your sense of security. It’s not just your relationship with your former spouse that changes; your relationships in the church, among friends, and with your extended family are also affected. There are many opinions and expectations to navigate.

The Challenges Divorce Brings to Your Well-being

Given the various complexities that divorce brings to your life, it isn’t surprising that it affects your well-being on several levels. For one thing, divorce can be stressful. There are financial costs involved, not to mention the logistical challenges that come with uncoupling. Stress often results in disrupted sleep, changes in appetite, and a negative impact on your overall health.

Emotionally, divorce is a source of grief, whether the relationship was good or not. Cherished dreams are being laid to rest, tears are shed for the years the locusts ate, and dealing with the heartache and pain you and your former spouse caused one another. There is fear of the unknown, and one may also have to grapple with a sense of failure.

Socially, divorce can change your landscape dramatically. Friendships, family connections, and church relationships can become strained or awkward. For their own reasons, the people in your life will choose sides, and that can have a devastating impact if it means losing friends and vital support at such a critical time.

Lastly, spiritually, divorce can leave you grappling with feelings of shame and guilt. You may begin to perceive yourself negatively and maintain unhealthy self-talk. Others experience a feeling of distance from the Lord, even in those situations where the decision was unavoidable.

Divorce can impact every aspect of your well-being, leaving you vulnerable to poor physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual health. If these challenges don’t get addressed, isolation, bitterness, and making use of unhealthy coping mechanisms are a true risk to keep a watchful eye on.

What to Avoid when Trying to Survive Divorce

Before launching into some healthy and effective ways to survive divorce, it may be helpful to take a detour and explore some common but unhealthy ways to try to survive a divorce.

It may be tempting, but avoid rushing into another relationship. Divorce can leave you feeling unworthy of love, and you may question your prospects or if you’ll even survive the world of dating post-divorce.

Whatever the case might be, take your time to heal and avoid trying to fill the void prematurely. Find your footing, work through your pain, and find joy before inviting another person into the deeper places of your heart and soul.

Another consideration is that you shouldn’t withdraw from the Lord or the church. Getting divorced can bring judgment from others, and your spiritual home may not feel safe any longer. You may feel shame or anger as you see how others around you are in light of this development, but you need to remain anchored in the Lord and among His people. That may mean finding a new spiritual home, but don’t withdraw from God or His people completely.

You should also avoid feeding revenge or bitterness. It can be tempting to narrate and re-narrate the ways your former spouse wronged you, or what should have happened. You can fuel anger, bitterness, and resentment as you dwell on what was or what should have been. Bitterness and the desire to get even may feel good, but they only serve to cloud your future and delay healing.

Do not ignore your physical and emotional needs. A relationship breakdown can take its toll on your body and mind. It’s not healthy to deny your grief or to ignore your needs at this (or any) time. These needs include the need to rest, so don’t overwork yourself. They also include the need for social interaction, to eat healthy food, expand your intellectual horizons, and connect meaningfully with God.

Lastly, you should also avoid making major decisions too quickly. Life may thrust some huge decisions upon you at this time, like needing to find a new home, changing jobs, or reentering the job market. Where it isn’t strictly necessary, however, avoid doing too much too soon. Give yourself the time you need to process what you’ve been through before making huge life changes.

Healthy Ways to Survive Divorce and Thrive

The Lord isn’t fond of divorce, given what marriage represents and the damage that divorce can cause (Malachi 2:16; Matthew 19:1-12; Ephesians 5:31-32). However, Scripture does speak to different circumstances for divorce (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15), and life after divorce can be more than just survival. It is possible to thrive. Some healthy ways to work through a divorce and flourish include:

Allow yourself to grieve Recognize and acknowledge the loss fully. Different days and experiences may reveal new dimensions of loss, like the loss of companionship or support, or how your former spouse could bring out parts of you that no one else can.

Some people journal, while others prayerfully reflect on their marriage, and still others use art or creative expression to explore and release their emotions.

Stay connected to others We need community, especially in the dark times. When you’re isolated, it can lead to more rumination, slowing your healing process. Connect with friends, your Bible study group, or a ministry that helps you feel safe. Don’t disengage from the Lord either. Rather, take your heavy and uncomfortable feelings and thoughts to Him, because He cares about you (1 Peter 5:6-7).

Prioritize self-care and growth Don’t neglect your well-being in this season. Your emotional resilience can be bolstered by taking care of the ‘little’ things like good sleep, nutrition, regular exercise, and finding spaces of rest. As you go, seek the Lod and ask Him to show you new opportunities, places of growth, and ways to begin rebuilding and serving in line with His purposes for you.

Forgive and release The way to undo bitterness and stop it from gaining a foothold in your heart is to forgive them and yourself. This is not a way to excuse wrongs, but it releases you from bitterness and the need to get even. This is the only way for you to move forward with your life.

Seek support and counseling Divorce can leave open wounds and scars that need healing. By speaking with a trained and licensed counselor, you can find support and wise counsel during a challenging season of life. With help, you can emerge wiser, stronger, and more deeply rooted in your faith. Contact our reception team to get connected with a counselor who will walk with you on this journey.

item.title: How Spiritual Maturity Is Linked to a Healthier Mind
item.description:
Growing faith doesn’t have to be just a spiritual journey. It can also be a journey toward good mental health. The deep connection between a spiritual relationship with God and a stable, grounded mind provides a profound basis for spiritual maturity.

“Bible Study”, Courtesy of Daiga Ellaby, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; This develops through years of navigating difficulty, learning to trust what cannot always be seen, and holding onto faith even when it seems distant. Along the way, there is a growth that quietly reshapes how a person thinks and processes emotion.

Some of the outward markers of a mature faith are familiar: deeper compassion, a longer view on hardship, and greater patience. However, the internal work to cultivate these qualities does something else. It builds a resilient, settled mind that can sustain genuine peace. This kind of growth comes with a promise that speaks directly to the peace available to those who trust in God.

The steadfast of mind You will keep in perfect peace, because he trusts in You. – Isaiah 26:3, NASB

Steadfast means fixed and anchored. These are qualities that describe other areas of mature faith. A mind that is anchored in the trust of God’s promise discovers that peace is no longer a destination. It becomes a natural outcome of having a deeper relationship with God.

The Link Between Spiritual Maturity and Mental Health

Health professionals are becoming more aware of the connection between spiritual well-being and mental wellness. An individual whose faith has been tested repeatedly tends to develop an inner stability not found elsewhere.

These individuals have cultivated a mature faith throughout the years, and they often report lower levels of anxiety and a greater ability to move through grief with greater strength. These are not accidental outcomes. They are the natural product of a life shaped by ongoing surrender and honest reflection about placing trust in something larger than oneself.

This is not to say that spiritually grounded people are immune to mental health challenges. Life is hard, and with it come tough moments, regardless of how deep one’s faith may run. It is the framework developed through years of spiritual investment that can significantly reduce the emotional weight a person carries.

The way a person can make meaning of a difficulty or find footing when the ground shifts is a pattern that Christian counselors often observe in those with a well-developed faith. This becomes the stabilizing force during seasons of uncertainty and significant life transitions. The pain is not erased, but the way it is held is changed.

For God has not given us a spirit of timidity, but of power and love and discipline. – 2 Timothy 1:7, NASB

This verse reflects a spiritual discipline that is intentional and practiced, deepening faith over time. The focus shifts from emotional reactivity to grounded, purposeful engagement with life. It is an engagement that is built through consistent spiritual investment rather than a single pivotal moment.

What a Rooted Faith Does for the Mind

When faith has grown roots through regular prayer, community, ongoing study, and the experience accumulated in a life of walking with God through hard seasons, it changes how a person relates to their thoughts and emotions. They are no longer swept away by worry or fear. They have learned to pause and return to what is known to be true. This practice builds strength to resist the pull toward catastrophic thinking.

This does not mean individuals should suppress difficult emotions or pretend that painful things are not painful. It compels them to create a consistent place to bring these emotions, where they can be managed without collapsing under them.

Emotional regulation is one of the strongest predictors of long-term mental health and resilience. A faith that is rooted, combined with consistent prayer and connection to an authentic community of believers, reduces the likelihood of processing hard seasons in isolation. Isolation is one of the most significant risk factors for declining mental health.

The presence of both spiritual and relational resources creates a life that is held in multiple ways and a mind that learns, over time, that it does not have to carry every burden alone. Scripture describes a practice that is active and ongoing rather than a single act of faith.

It does require a rhythm developed over time to gradually reshape how the mind processes stress, fear, and uncertainty. Scripture invites a person to meet anxiety with prayer and gratitude when making requests known to God.

Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and pleading with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. – Philippians 4:6, NASB

Spiritual Maturity and the Practice of Peace

One of the most rewarding mental health benefits of spiritual maturity is the deepened capacity for peace. This is not the absence of problems, but a settled mindset that persists as a person experiences them.

Those who have been walking in faith for years describe a meaningful shift in how they approach difficult situations. The overwhelming feelings they once carried have gradually been met with steadiness. This shift comes from a growing trust that something larger and more purposeful is at work, even in the hardest and most disorienting seasons of life.

When it comes to mental well-being, this internal shift carries significant weight. Persistent anxiety and chronic stress are two common concerns that Christian counselors encounter in daily work with clients. Spiritual maturity offers a perspective on these experiences that goes beyond immediate circumstances and frames the present difficulty within the context of a God-authored story.

The result of this reframing is a healing potential that situates hard things within a narrative that includes hope, purpose, and forward movement. When this perspective deepens as the person continues to walk in faith, it has a cumulative effect on the mind.

And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:7, NASB

This Scripture presents an image of peace as a guard over the heart and mind. This points to the reality that peace is not passive or fragile but protective. It is this protection that becomes more established, reliable, and accessible as a person cultivates faith and matures over a lifetime.

When Faith and Mental Health Work Together

Mental health care and faith are not competing forces. The most effective healing journeys often unfold when they work together. A person who is actively investing in spiritual growth is also cultivating a stable sense of identity that is not connected to performance or achievement. The result is an expansion of the capacity for hope even in difficult circumstances. These benefits are concrete qualities that support the goals of meaningful, lasting mental health care.

There are seasons when the weight of life requires more than spiritual practice alone. Grief, trauma, relational wounds, and clinical mental health conditions are real, and they deserve professional support. This is where Christian counselors bring a distinctive advantage.

A faith-based counselor understands the spiritual dimension of a person’s life, and they are equipped to help integrate faith into the healing process. This offers a meaningful, practical, and deeply personal strategy for those seeking genuine inner wellness and spiritual maturity.

Learn how your spiritual maturity and mental health connect

There are no shortcuts in developing spiritual maturity. It is a process with no finish line to declare the work complete. The growth that accumulates along the way, as trust deepens and views on hardship broaden, also produces genuine, measurable support for a healthy mind. Spiritual maturity is not a badge or a marker of having arrived somewhere. It is a way of life built one season at a time through the easy and hard years a person navigates.

Those who find themselves at the intersection of spiritual growth and mental health should know that the two need not exist in separate lanes. A maturing faith is a resource for lasting inner wellness, and pairing it with the right professional support makes a meaningful difference in how a deepening faith shapes mental health.

If you are ready to integrate your faith and mental health, please reach out to our reception team to be connected with a counselor who understands both and can help you begin this process. The reception team can provide you with more information about faith-informed counseling and how it can support this journey.

item.title: Considering Therapy? Discover Topics Covered in Therapy for Women
item.description:
Women are more likely to seek help for their mental health, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. This is good news. But you don’t have to wait until you feel like you can no longer bear a situation. Counseling centers use therapy for women for a multitude of topics.

Common Topics Covered in Therapy for Women

Women assume roles inside and outside the home. They serve as caregivers to families, friends, and the church. Many mothers and grandmothers also volunteer for organizations, including those in which their children or grandchildren are involved.

They pour out so much of themselves into others that they may not notice that they themselves are depleted. Hormonal shifts, life events, and other problems can take a toll on their physical and mental health.

We talk with women about a variety of topics at our center. The following are the common topics covered in therapy for women.

Trauma-Specific

Whether from abuse, neglect, abandonment, violence, or natural disasters, we see women trying to move past trauma. Trauma brings about nightmares, anxiety, depression, negative thoughts, fears, and a host of other issues. Trauma-specific issues often affect physical health.

Your counselor will get to know you and discuss a treatment plan for your specific situation while addressing you as a whole person. Christian counseling is more than just the mind. We want to help you thrive in your physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual health.

Body Image Issues

Body image issues can stem from societal pressures, childhood experiences, or sudden changes in body composition. However, not every thought is true. You should always challenge negative thoughts, a skill you can learn in counseling. Sometimes perception plays a huge role in how women view themselves. Body image issues can lead to body dysmorphia, eating disorders, and low self-esteem.

Relationships

Relationships with a significant other, parents, children, and extended family can cause distress if there is contention. Toxic relationships and friendships that leave you drained and feeling worse after being around them will erode your confidence. Some of these relationships feel painful. Counseling can show you how to be assertive and place distance if needed by teaching you how to set (and enforce) boundaries.

Life Events

One of the most common topics we cover in therapy for women is the transition into roles during major life events. All major life changes come with some stress, even the good ones. Stress and doubt may prevail as a woman tries to adjust or adapt to her new normal. Graduations, marriages, deaths, births, moves, and career changes can leave a woman feeling out of control and on edge.

Anxiety and Depression

Anxiety and depression are common mental health disorders we treat at our center. Chronic stress, hormonal changes, life changes, chemical imbalances, and other factors contribute to mental health conditions.

Arming a woman with strategies and techniques to overcome anxiety and depression and move forward is our goal. We want every woman to leave a session feeling empowered, not only by herself, but with God’s help.

Contact Us to Learn More about Therapeutic Approaches in Christian Counseling

Our office would love to work with you. Our representatives can connect you with a Christian counselor specializing in therapy for women. Therapeutic approaches can include talk therapy, group therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), and more. Contact us today for an assessment.

Photos:

item.title: How to Care for Yourself in This Economy
item.description:
When we hear the term “self-care,” many of us think of spa days, resorts, and beach houses. And for many of us in this economy, those options are out of the question. However, there are several effective free or low-cost alternatives to help you care for yourself when you feel overwhelmed and stressed.

Daily Habits to Care for Yourself

You want to be healthy, physically, mentally, and spiritually. But how do you care for yourself during a downturn in the economy and busy days trying to make ends meet? The answer: you build daily habits into your life that are either free or low-cost.

The following are several tips you can try to care for yourself in this economy.

Make Movement a Part of Your Day

Movement does not have to mean grueling workouts at the gym for hours six days a week. Movement can be a few days of walking for 10 to 30 minutes and strength training every other day, three days a week. It can mean stretching before bed or Saturday morning Pilates. It can look like playing catch with the kids or walking the dog. Make it a part of your daily routine like brushing your teeth.

Stay Hydrated

Most people do not drink enough water to stay hydrated. Dehydration can lead to headaches, fatigue, rapid heart rate, and a drop in blood pressure. In extreme cases, dehydration can cause confusion, dizziness, fainting, kidney stones, and seizures. Depending on your climate, you may need to drink more than 64 ounces of water daily to stay properly hydrated. Consult with your physician.

Choose Your Meals Wisely

Ultra-processed foods can worsen anxiety and depression symptoms and trigger physical responses, like chronic inflammation. Caring for yourself includes eating nutritious foods to care for the body God gave you. Create a menu of healthy meals before grocery shopping to ensure you have what you need on hand.

Enjoy Green Spaces

There is something about standing in God’s green spaces, listening to nature, and inhaling fresh air. Green spaces have been shown to calm the nervous system. By sitting or strolling in nature, you activate the parasympathetic nervous system, calming the fight-or-flight response. Try to get outdoors more, whether it is to enjoy your morning coffee, during your lunch break, or for an after-dinner stroll.

Make a “Six Most Important Things” To-Do List

Mary Kay Ash, the founder of Mary Kay Cosmetics, had it right. She encouraged her consultants and directors to create a list of the six most important things to do the next day. This list narrowed focus and made it easier to get more done because people didn’t feel pulled in different directions while also keeping the list short. Create your list the night before, and move any tasks you do not complete to the top of the next day’s list.

Calm Your Nervous System

Triggering the parasympathetic nervous system is easier than we give it credit for. Most of us notice when we trigger anxiety, but pursuing calming hobbies and interests can be the catalyst for relaxing our bodies and minds. Consider pursuits like reading, listening to music, fishing, crocheting, or praying.

Serve the Community and Be Social

Serving the community may seem counterintuitive to caring for yourself, but volunteering to meet another’s needs can leave you feeling purposeful. Socializing with others at events, like church, the library, or local gatherings, keeps you from feeling isolated and provides opportunities for connection.

Create a Morning or Evening Basket

Start and end your day on a relaxing note by creating a morning or evening basket or comfort kit. Consider adding items that make you feel good and offer a few minutes of luxury. For example, you could include a bottle of lotion or a tube of hand cream, a novel, a puzzle book, a ball of yarn and a crochet hook, a devotional, or several herbal teas.

Get Help for Negative Thoughts

Negative thoughts have a way of sneaking in when you’re tired, overwhelmed, and stressed. Beat them at their own game by having a reframed mantra. First, identify the negative thought. Next, ask yourself whether this is really true, and flip the script by rewording the negative thought into a positive mantra to repeat aloud to yourself.

Help is Only a Call or Click Away

If chronic stress, overwhelming responsibilities, and worry about the state of the world have you feeling anxious or down, reach out to our office today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor. Your Christian counselor will address you as a whole: physically, mentally, and spiritually. Call or complete the online form today to get started. It is time to care for yourself so you can serve the Lord to the best of your ability.

The post How to Care for Yourself in This Economy appeared first on California Christian Counseling.

item.title: Severe Anxiety: Dealing with Medical Anxiety
item.description:
If you are one of the millions of people who suffer from medical anxiety, you know how crippling it can be. Logically, you may understand that seeking medical attention is the right thing to do to protect your health, but trying to get yourself to actually make and keep an appointment seems threatening and nearly impossible.

The difficult conundrum with medical anxiety is that it operates on an unfortunate and continual loop. When you fear the one thing that can stop the anxiety, it can make you feel not only trapped, but hopeless.

Can you get over medical anxiety? Yes, you can. Just like other fears and anxiety-based behaviors, through therapy and prayer, you can overcome these limitations and live a normal and healthy life. Read on to learn more.

What causes medical anxiety?

While you might be predisposed to anxiety through your biological makeup, most people aren’t born with this fear. It is something that develops after experiencing a medical trauma.

Maybe your beloved mother died of cancer, and now you fear every small anomaly you discover on your body. Or maybe you got an unfavorable diagnosis, and your anxiety has convinced you that every subsequent doctor visit will result in the same terrifying news.

There are a number of ways and reasons someone might develop medical anxiety. Whatever the cause, the resulting consequence is often insufficient healthcare, missed medical appointments, and delayed checkups. This can lead to an unhealthy lifestyle.

What characteristics make up medical anxiety?

Medical anxiety varies in type and severity. Some suffer from illness anxiety disorder (IAD), which is commonly known as medical anxiety or health anxiety. The definition, as given by the National Institutes of Health, is a psychiatric condition characterized by intense, persistent, and excessive fear of having or developing a serious, undiagnosed disease.

Some people have milder cases of medical anxiety and may simply refer to their condition as “white coat syndrome,” meaning they fear things related to doctors or medical facilities.

What does having medical anxiety actually look like? Here are some characteristics you might experience.

You catastrophize

If you have medical anxiety, you will likely assume the worst-case scenario is imminent for all things health-related. That little headache you have can become convincingly similar to a brain tumor. That skin tag, which is a normal part of aging, can look suspiciously close to a cancerous growth through the lens of anxiety. When you live in a constant state of threat, your brain scans for any new or additional information that could be a sign of a bigger threat.

You feel overwhelmed

Another unfortunate element of medical anxiety is the feeling of being overwhelmed. It’s not unusual for people to postpone routine checkups or visits for minor ailments. For those with medical anxiety, those missed appointments happen often and aren’t due to scheduling mishaps.

With every missed appointment, medical conditions can compound. A minor issue can develop into something more serious. When that happens, not only does the need to seek medical attention grow, but the fear of receiving devastating news grows right with it. Even if you want to get back on track with your health goals, seeing the number of appointments you would have to face can make the whole process feel like too much.

Your mind starts to reel as you recall the date of your last dental appointment. You notice your eyeglasses aren’t quite as effective as they used to be, and you don’t even remember the date of your last blood test. You know you should make those appointments, but trying to force yourself to do the thing you fear can feel nearly impossible, and the sheer number of these necessary appointments can feel overwhelming.

You’re preoccupied

When you suffer from medical anxiety, you have a persistent preoccupation or intense focus on having or contracting a serious illness. You may not have any real symptoms that would indicate imminent danger, but your anxiety reacts as if there is an actual risk.

You may try to comfort yourself by doing independent research on symptoms or early warning signs of danger. This information rarely brings peace and might easily trigger an even greater degree of anxiety.

You seek reassurance

Another common pattern in someone with medical anxiety is the constant need for reassurance. You might find yourself asking a spouse, family member, or friend if they think something is wrong with you. You go into painstaking detail about your symptoms, hoping they’ll tell you that you’re okay.

That works for a while. You feel relief, and your fears subside. But that peace is short-lived. Before long, the doubt will resurface, and you will wonder if they’re telling you the truth or if they are even confident in their own answer.

Your behavior changes

Your medical anxiety might not just affect your mind and emotions, but dictate your behavior too. You might excessively check for signs of illness, scanning your body for any anomalies or symptoms. Conversely, you might avoid medical offices and information altogether.

Getting Over Medical Anxiety

There may not be a magic switch that you can flip to suddenly feel fearless, but with slow retraining of your mind and body, you can learn to respond differently to your medical anxiety.

Therapy

One of the most effective ways to overcome this crippling fear is through therapy. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) can help you identify the thought patterns that fuel your anxiety and challenge them with truth. Instead of immediately jumping to worst-case scenarios, you can learn to pause and question those thoughts. You can also learn how to replace them with more realistic and reassuring ones. Eventually, this will weaken anxiety’s power over you.

Exposure therapy is another effective approach to overcoming medical anxiety. While exposure to the thing you fear the most might feel terrifying, you don’t have to force yourself into overwhelming and scary situations all at once. You can learn to take small, manageable steps instead.

Maybe you start by simply looking up a nearby doctor or scheduling an appointment. Even if you later cancel that appointment, you’ve made progress by exposing yourself to the idea of going to the doctor. Maybe you sit in the waiting room of a doctor’s office before you even make an appointment. Exposing yourself to the environment in a non-threatening way and knowing that your name won’t be called can help you build up a tolerance for medical environments.

Each step you take to expose yourself to medical situations can help build confidence. It trains your brain to feel safe, even when the threat feels imminent.

Trusting God

Much of the fear behind medical anxiety stems from a lack of control. You don’t know what’s going on inside your body, and that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But the good news is that God knows.

God created you wonderfully, and He knows every detail about you. While He never promised a life free of difficulty, He does promise His presence even in the face of adversity. When your brain starts to spiral into the “what ifs,” you can center yourself on what is the absolute truth. That God is with you and your life is ultimately in His Hands. Your lack of control doesn’t have to be a deficit, but can be viewed as faith.

Help For Medical Anxiety

If you need help getting past your medical anxiety, schedule an appointment with a Christian therapist. These professionals at this practice can help you overcome this crippling fear that not only affects your mind but can also impact your overall physical health. They can point you back to the all-knowing, all-powerful God who loves you and wants you not to live in this fear any longer.

Resources:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11211185/

item.title: Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy: Re-opening Closed Hearts
item.description:
Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFCT) is a highly effective, evidence-based approach that has become the gold standard for couples therapy. Built on the science of attachment theory, it was developed in the 1980’s by world-renowned psychologist and couples therapist, Dr. Sue Johnson.

Johnson posited that relationship conflicts and arguments are rarely about superficial issues. Instead, they are typically driven by a deep, underlying, often subconscious fear of disconnection, abandonment, or unworthiness.

Loving connection provides the dependable web of intimacy that allows us to cope with life and live life well. – Dr. Sue Johnson

The main focus of EFCT is to help distressed couples break the negative interaction cycles fueling their distress. It does this by addressing the underlying emotional needs and attachment patterns in the relationship, providing insight into why these dynamics exist, and teaching new ways of relating to one another. This is done with the goal of fostering deep emotional healing and the formation of a secure, lasting connection.

How It Works

According to Johnson, the conflict is never about the actual matter a couple is fighting about. Couples experiencing relational distress are struggling with basic attachment issues and unhealed childhood wounds they may not even be aware of. These can include feeling helpless, worthless, unlovable, inadequate, or abandoned.

As these underlying emotions get triggered and stirred up, it causes them to enter defense mode and close their hearts to each other. The signals they send tend to be distorted and misinterpreted. They may resort to anger, for instance, to try and get a response, or shut down to cope with difficult feelings or their partner’s reactions.

Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy is specifically designed to reopen closed hearts. It addresses the emotional disconnect, decodes negative patterns of interaction, and helps partners shift. They move from defensive, guarded positions to vulnerability and reconnection. They learn to reframe their arguments from perceived personal attacks to understandable responses to a sensed lack of emotional safety.

The therapist helps partners uncover the vulnerable emotions that lie deep below the surface. Together, they identify their masked attachment needs and start to understand how their attachment-related fears of loss are affecting their relationship. This helps them begin openly sharing their vulnerabilities with their partner to seek closeness and empathy, and new patterns of interaction are developed.

As they learn to become more empathetic, responsive, and attuned to each other, this leads to greater trust, emotional intimacy, and bonding. These changes foster deeper connection and attachment security.

The Science Behind Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Our relationships are not just emotional experiences. They are deeply rooted physical processes that continuously alter our brain’s wiring.

The need for a safe emotional connection with a loved one we can depend on is biologically wired into our nervous system. It is vital to our survival during infancy and times of crisis, as well as to the maintenance of our physical and mental health.

Functional MRI studies have shown that the presence of a secure loved one has a soothing effect on the nervous system. It calms the threat response and alters its neural activity in a way that fosters emotional safety and connection. Feeling rejected, isolated, or as though you do not matter, on the other hand, has a traumatizing effect.

Relationship distress is a survival-based reaction to the loss of connection. By helping couples identify and express their core emotional vulnerabilities, Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy enables them to rewire maladaptive emotional responses and restructure emotional experiences. Then they can rebuild connection and create a sense of emotional safety and trust.

What to Expect in an Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Session

During an Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy session, the therapist observes the dynamics between you and your partner. They take an active role in helping you identify the hidden vulnerabilities beneath the surface of your behaviors that are contributing to the conflict in your relationship.

A therapist also recognizes the recurring, predictable pattern of your fights in sessions. They help you learn to view this destructive pattern – not your partner – as the enemy, and guide you through new ways of interacting that foster a safe, secure connection.

The Three Stages of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Emotions are the foundation of human relationships. They influence the way we communicate and respond to one another. When our emotions are acknowledged and validated, we feel heard and understood, and our satisfaction with the relationship is enhanced. On the other hand, when partners ignore or dismiss them, it can lead to conflict, disconnection, frustration, resentment, and destructive interactions.

EFCT consists of nine specific steps, divided into three stages, that help guide couples through a process. These steps help them become attuned to subconscious emotions and unmet needs, reprocess their distressed responses, and transform negative patterns of interaction into positive, secure attachment bonds.

Stage 1, De-Escalation (steps 1-4): In this first stage, the therapist lays the groundwork for change by tracking the way you and your partner interact. They help you become aware of your negative patterns of behavior, such as criticizing, attacking, being defensive, withdrawing, or shutting down.

They work to help you understand the deeper emotions and unmet needs that are triggering these behaviors, see how your insecurities and fears are impacting your relationship, and redefine the problem as being the negative cycle you are caught up in rather than blaming each other for it.

Stage 2, Restructuring Emotional Bonds (steps 5-7): This stage is devoted to creating a sense of security and restoring the emotional bond between you and your partner. The therapist guides you through new interactions that promote emotional engagement and move you beyond defensive reactions to more authentic communication.

In this, you learn to be vulnerable with each other, share deep underlying emotions and needs without fear of being judged, respond in supportive, empathetic ways, and engage in constructive dialogues with one another rather than destructive arguments.

Stage 3, Consolidation (steps 8-9): In this last stage, the therapist helps you and your partner integrate what you have learned into your day-to-day interactions and rehearse the skills you have developed to solidify these new patterns. You can practice comforting and connecting rather than disconnecting in the face of challenging emotions.

Specific Techniques Used in Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Trying to change your behaviors without dealing with the unspoken issues that lie beneath the surface of your responses is ineffective, which is why EFCT is not just about better communication. It is about helping you identify and address these underlying emotions and share them with your partner.

The following are examples of the types of techniques used to enhance emotional awareness, facilitate the expression of previously disowned needs and feelings, and encourage deeper connection, empathy, and understanding between partners to create a deeper emotional bond.

Emotionally Focused Conversations: An emotionally focused conversation is a structured dialogue that helps create an environment of empathy and compassion in which each partner is encouraged to discuss his or her thoughts and feelings without being interrupted.

Hold-Me-Tight Conversations: A hold-me-tight conversation is a guided dialogue that encourages partners to be vulnerable and share their deepest fears and needs, and talk through how they each hear the revelation. It aims to slow down the negative interactions and help the couple become more empathetic, emotionally responsive, and engaged with one another, transforming relational distress into emotional connection.

Reflection and Validation: Reflection and validation are techniques used to help couples recognize and articulate their needs and feelings by deepening their self-awareness and helping them recognize and process their hidden emotions.

Using empathic supposition, the therapist mirrors their words back to them in a clearer, more detailed way. They highlight core meanings or name emotions to help them see perspectives they may have missed, validate their experience, and reinforce its importance in the relationship.

Attachment-Focused Interventions: In attachment-focused interventions, the therapist helps partners recognize their attachment style and how it is influencing their interactions. They gain insight into their emotional responses and learn to navigate relational challenges in a healthier, more effective way.

Enactments: Enactments are role-playing exercises that help couples practice the new communication skills they have learned in a supportive, non-judgmental environment under the guidance of the therapist.

Are you interested in learning more?

If the information in this article resonates with you, and you would like to set up a risk-free appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors at our location, please give us a call.

References:

item.title: Perfectionism and Anxiety: Is Pride Just Insecurity in Disguise?
item.description:
Some of the most prideful people are often the most insecure. There’s a common misconception that prideful people are bold, arrogant, and think quite highly of themselves. Of course, this is true in many cases, but it may not be typical.

More often, pride comes out of insecurity. Pride manifests in the places where people are the most unsure of themselves or are the most afraid of being exposed. Pride really shines in those fragile parts of their lives where they’re the most desperate for approval.

Pride and insecurity might look like opposites on the surface, but if you dig deep enough, you’ll find that they often share the same root. Someone who is insecure will often try to prove that they are worthy. Outwardly, this looks like confidence, but it’s actually more of a defense mechanism.

Insecure Pride as a Defense

Pride can be difficult to spot sometimes because it wears a lot of different masks. One of those masks is defensiveness. In the real world, this might look like someone’s need to win every argument or to be looked upon as the smart one in the friend group. It could also manifest as a refusal to apologize or to admit weakness. Sometimes it even shows itself as perfectionism and anxiety.

Someone who appears prideful might actually feel inadequate, and they might become highly critical of others. If they can’t measure up to the accomplishments of someone else, they might criticize and try to bring that person down to their level.

Prideful people also have a difficult time apologizing or admitting their own mistakes. They might cover up their failings or try to project them onto someone else. This can manifest as phrases such as “You made me do it” or “If you hadn’t done that, I wouldn’t have done this.” Prideful people rarely take responsibility for their own failures because they don’t want to add another mistake to what they believe is an already lengthy list of their flaws.

As destructive as they are, prideful behaviors are sometimes praised and admired because they can look quite attractive. They might look like confidence to the world, a trait often praised in our society. This praise reinforces the behavior because it also feeds the person’s ego. This creates a cycle of behavior. But when you look a little deeper, under the fake confidence, you will likely see that these behaviors are protecting fragile self-esteem.

The Cycle of Pride

When someone fears being rejected, they might present themselves as superior in an attempt to convince themselves and their audience of their worth. Because they don’t believe they can meet someone else’s standard, they puff themselves up, trying to appear better than others.

Pride and insecurity are both part of a larger cycle. Insecurity creates a fear of exposure. Protective pride in the form of arrogance or perfectionism creates a temporary ego boost, which pressures you to maintain this false mask. And the knowledge that you’re falsely elevating yourself or are inauthentically being propped up by others creates even deeper insecurity.

Pride in the Bible

The Bible has quite a lot to say about pride. Scripture consistently warns that pride can lead to a destructive path. Proverbs 16 tells us plainly that “Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18, NIV)

What does pride mean in this context? In this passage, pride does not refer to confidence or feeling good about yourself. Feeling confident in the creation God made you to be is not a detriment, but a goal. Biblically speaking, pride refers to an inflated view of oneself that pushes God and others out of their proper place. It is a posture of the heart that believes it’s better than anyone and doesn’t need correction.

The Hebrew word used here in Proverbs for pride is gaon. At its core, it means height or majesty. When used negatively, as it is in this context, it refers to an inflated view of oneself that pushes God and others out of their proper place. It’s the idea of rising above others in a falsely elevated way.

This can happen through arrogance, prideful elevation of oneself, self-exaltation, or a sense of superiority. Proverbs 16:18, in the original text, also uses a related idea, ruach gavoah, which means a high or lofty spirit. Together, these terms paint a picture of someone who has lifted themselves to appear more important than they actually are.

Having pride has become a badge of honor in modern culture. Biblically, elevation belongs to God, not us. By puffing up (gaon), we create an attitude that eventually causes the fall that Proverbs warns about.

Scripture also helps us understand that pride can hide insecurity. In Luke 18, Jesus tells a story about two men who went to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee, a man who would have been respected in his day for his religious devotion. The other was a tax collector, someone whom most of his contemporaries would have called corrupt.

The Pharisee prayed confidently: “‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people, robbers, evildoers, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.’” (Luke 18:11-12, NIV)

The tax collector took an opposite posture. Scripture says he stood at a distance and wouldn’t even look up to heaven. He didn’t have a long and eloquent prayer, but simply said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, NIV)

The result might surprise you. The tax collector, not the prideful Pharisee, went home justified before God (Luke 18:14) because the tax collector was honest. He wasn’t comparing himself to anyone or trying to prove his worth. He simply admitted his need while the Pharisee was busy defending his own worth.

Pride Is Exhausting

Maintaining an image, like the Pharisee in our example, takes a lot of effort. If your identity depends on appearing strong, capable, or morally superior, then you are constantly attempting to manage how others see you.

Every interaction or conversation, the ones most people don’t give much thought to, becomes heavily important when you are protecting your curated image. Constructive criticism is viewed as an attack, and every mistake is seen as an enemy. That responsibility can be downright exhausting.

God Is Our Peace

What brings peace and can quiet those insecurities and squelch that pride?

Humility is often misunderstood. Many people assume that humility is thinking poorly of yourself. But that’s not biblical humility at all. Humility is simply seeing yourself accurately. It is the ability to recognize your strengths without exaggerating, as well as your weaknesses without cover-up. This accurate self-assessment actually creates emotional freedom.

Humility recognizes grace. When you can admit your frailties, limitations, and mistakes, you leave room for God’s forgiveness and grace. Your IQ, test score, paycheck, or social media presence isn’t going to ever be good enough to get you to Heaven.

“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith – and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God –  not by works, so that no one can boast.” (Ephesians 2:8-9, NIV) That realization alone can be humbling and remove the need for pride.

Therapy Can Help

Many prideful behaviors stem from old insecurities. Maybe the mistakes you made as a child were harshly criticized or constantly compared to others. Pride then can become a shield or a way to compensate for that lingering sense of inadequacy.

Therapy can help you trace your prideful behaviors back to their roots. When you stop trying to maintain a perfect image, you open yourself up to growth. You can finally deal with the underlying issues. When you do this, something beautiful and authentic happens.

You will begin to feel safe enough to acknowledge your own limitations, fears, or weaknesses. You will find a place of humility. And with this self-actualization, the need for pride and the perfectionism and anxiety that often come with it will start to fade, leaving room for the awesome work God wants to do in you.

If you need help addressing issues of insecurity or pride, call our offices and make an appointment. Specially trained therapists can help you grow in your humility and embrace the grace of a God who does not require perfection.

Resources:
https://biblehub.com/lexicon/proverbs/16-18.htm
https://enduringword.com/Bible-commentary/luke-18/

The post Perfectionism and Anxiety: Is Pride Just Insecurity in Disguise? appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Why Traditional Therapies Don’t Always Help Adults with Borderline Autism
item.description:
Have you always felt like there’s something a little different about you, but not different enough for you to know exactly what makes you different? Maybe you’ve done a good job keeping up with the world around you, even though most times you have a harder time fitting in than others.

Maybe you’ve been working hard all your life, socializing, and checking all the boxes, but it still feels like things take more effort than they should. Like social situations leave you completely drained, or unexpected noises, change, or confusion throw you off for hours or even days.

You might have even heard that there’s something called borderline autism in adults, without understanding what it is. This condition is not an official diagnosis, but it does describe real experiences people, much like you, experience every day. People in this group show some traits of autism, but not all, and because of that, traditional therapy may not always be the help you need.

Let’s break down why that happens and what can actually help.

What Borderline Autism in Adults Feels Like

Borderline Autism in Adults exists in a grey area between neurotypical functioning and a clear autism diagnosis. You may not have the signs or mirror the typical idea of someone with autism. In school, you probably did just fine, and socially, you also learned how to copy the behavior of people around you over the years, smiling when you’re supposed to, making small talk, and blending in.

However, after all these years, these seemingly simple social actions have felt harder for you than they look from the outside. Many adults with borderline autism have spent years feeling different without knowing why, having to force themselves to act neurotypical. Unfortunately, these efforts come at a huge cost, causing stress, exhaustion, and identity confusion.

You might not have had a diagnosis growing up, and no one saw what was going on because you didn’t act out. You stayed quiet and always followed the rules. As an adult, you may have been told you have anxiety, ADHD, or depression, and while that may explain some parts, it probably doesn’t explain all of it.

Small Signs That You’re Living with Borderline Autism

There are signs, however, that can help you identify what living with borderline autism might look like. Some of them are:

  • You struggle to follow conversations, especially in groups.
  • You feel uncomfortable in noisy places or crowded rooms.
  • You have a strong need for structure or routine.
  • You stay deeply focused on a specific topic or interest once you’ve started.
  • You deal with big mood swings or getting emotionally stuck over small things.

If you’ve tried therapy before and always left feeling like it didn’t really help, you’re not imagining things. Most mental health approaches are built around standard diagnoses and don’t always work for people with borderline conditions, especially with autism.

This is because traditional therapy usually focuses on fixing you. A lot of therapy is designed to change how you act so you’ll fit in better. Yet if you’re already good at masking, or pretending to be fine when you’re not, this just adds unnecessary pressure. You don’t need fixing, but rather you need support that helps you understand yourself.

Additionally, most social skills training feels unnatural. Some programs teach step-by-step responses for social situations. That might help in a textbook way, but real-life conversations aren’t scripts. If you’ve ever left a conversation feeling like you missed something, even when you said the right things, this might be why.

Likewise, medication isn’t always helpful. Doctors might give you medication for anxiety or mood swings. While that may help with some things, it doesn’t deal with your deeper issues like sensitivity to light, noise, or how exhausting everyday social stuff feels.

Therapies designed for more severe autism cases do not always adapt well to adults with borderline traits. That’s because some of these approaches do not fit the life experiences you deal with daily.

What Life Feels Like Day to Day if You Have Borderline Autism

Borderline autism can leave you socially exhausted. Even a short chat can leave you mentally wiped out. Small talk feels confusing, and group conversations move too fast. You might replay things in your head for hours afterward, trying to figure out what people meant or if you said something wrong.

It can also come with sensory issues. Certain sounds, lights, or fabrics bother you more than they seem to bother others. Maybe just a simple flicker of fluorescent lights, a tag in your clothes, or too many people talking at once can throw you off. These things are hard to explain but easy to feel.

There could also be significant mood crashes. Something small, like an unexpected change in plans or a misunderstanding, can throw your whole day off. You might not always know why you’re feeling down over something others seem to be ok with, but just know it happens.

You probably have one or two things you’re really into. Not in a casual way, but in a way that brings you comfort, focus, or joy. Other people might tell you you’re too into it or not get why you get so focused on it once you start, but it matters to you.

You might be great at your job but still feel unsure when it comes to things others seem to naturally understand, like office politics, vague feedback, or unsaid rules. It’s not that you’re bad at your job; you’re just working twice as hard to understand what others seem to pick up without thinking.

If standard therapy hasn’t worked for you, don’t give up. There are other ways to get support, ways that meet you where you are, not where someone thinks you should be.

Some Therapies That May Help

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy helps you understand and work through unhelpful thoughts, like beating yourself up after social interactions or feeling like a failure when you’re just overstimulated.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy teaches skills for handling big emotions, staying calm during stress, and setting healthy boundaries. It’s especially useful if your emotions feel intense or fast-changing.

Sensory Support involves working with a therapist who understands sensory sensitivities. They can help you slowly build comfort with difficult things, like certain textures or sounds, without pressure.

Creative Therapies include art or music therapy, which give you a way to express yourself without needing to explain everything with words. It can be a break from masking and a way to let your real self breathe.

Occupational Therapy isn’t just for physical rehab; it’s also for creating routines that work with your brain, not against it. It can help with organizing your day, managing time, and building habits that lower stress.

Routine and Adaptive Planning build structure, which is comforting to you. Life isn’t always predictable. Therapy that helps you build routines and also handle change can make a huge difference.

Support for Deep Focus helps you reimagine your ability to hyperfocus. Instead of seeing your intense interests as a problem, some therapists and coaches will help you use them to reach goals, whether that’s through a career, hobby, or creative project.

Support Groups create community with others who also live the same challenges. You don’t have to explain every detail; they just get it, and that alone can lift a huge weight off your shoulders.

You deserve support that fits you, so if other solutions haven’t worked yet for you, it doesn’t mean you’re the problem. It just means you haven’t found the right kind of support yet.

You don’t have to keep pushing through life feeling misunderstood, worn out, or like you’re faking your way through every day. The right help is out there; help that makes sense for how you actually experience the world.

If any part of this sounds familiar, it’s worth talking to someone who can help you find relief. Contact our office today to make an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our association.

item.title: The Trauma of Aging: Where to Find Support
item.description:
Is “trauma” too big a word for this situation? Aging isn’t a dramatic event with alarms, flashing lights, and a solitary life-changing moment. Yet, the evidence of aging in your own life and body can hit harder than you would ever expect. You knew you’d grow old, or at least you hoped you would. But you never knew what aging would actually feel like.

Saying that aging is trauma may not be clinically precise, yet it is emotionally true. Aging is not the trauma of tragedy or catastrophe. It’s natural, normal, and can be anticipated. But those small cumulative losses of independence, stamina, and your youthful good looks can chip away at the self-worth you’ve tried hard to build and maintain.

It feels like trauma

Aging, while natural, can be experienced like a traumatic event for some people. Aging, of course, does not happen in a single moment, but it can still make you feel as if you’ve experienced trauma. It deals with loss, grief, accumulated stress, and unrelenting reminders of your own mortality.

That ongoing exposure to loss and change can feel trauma-like, especially if it triggers anxiety, depression, panic, or reactivates previous trauma such as illness, neglect, abuse, or medical trauma. And it’s more prevalent in cultures that don’t value the aging process, as we see in the modern Western world.

Some therapists might label this as an existential trauma or cumulative trauma rather than a single event. But in strict clinical terms, aging itself is not classified as trauma in the same way that PTSD is defined. True trauma involves a singular or series of traumatic events that involve a threat to life or safety.

But, and this is a big but, your emotions can still feel similar to actual trauma from age-related events. True trauma is often associated with aging, such as medical procedures, loss of a spouse, chronic pain, or serious illness.

This means that aging, while not the singular trauma itself, is often the context in which true trauma can happen. And the process of aging can evoke emotions often associated with trauma because of your personal sense of loss.

I miss my strength and independence

Aging comes with a lot of changes, but these changes aren’t always obvious at first. The gradual loss of strength and stamina can truly alter how you interact with the world around you. What used to come easy, like a long walk or lifting heavy objects, suddenly requires more effort and even forethought. And for many, especially those who value their independence or are known for their physical strength, this is the most difficult age-related adjustment to accept.

But God doesn’t value you for what you can do, what you can lift, or how fast you can do it. In fact, having your own abilities stripped away can also strip away pride. When you can do all things by yourself, you no longer have to rely on God or others. “Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to Him, and He will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5-6, NIV).

Aging forces you to confront the truth about your body and its limited strength. “Leaning on God” does not just include your own “understanding” but your practical daily needs as well.

This mind shift can push you away from the feelings of loss toward surrendering your own pride. It can teach you gratitude as you learn to rely on family, friends, and community, and yes, to trust God to provide all these things for you. It also teaches patience, as you cannot always take care of your own needs in an instant. It might also teach you empathy for other people in your situation or push you toward asking for forgiveness for past impatient behavior.

I miss my village

With time comes seasons. And seasons change. As you age, not only do you have to deal with your own age-related issues, but you are affected by the changing seasons in others’ lives as well.

Spouses, family members, and lifelong friends pass away. People move after they retire. Adult children become increasingly independent, and you become acutely aware of the shifting dynamics.

You might suddenly feel out of place in a culture that is hyper-fixated on youth. You can no longer relate to the newest trends, and you don’t quite understand all the jokes that everyone else seems to find amusing.

But these circumstances, while they might feel lonely in the moment, are also reminders of the consistency and faithfulness of our never-changing God. The God you knew in your youth, He’s the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8, NIV). And even if you haven’t known God for long, you can be assured that He will never leave you or forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

I Miss My Good Looks

The world is obsessed with youth. Models in magazines have flawless skin and near-perfect physiques. The beauty industry is a multi-billion-dollar business built on the shallow fact that people crave beauty, from themselves and those around them.

So, when you look in the mirror and discover a new gray hair or a wrinkle that has gotten a bit deeper, the emotional impact you feel might feel can hit harder than you know it should.

You know that vanity isn’t a virtue you should be aspiring toward. You probably don’t even want to admit it because it seems so shallow. Yet it can shape how you see yourself and how worthy you feel of love, attention, and belonging.

And when you notice the physical changes in your appearance, it can not only undermine your self-esteem but can be a reminder of the loss of youth, and worse, the progression of aging.

But if you stop and ponder the Word of God, you will realize that maybe you shouldn’t have relied on your looks at all. Maybe this aging process actually weeds out a part of your being that shouldn’t have been there in the first place. That same God is using this process to refine you. Even those gray hairs are tools to draw you closer to the Almighty.

In that way, your focus shifts from what is being taken away from you to what is being revealed and rewarded. 1 Peter 3:3-4 says, “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles and the wearing of gold jewelry or fine clothes. Rather, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit which is of great worth in God’s sight” (NIV).

Not only does your aging body help you focus more on what is truly important, your inner self, but it is in itself a reward. “Gray hair is a crown of splendor. It is attained by a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31, NIV).

Therapy

By the time you hit your golden years, you might think that you have everything figured out. You know how to manage your stress reasonably well. You’ve had trauma in your life and survived. But the scars you carry and that underlying, unresolved trauma can cause you to feel anxious, hypervigilant, or angry.

Even if you don’t feel the effects of past trauma, you will likely face new traumas as you age. Medical issues for you and your spouse, transitions such as retirement, moving into elderly care homes, or dealing with other age-related traumas exist.

Christian therapy can help you through these mental and emotional issues and transitions. It can help you understand your body, celebrate your life, and give you hope for a peaceful future. It can help you face your own mortality with acceptance and remove the fear and anxiety surrounding death.

If you’re struggling in the aging process, know that there’s help available to you. At Spokane Christian Counseling, we are here to assist you in overcoming your age-related fear, trauma, and anxiety. Contact our reception team today to help you live more peaceful tomorrows.

The post The Trauma of Aging: Where to Find Support appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: Why the Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women Are Missed During Major Life Changes
item.description:
When people think of bipolar disorder, they imagine mostly crazy mood swings, risky decisions, or extreme behavior. That’s true in many cases, but for many women, the signs can be harder to recognize, especially during big life changes.

The signs of bipolar disorder in women blend into the background of everyday stress, hormonal shifts, responsibilities, and the pressure to keep everything going. This is why mental health challenges like this go unnoticed, particularly during times like pregnancy, postpartum, menopause, or even during job changes or caregiving responsibilities.

Let’s look at why this happens, how it may happen, and what to do when it doesn’t feel quite right to check if bipolar disorder might be a factor.

Why Life Changes Make Things Less Clear

Throughout their lives, women go through major physical and emotional changes. These times naturally bring mood shifts, exhaustion, and irritability. Feeling tired, anxious, or emotionally sensitive after having a baby? That’s normal. Feeling irritable and foggy during menopause? Also normal.

But sometimes, these feelings are more intense than expected, or they come with bursts of energy, racing thoughts, or unexpected behavior.

That’s where things get confusing. Some signs of bipolar disorder in women are quite similar to normal hormonal changes, and they’re often brushed off. A woman might be told she’s just overwhelmed or going through a phase. And while those things may be true, they don’t explain everything.

Think about these examples:

  • A woman who just had a baby hasn’t slept in days. Suddenly, she feels full of energy in the middle of the night and starts reorganizing the house. A few days later, she crashes into sadness she can’t explain. This could actually be more than postpartum blues.
  • Another woman in her late forties starts feeling detached and flat. Then, out of nowhere, she feels jumpy, irritated, and full of restless energy. She may be experiencing a mixed episode.
  • Or a woman with a demanding career goes through phases where she works nonstop, filled with ideas and confidence, only to retreat completely the next week, feeling like she can’t get out of bed. She might be showing real signs of hypomania and depression.

In each case, the emotional ups and downs are real. But so is the possibility of bipolar disorder. And when the two collide, it’s easy to miss what’s really going on.

Why Functional Women Are Overlooked

One of the biggest reasons bipolar disorder goes unnoticed in women is that many of them are still functioning. They’re going to work, caring for kids, managing households, and caring for others. They may even seem more productive than usual during hypomanic phases. When they crash into depression, it’s chalked up to burnout or stress.

Just because someone is still getting things done doesn’t mean they’re feeling okay or mentally well. A few signs that are sometimes ignored in women who seem to be functioning well:

  • Feeling extremely motivated or wired for days, followed by a stretch of low energy or sadness
  • Making decisions on impulse, like sudden purchases, trips, or even quitting a job
  • Talking faster than usual or jumping from one idea to the next
  • Being emotionally sensitive or reactive, without a clear reason
  • Experiencing deep sadness that doesn’t respond to typical coping strategies
  • Having trouble sleeping during energetic phases and oversleeping during low ones

Many of these patterns can be subtle. They don’t always disrupt a woman’s ability to function, but they do affect her relationships, her sense of self, and her long-term mental health.

When Self-Doubt Gets in the Way

Many women live with their symptoms for years without seeking help, not because they’re fine, but because they second-guess themselves. They wonder if they’re just being too emotional, too dramatic, or not strong enough. They blame themselves for not keeping it together or for needing rest when others seem to manage just fine.

This self-doubt is one of the reasons the signs of bipolar disorder in women go unnoticed. Instead of speaking up, women push through. They adjust to the highs and lows, explain them away, and hope things will even out eventually. Some even feel guilty for bringing it up, especially if they’ve already been told it’s just stress or just hormones.

But guilt isn’t a diagnosis, and doubting yourself doesn’t mean you’re imagining things. You know when something feels off. Trusting that feeling is not weakness, it’s wisdom. Being open about your experience doesn’t make you difficult or dramatic. It makes you honest. And honesty is the first step toward support and answers.

In some cases, the signs of bipolar disorder in women are less obvious. They’re woven into personality, habits, or even coping strategies. If you’re wondering whether bipolar disorder might be part of your story, or someone else’s, there are a few less conventional clues to consider.

Other Clues That Don’t Always Get Noticed

  • You’ve been treated for anxiety or depression, but it doesn’t seem to fully explain what you feel. Maybe the medication helps a little, but not enough. Or maybe you’ve always felt like something’s missing from the diagnosis.
  • You feel like there are two versions of yourself. One is full of energy and ideas, the other is tired and disconnected. You swing between them, but you don’t know why.
  • Your moods seem tied to your cycle, seasons, or stress, but the emotional swings feel too strong to be typical. You feel like you’re on a rollercoaster you didn’t sign up for.
  • People say you’re intense or moody, but you’ve always felt like you’re just trying to keep it together. You may have learned to mask your symptoms or push through them, but that doesn’t mean they’re not affecting you.
  • You’ve done things on impulse, like spending sprees or sudden changes, that felt exciting in the moment but later left you confused or regretful.

All of these aren’t things everyone thinks of when they hear bipolar disorder, yet they’re part of what many women experience when living with it. This is especially true for bipolar II or mixed episodes, which are more common in women and harder to recognize.

If any of this sounds familiar, it’s worth exploring further. Bipolar disorder is treatable, but only if it’s properly diagnosed. Many women spend years being treated for depression or anxiety without realizing there’s a deeper pattern underneath it all. And because the signs of bipolar disorder in women aren’t that easy to pick out, it’s important to advocate for yourself, or for someone you love.

What You Can Do Next

  • Start keeping track of your moods, energy levels, and sleep. Even short notes can help spot patterns.
  • Don’t ignore symptoms just because you’re keeping up with daily life. Mental wellness isn’t only about functioning; it’s also about feeling like yourself.
  • Find a mental health professional who understands the signs of bipolar disorder in women.
  • Ask about things like bipolar II or rapid cycling. These are more common in women. They are more subtle but still serious.

If what you’ve read here feels familiar, don’t ignore it. The signs of bipolar disorder in women are real, even if they’ve been misunderstood or overlooked in your life until now. You don’t have to figure this out by yourself, and you don’t have to wait until things get worse to reach out.

Talking to someone who understands women’s mental health, especially during life changes like postpartum, menopause, or times of high stress, can bring a sense of clarity that’s been missing for years. The right support can help you make sense of your moods, your energy, and the parts of yourself that feel unpredictable or exhausting.

You can speak with a licensed Christian counselor who truly listens and understands what you’re facing. Call one of the numbers on your screen or browse the counselors listed on this site to find someone who fits your needs. Whether you’re ready to book a session today or just want to ask a few questions first, someone is here to help.
