item.title: How to Keep Your Children from Inheriting Your Trauma
item.description:
Most parents want to give their kids the world, not their trauma. They want to make their life easier, surprise them with much-desired gifts, and set them up for a comfortable and secure future. They want to make sure that their legacy lives on in the lives of their offspring, even after they’re gone. They think about homes, heirlooms, and savings accounts that they’ll someday pass down, assuring their children will get what is rightfully theirs.

This likely sounds like a great undertaking. If we get everything right with no unpredictable events, life will go well for our children. In the real world, this is not possible. Jesus assures us, “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Not everything parents pass down fits into a box or a bank account. In all that focus on giving their kids the best, many parents forget something more important. Parents fail to protect their children from experiencing things like their unresolved pain, old wounds, unhealthy patterns, and harmful parenting practices that are excused because it’s how the parent was raised.

As noble as it is to set your children up for a successful future by giving them monetary gifts, it’s more important to be mindful and self-aware of the internal emotions or activators that cause the parent(s) to react vs. respond to a challenge or struggle. Not passing along negative and detrimental behaviors is critical to decreasing the growth of generational wounds, which decrease the quality of life within the family unit. When parents live in the aftermath of trauma, it changes the way they see the world and how they interact with their children. Poor self-awareness of internal negative thoughts and emotional responses can lead to poor judgment, harming the children, and inadvertently creating trauma for the kids.

Being Raised in the Aftermath of Trauma

Realistically, we can’t eliminate big trauma-inducing events from our lives. You will inevitably face big life moments during your children’s formative years. Death of a loved one, financial struggles, marital issues, health scares, and other difficult moments are bound to happen.

Matthew 5:45 tells us that rain will fall on both the just and the unjust, meaning that no matter how good a person you are, you will face hardships because you’re human and because we are living in a fallen world.

God never promised that He’d remove major obstacles, just that He’d help us walk through and overcome them. As scary and tense as these events might be, they’re not actually what will mentally and emotionally wound your children. What will cause long-lasting negative consequences is your inability to recognize when you are reacting to these traumas.

Trauma, left unprocessed and unhealed, has a way of shaping the way you react vs. respond to stress. Without deliberate and conscious effort, that response is likely to be unhealthy. Stress and trauma aftermath have a way of chipping away at your patience and creating unreasonable fears that can creep into every aspect of your life. Unfortunately, that includes your parenting.

How Trauma Transfers

Children, whether they’re toddlers or teens, look to you as their guidepost and compass. They watch you. They study how you react or respond, and how you cope. And in those moments of crisis when you feel overwhelmed and ready to fall apart, they’re watching.

When you don’t even realize that you’re teaching, you’re showing them how to speak to themselves and how to respond to others, even those who’ve been hostile toward them. You’re showing them how to handle difficult moments, and without even realizing it, they will begin to mirror these actions.

You can also inadvertently transfer your pain and woundedness directly, not just by your example of self-regulation, but by how you treat them during a crisis. Beyond just watching and learning from your example, you’re also molding your child(ren) through your actions.

It’s great if you have composure amid adversity, but sometimes that strength can also make you behave in ways that appear hostile or emotionally unavailable. While you might be handling the crisis itself like a boss, the stress of the situation may appear in more subtle ways. Your tone with them might become sharper or your patience short. You might unconsciously emotionally shut down or place unreasonable expectations on your child.

Though they may seem unrelated and relatively small compared to the big crisis you’re juggling, these subtle but toxic moments can leave a lasting imprint on your child, which may even injure your relationship with them.

How To Interrupt the Transfer

No parent intends to traumatize their child/children. You don’t want to transfer your past or present woundedness to your child, but how do you prevent it? You’ve taken the first step in preventing it by reading this article. By recognizing that trauma can transfer to your child, you are making steps toward preventing it.

How exactly it is transferring may be a little more difficult to decipher because trauma doesn’t always manifest in obvious ways. Yelling or complete emotional withdrawal are easier to identify and control, but subtle trauma responses are often just as damaging.

They show up in patterns such as emotional dysregulation, constant tension, overprotectiveness, emotional unavailability, or inadvertently placing your fears and insecurities onto your child. Children are incredibly perceptive and sense stress incredibly well. They often internalize it even when they don’t verbalize it. Young children are not equipped with the emotional vocabulary to verbalize their feelings, nor are some adults.

To interrupt trauma transfer, ask yourself if you’re reacting out of fear, unresolved anger, grief, or another pain in your past. Am I projecting my anxieties, fears, or overthinking onto my child?

Research shows that children of parents who’ve experienced significant unresolved woundedness, anger, resentment, bitterness, and trauma memories are two to three times more likely to develop anxiety, depression, or PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder). Chronic parental stress can also affect a child’s emotional regulation, alter stress hormone levels, and increase vulnerability to mental health challenges.

The good news is that by recognizing your unresolved trauma responses and identifying negative behavioral patterns in yourself, you can actively work on processing your trauma properly.

Therapy

While you can do some of the work yourself, in trying to identify your negative behavioral patterns and what is triggering (activating) them, it’s wise to employ the help of a professional Christian therapist. In therapy, you can work on resolving your own trauma or the ones that you’ve inherited. You can learn to identify how to become more self-aware of your internal struggles in your thoughts, emotions, and what your body is holding and where it holds it. Identify where you hold anger, anxiety, and bitterness in your body. Seek to grow in self-awareness regarding the responses you’re exhibiting that could be impacting your children.

With the help and guidance of a professional therapist, you can then deal with it. And you can also develop healthier coping mechanisms with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and trauma-focused therapy. You can invite God into the equation, too. Your therapist can point out Scriptures and use biblical principles that can help you interrupt negative and destructive patterns.

By recognizing your responses, the behavior you exhibit in front of your children, and your triggers (those things that cause those behaviors), you can respond intentionally rather than react impulsively. Consistently applying coping strategies will help you break from harmful patterns and give you the skills to create newer, healthier, and more productive ones. You can experience a healthier YOU, a healthier family, more peace and joy, and tools to improve the legacy of your family.

The benefits go way beyond you living a better life. In doing the work now to heal, you are creating a more emotionally safe environment for your children, ensuring they inherit the family heirlooms, not trauma.

God and Trauma

Maybe you inherited old pain and old patterns from long-ago trauma. Maybe you’re still haunted by choices made long before you were born. The Bible doesn’t ignore the fact that trauma can pass from generation to generation. In Exodus 20, God warns of the consequences of sin and brokenness. While they can and often do ripple through families, He promises redemption and healing to those who turn to Him.

This means that while a legacy of pain can affect you, you can heal from it. It also means that it doesn’t have to affect your children and their children. Just as you want to pass down homes, heirlooms, and savings to your children, you also have the power to pass along faith, wisdom, and emotional health.

When you address your own woundedness and lean on God for guidance, you ensure that what you leave behind is a healthy legacy of restoration, redeeming and refreshing the soul. With God, you can create a firm foundation for generations to come.

Learn how to break free from unresolved woundedness and pain through Christian counseling. Contact our reception team today to learn more.

item.title: The Real Reason You Constantly Feel Guilty
item.description:
Some people go through their entire lives feeling guilty, without ever feeling as if they can atone for their mistakes or be fully forgiven and accepted. Guilt can be a helpful response to something. When you make a mistake, your moral compass tries to steer you back to your values with a sense of guilt and shame. Usually, these emotions are resolved when you make things right.

When guilt and shame persist for years, that’s a sign that something is stuck. Guilt that persists for years and decades, however, is not a prolonged attack of conscience. Feelings of constant guilt are your body’s default way of trying to keep you safe. You can resolve persistent guilt, but it will require you to be vulnerable with someone.

Your Conscience as Your Guide

To understand why you constantly feel guilty, you must understand what appropriate guilt looks and feels like, and then compare it with your experience of feeling guilty. Appropriate guilt doesn’t persist for years or decades. It is an immediate cognitive response that acts as a motivator to change the situation, and usually it is clearly connected with wrongdoing.

Let’s say that there is a coworker whom you dislike. One day, you are talking about this coworker with another friend at work, saying unkind things about them and laughing cruelly. You discover that they have walked into the room behind you and have heard you mocking them. Even though you dislike them, you will still likely feel terrible about having been caught in the act of being mean about them.

In a scenario like this, guilt is a response to being caught behaving badly. It is appropriate and will likely motivate you to apologize and perhaps even amend your working relationship with this person.

Appropriate guilt is a logical response to wrongdoing. Once you have done the work to resolve the issue and make amends, that guilty feeling should subside and make way for other emotions like relief, gratitude, and determination to avoid further wrongdoing. In this way, it’s a helpful emotion. What happens when you can’t stop feeling guilty, though?

A Frozen Nervous System

You can’t think yourself out of feeling guilty, and positive affirmations can’t make you feel better. This is because persistent guilt is not an emotion you need to process, nor is it a thought you need to challenge. Constant guilt is a sign that you don’t feel emotionally safe.

In the example of being caught gossiping about your coworker, you had a physical response to being caught in the middle of wrongdoing. In that moment, you were suddenly unsafe because one of your flaws was exposed. That might have affected your reputation in the workplace, your friend’s reputation, or even your job itself. Guilt motivated you to take action by apologizing, so that you could feel safe again.

Persistent guilt and shame often stem from childhood experiences of constantly being criticized, and it is often attached to conditions like OCD, trauma, depression, and perfectionism. It might be stored in your mind as memories or a harsh inner voice constantly criticizing you. It cannot be resolved in your thoughts alone. Persistent guilt is stored in your body, and the only way it can be resolved is to feel safe, seen, accepted, understood, and loved.

The Fig Leaf

In the book of Genesis, we are told that Adam and Eve’s first actions after eating the forbidden fruit were to make fig leaf coverings to hide their nakedness. After that, they hid when God came looking for them. Guilt always combines with shame. This causes us to cover up and hide ourselves away from connection and relationships, especially with those who know us best.

Covering up or isolating yourself will not help. This is not how we feel safe. If anything, isolating yourself will make you feel less safe as you cut off your much-needed emotional support.

You might constantly feel guilty because you were told throughout childhood that there was something flawed about you. Your parents might have been your first bullies, and you have been covering up your authentic self for decades. When you mask important parts of yourself like this, others can’t see you, accept you, or validate you.

You might feel guilty because you do not allow yourself to be seen by others. The only way you will stop feeling guilty all the time is when you are exposed and vulnerable to someone. You need to allow them to validate and love you for being exactly who you are.

Your nervous system will only come out of panic mode, and your guilt will only be resolved, when you can be vulnerable with someone who remains steady and shows you complete acceptance. Only then will you be able to drop your defenses and pretenses, stop performing or trying to earn love, and accept your flaws.

When this happens, your nervous system learns that it is possible to feel safe, possibly for the first time. You’re not perfect; you will make mistakes in the future, but you don’t have to be perfect to be seen, accepted, and loved. This is what safety feels like.

Signs You’re Moving Away from Constantly Feeling Guilty

When you feel safe, you don’t have to continue monitoring yourself, masking your behavior, or keeping your opinions to yourself. You can express your thoughts and state your preferences. You don’t have to hide behind a carefully constructed mask of politeness and peacekeeping. It’s not about acting out-of-character; this is you being your authentic self.

One of the signs that you are resolving your guilt is that you stop apologizing. Before, you were likely apologizing for everything, even when you were doing nothing wrong. When you’re not feeling guilty all the time, you will stop apologizing as if everything is always your fault.

On the other hand, without persistent guilt, you can take accountability for your mistakes and own up to your failures. Sometimes, persistent guilt causes you to cover up your mistakes or gaslight your way out of issues. When you can feel appropriate guilt for your wrongs, you can make amends whenever necessary, without your feelings getting overwhelmed by the incident.

Most importantly, you will know that you have left persistent guilt behind when that harsh inner critic is finally silenced. Perhaps it was an echo of your mother or father’s voice, always criticizing, demeaning, and mocking your every action. Maybe it was your own voice telling you that you were constantly getting things wrong.

When you have stopped feeling guilty all the time, you will only hear that voice occasionally, and usually only when you have done something that can be resolved. Even better than the inner critic voice being silenced, however, is when you begin hearing a small whisper that tells you, “Good job,” “Well done,” and “You deserve good things.”

You may have carried guilt and shame for the longest time, without knowing why and without knowing how to be free. You don’t have to continue like this, but you can’t go on alone. When you meet someone who keeps calm, steady, and accepting when you are vulnerable, you will find the guilt fades. There are people in the world who want to see you, validate you, and love you.

When you go for counseling, you get to be yourself with someone who will never judge you. For many people, this is the first time they have ever felt seen, understood, and validated. If you would like to begin meeting with a counselor, we can help. Please consult our online catalog or speak with our reception team to find someone who can help you overcome persistent guilt.

item.title: Navigating Anxiety in Pregnancy with Faith and Support
item.description:
In pregnancy, one of the most precious seasons of life, there is a certain kind of loneliness associated with anxiety. Women absorb a social message that frames pregnancy as purely celebratory and leaves little room to honestly name fear, worry, or the sense of being overwhelmed. Anxiety in pregnancy can feel particularly difficult.

Anxiety during pregnancy can show up as a persistent worry about the baby’s health, fear of childbirth, or a feeling of dread that doesn’t go away. These are real experiences, and they deserve to be taken seriously rather than labeled as hormones or nerves.

Perinatal anxiety occurs during pregnancy or the postpartum period and is more prevalent than prenatal depression, yet it receives minimal public attention. A woman who white-knuckles through appointments, sleepless nights, and daily responsibilities while appearing calm is often struggling with an unseen emotional battle.

Some Christian counselors specialize in perinatal mental health, and they understand that this emotional labor is exhausting. These counselors can offer a space for a woman to finally let go of this anxiety and acknowledge that it is not a failure of faith or gratitude. Rather, it is an act of honesty before God in seeking to be the whole person He created.

How Nutrition Shapes the Anxious Mind During Pregnancy

The connection between nutrition and mental health in women is not new. The gut and brain are in constant communication through the gut-brain axis, and pregnant women are not immune to this connection. The food they consume will influence this system and their mental well-being.

Consuming highly processed foods, refined sugars, or inflammatory ingredients has been linked to mood instability and anxiety. But choosing a diet rich in whole foods, lean proteins, and omega-3 fatty acids will support emotional regulation. This does not mean that nutrition will eliminate anxiety, but it will help in the bigger picture of reducing anxiety.

Certain nutrients need attention during pregnancy. Magnesium is important for calming the nervous system, B vitamins support neurotransmitter function, which helps regulate mood, and omega-3 fatty acids support brain development in the baby and emotional resilience in the mother. Women who are pregnant should monitor their iron intake, as low iron levels can trigger feelings of fatigue, irritability, and anxiety.

Maintaining a healthy diet requires eating with intention during pregnancy and is considered a form of daily care for both mother and baby. This allows the woman to feel a sense of agency in a season that feels unpredictable.

Anxiety in Pregnancy and the Cycle that Nutrition Can Help Break

Anxiety in pregnancy tends to feed on itself, which makes it a frustrating dynamic during this time in a woman’s life. Poor sleep can lead to an increase in anxiety, which leads to poor eating choices, which leads to blood sugar instability, leading to more anxiety. It is a vicious cycle that can quietly consume a woman before she even realizes what is happening.

The crash that follows a high-sugar comfort food binge intensifies feelings of worry and emotional instability. The caffeine that women rely on out of exhaustion can amplify physical symptoms of anxiety and make it harder to distinguish between a caffeine response and genuine emotional distress.

To break the cycle, there must be intentional awareness and gentleness. This doesn’t mean she should focus on achieving a perfect diet or adding another expectation to an already full plate. It simply requires building small, sustainable shifts that will support the nervous system over time.

By prioritizing meals, choosing healthy food, and staying adequately hydrated, the expectant mother can move forward even on difficult days. An expectant mother should approach nutrition as an act of self-compassion rather than another standard to meet. The pairing of nutritional shifts and emotional and spiritual support builds a complete foundation for managing anxiety during pregnancy.

Building a Support System that Honors Body, Mind, and Spirit

Learning to navigate anxiety in pregnancy is not a solo endeavor. The competing demands of daily life, existing relationships, and preparations for a new baby can leave a woman feeling as though there’s no space to ask for help. These are the narratives women absorb from families, faith communities, and a broader culture to reinforce a standard of quiet endurance.

In this framework, strength looks like managing without showing the strain. But honest strength involves knowing when a situation is more than a person can carry and choosing to reach out.

Christian counselors can offer a unique form of support for expectant mothers dealing with anxiety. These counselors hold both the clinical and spiritual insight of what a woman is experiencing and understand that fear and faith can coexist.

They are not asking women to choose between addressing their mental health and honoring their beliefs. Instead, they are assisting the mother-to-be in connecting nutritional awareness, community support, and spiritual grounding. They work to build a structure that can hold the emotional complexities of pregnancy.

This type of care assists women through a season, producing lasting change rather than temporary relief. What this looks like in practice is a counselor who understands both the physiological realities of pregnancy and the spiritual questions that surface alongside them.

Rather than offering a checklist, a skilled Christian counselor helps the expectant mother build a grace-filled, realistic plan. This plan accounts for hard days, honors her faith, and draws on professional insight to carry her through the moments when anxiety feels louder than hope. Working together, they highlight the importance of the instruction in Ecclesiastes:

Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up! – Ecclesiastes 4:9–10, ESV

Support During Pregnancy

Anxiety during pregnancy does not disqualify a woman from experiencing the beauty of what God is doing through her. Although anxiety during pregnancy is real and affects countless women across all backgrounds and faiths, it does not have to overwhelm the entire experience.

The body and mind are connected. By addressing intentional nutrition, professional support, and spiritual anchoring, we offer a holistic and honoring response to what many women face. Seeking help is not a weakness. It is wisdom.

Anxiety in pregnancy does not have a single solution, and no two women will walk through it the same way. What remains constant is that support is available, God is present, and the decision to reach out is always worth making. A woman who chooses to address her anxiety is not showing weakness; she is showing the kind of quiet, determined care that good mothering is built on.

Navigating peace during pregnancy is not a straight line and comes with days that feel manageable and days that don’t. If the right emotional, nutritional, and spiritual support is in place, women do not have to face this journey alone. Hope anchors itself in God’s care. He sees every sleepless night, every worried thought, and every prayer whispered over a growing life.

Women who struggle with anxiety in pregnancy are encouraged to contact our reception team and get started building a faith-based care plan to help navigate this special season in their lives. Our team is standing by to answer any questions or schedule an appointment today.

item.title: It Is Not Too Late: Parental Regret and Reconciliation
item.description:
Many parents experience moments of regret in their relationships with their children. It could be a harsh word spoken in anger, years of emotional distance that was never addressed, or a relationship with a child that slowly drifted into something unrecognizable. These are the kinds of things that stay. Regret over these moments is a weight that doesn’t fade, and for many parents, it quietly shapes every interaction that comes after.

Many adult children carry wounds that become part of how they move through the world. It’s hard to address parental regret and the hope of reconciliation in a single conversation or a grand gesture. It is a process, layered and complicated by grief, pride, and hidden pain.

Both parents and adult children need to move toward healing with intention. That kind of intentionality is harder than it sounds when the wounds run deep, and the history between them is long and complicated. Still, we can rest on the promise in Scripture: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NIV)

Understanding the Weight of Parental Regret

Parental regret extends beyond wishing things had gone differently. It carries a particular kind of anguish with the knowledge that the people most affected were children who had no choice in the matter. That weight often shows up as a sense of helplessness, as though a parent feels trapped in an identity they can’t escape. And for many, that feeling doesn’t go away on its own.

This is similar to moral injury, which occurs when emotional damage stems from the gap between who a person wanted to be and who they actually were. That type of shame lingers long after the moment has passed. Most parents manage it privately rather than address it directly. That isolation only deepens the wound over time.

Parental regret is especially complex because of its intersection with love. Loving someone and knowing you caused them harm produces a grief that is hard to name. It shows up as depression, as anger turned inward, or as a quiet belief that repair is no longer possible.

Parents in these situations find themselves maneuvering between the desire to reach out and the fear that doing so will only cause more damage. That leaves the relationship stuck in a painful place, where both individuals carry wounds that were never named out loud. But God knows, and we can invite Him into our pain. “Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts.” (Psalm 139:23, NIV)

The Emotional Landscape of Adult Children in Parental Regret and Reconciliation

The decision to address parental regret and reconciliation is not simple for adult children. It involves navigating painful memories, weighing the emotional cost of restoration, and sitting with feelings that don’t have easy answers. Adult children often grieve for the parent they needed and the relationship they never had. Both of those things are true at the same time. Both deserve space rather than a rush to resolution.

Reconciliation doesn’t automatically restore what was broken. It requires trust, and trust takes time to rebuild. The idea of opening the door again often feels like a risk for adult children who have tried before without anything changing.

There is also a quiet social pressure to forgive quickly or to minimize what happened to preserve family harmony. That pressure produces reconciliation that looks good but is far from the real thing. When an adult child goes through the motions without genuine safety or acknowledgment, it can deepen the wound rather than begin to close it.

Christian counselors emphasize that there is no way to manufacture or hurry genuine reconciliation. It is only reached through an intentional choice free from manipulation or guilt, and grounded in honesty about what happened. Scripture helps us in this: “Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.” (Colossians 3:13, NIV) This shows us how to handle these hard situations.

What Makes Parental Regret and Reconciliation Possible

The reconciliation that happens between a parent and a child does not come from both parties pretending the past didn’t occur. It only takes shape when both people are willing to face it honestly, with genuine acknowledgment of harm, rather than an apology offered to relieve personal guilt. Accountability forms the foundation of repair. It only holds when someone chooses to face what they did without deflecting.

When a parent takes responsibility without minimizing, without deflecting, and without asking the adult child to move faster than they are ready, it gives the adult child permission to be exactly where they are. That can feel vulnerable for the parent who doesn’t know how that honesty will land.

Faith plays a significant role in this process for families. Biblically, there is a call toward reconciliation rooted in truth and grace, not a mandate to ignore boundaries or overlook pain. Christian counselors help families understand that forgiveness and reconciliation are related but not the same.

Forgiveness can begin in the heart long before reconciliation is possible. Sometimes reconciliation has to wait until safety is established. When both take root, the result is a relationship that is more honest and grounded than what existed before. Jesus put a high value on reconciliation.

“Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift.” – Matthew 5:23-24, NIV

Mental Health, Faith, and the Journey Toward Healing

Repairing a parent-child relationship has a deep impact on mental health that is hard to keep hidden. The emotional work involved isn’t always easy to see from the outside. Depression, anxiety, and difficulty forming attachments in adulthood connect back to unresolved relational wounds. This is particularly true when those wounds go all the way back to the earliest relationships a person ever had.

The way parents connect with children at a young age is a big influence on the ability of the child to develop emotional regulation and experience intimacy throughout their lives. Because of this, the stakes of parental regret and reconciliation extend beyond the family unit. Moving toward reconciliation isn’t just about repairing one relationship. Reconciliation focuses on reclaiming and healing something that was hurt long ago.

Parents who grapple with regret find that the mental health implications run just as deep. Chronic guilt and shame, when left unaddressed, lead to withdrawal, self-isolation, and a diminished sense of personal worth. Parents carry an internal picture of what a good parent looks like. When they believe they missed that mark, it builds a kind of trap that doesn’t open easily without the support of a therapeutic relationship.

Shame does not have to be the outcome. When parents find their way into a space where their story can be heard without judgment, that cycle can begin to shift. It doesn’t happen overnight. But it does happen.

Christian counselors work at the intersection of faith and clinical support. That combination matters here because this kind of healing rarely happens without both.

Pursuing Healing

Reconciliation does not erase what happened or negate the pain that came from it. It is a painfully slow and tender decision to build something new from the rubble of what fell apart. Everyone involved must show up with honesty, patience, and a willing heart – and stay present even when it gets uncomfortable.

Not every relationship heals completely. That does not mean anyone has failed. It means grace is still needed. For those who take the first steps toward addressing parental regret and reconciliation, the healing potential is real. Scripture teaches us that grace goes beyond what any of us can accomplish alone. Something new can take place even in the middle of the chaos of regret and reconciliation.

And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose. – Romans 8:28, NIV

If you are facing the challenge of reconciliation and carrying a weight of regret, you do not have to navigate it alone. The first step toward something better is reaching out. Contact our reception team to learn more about parental regret and reconciliation and to get connected with a counselor who understands the complexities of family relationships.

References:
https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/forgiveness
https://www.verywellmind.com/what-is-estrangement-5207492
https://psychcentral.com/health/living-with-regrets-and-how-to-deal-with-them
https://psychcentral.com/lib/when-parents-and-children-are-estranged
https://www.verywellmind.com/how-to-rebuild-trust-in-a-relationship-5207498

Photo:
“Father and Son”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post It Is Not Too Late: Parental Regret and Reconciliation appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.

It only takes shape when both people are willing to face it honestly, with genuine acknowledgment of harm, rather than an apology offered to relieve personal guilt. Accountability forms the foundation of repair. It only holds when someone chooses to face what they did without deflecting.

When a parent takes responsibility without minimizing, without deflecting, and without asking the adult child to move faster than they are ready, it gives the adult child permission to be exactly where they are. That can feel vulnerable for the parent who doesn’t know how that honesty will land.

Faith plays a significant role in this process for families. Biblically, there is a call toward reconciliation rooted in truth and grace, not a mandate to ignore boundaries or overlook pain. Christian counselors help families understand that forgiveness and reconciliation are related but not the same.

Forgiveness can begin in the heart long before reconciliation is possible. Sometimes reconciliation has to wait until safety is established. When both take root, the result is a relationship that is more honest and grounded than what existed before. Jesus put a high value on reconciliation.

“Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift.” – Matthew 5:23-24, NIV

Mental Health, Faith, and the Journey Toward Healing

Repairing a parent-child relationship has a deep impact on mental health that is hard to keep hidden. The emotional work involved isn’t always easy to see from the outside. Depression, anxiety, and difficulty forming attachments in adulthood connect back to unresolved relational wounds. This is particularly true when those wounds go all the way back to the earliest relationships a person ever had.

The way parents connect with children at a young age is a big influence on the ability of the child to develop emotional regulation and experience intimacy throughout their lives. Because of this, the stakes of parental regret and reconciliation extend beyond the family unit. Moving toward reconciliation isn’t just about repairing one relationship. Reconciliation focuses on reclaiming and healing something that was hurt long ago.

Parents who grapple with regret find that the mental health implications run just as deep. Chronic guilt and shame, when left unaddressed, lead to withdrawal, self-isolation, and a diminished sense of personal worth. Parents carry an internal picture of what a good parent looks like. When they believe they missed that mark, it builds a kind of trap that doesn’t open easily without the support of a therapeutic relationship.

Shame does not have to be the outcome. When parents find their way into a space where their story can be heard without judgment, that cycle can begin to shift. It doesn’t happen overnight. But it does happen.

Christian counselors work at the intersection of faith and clinical support. That combination matters here because this kind of healing rarely happens without both.

Pursuing Healing

Reconciliation does not erase what happened or negate the pain that came from it. It is a painfully slow and tender decision to build something new from the rubble of what fell apart. Everyone involved must show up with honesty, patience, and a willing heart – and stay present even when it gets uncomfortable.

Not every relationship heals completely. That does not mean anyone has failed. It means grace is still needed. For those who take the first steps toward addressing parental regret and reconciliation, the healing potential is real. Scripture teaches us that grace goes beyond what any of us can accomplish alone. Something new can take place even in the middle of the chaos of regret and reconciliation.

And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose. – Romans 8:28, NIV

If you are facing the challenge of reconciliation and carrying a weight of regret, you do not have to navigate it alone. The first step toward something better is reaching out. Contact our reception team to learn more about parental regret and reconciliation and to get connected with a counselor who understands the complexities of family relationships.

item.title: How to Stop Worrying: Is Certainty Your Idol?
item.description:
Most people have one fear or worry that looms larger than all others. Maybe you’ve been labeled the “worry wart” in the family because you tend to overthink or anticipate negative outcomes. Or maybe you don’t worry about everything, but you have that one thing that triggers you. You just don’t know how to stop worrying.

Whether you’re in a constant state of fear or you have that one unresolved trigger that has turned into more than a hyperfixation or phobia, you may be dealing with something deeper than anxiety alone. Beneath the surface, there may be a persistent need for clarity. You hold tight to the idea of living a secure, certain life. But could certainty be an idol?

What is an idol?

When we think of idols, we often conjure images of golden statues or ancient altars. Images of gold figures glisten in the desert sun, or chubby little gods may come to mind. But idols in the modern world, especially in the Christian faith, are rarely as obvious as a tangible item sitting on a home altar. An idol is anything you rely on to provide security or peace that isn’t God. An idol is anything that functions as a savior.

When certainty becomes a definitive goal, worry can become a ritual. You may not even realize you’re doing it, but when you crave certainty, you might start to believe that your worry is the catalyst to certainty. This is where certainty fails as a god. An idol might promise a reward, but it can’t deliver on it. You might chase certainty to find peace, but the chase only causes more chaos.

Is it a spiritual issue?

Overthinking about a problem or mentally preparing for a potential negative outcome can unconsciously convince you that, through this coping mechanism, you can somehow control the universe. As a result, you sacrifice your sleep, your relationships, or even your physical health at the altar of certainty. You hope that your mental suffering will act as an offering to the god of certainty.

Is a hyper-fixation automatically an idol? Hyper-fixation, even when it feels overwhelming and obsessive, isn’t automatically an idol. In many cases, a hyper-fixation can be the result of biological influence, trauma, and learned patterns of thinking. It’s a biological and psychological issue, not a spiritual one.

The nervous system often shapes anxiety, rumination, and intrusive thoughts. They are not simply created by personal choice. It’s important to acknowledge this in your own life and others’, because not every intense or persistent thought pattern is a spiritual issue.

The pattern of worry or need for certainty may have started as a way to cope or protect yourself in unpredictable situations. In a way, it may serve its purpose by making you feel more prepared for difficult situations. But without even knowing it, your need to prepare or your need for certainty can become a way you try to gain control rather than relying on God in moments of unpredictability.

You can’t automatically attribute the feelings of worry or anxiety to the sin of idolatry. If you do, you risk over-spiritualizing a biological reality and turning a biological and psychological survival response into a moral failure.

However, in some cases, these thought patterns can have a spiritual element. If you’re dealing with a need for certainty, it might be worth exploring whether or not there is a spiritual root.

Habakkuk teaches about worry

In Habakkuk 1, the prophet is witnessing the collapse of his society. His worry is rooted in real-world trauma, not necessarily a biological tendency. He’s dealing with violence, paralyzing laws, and justice that never prevails (v. 4). His anxiety is a rational response to an irrational world. Habakkuk’s trauma-informed response is exactly what a dysregulated nervous system looks like today.

Habakkuk does what many of us do in times of crisis or uncertainty. He asks, “Why?”

Seeking Certainty

Habakkuk’s “why” was a desperate cry and longing for clarity and a predictable end. He’s looking for a way to make the chaos all around him finally make sense. The book begins with a cry of anguish. “How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen?” (Habakkuk 1:2, NIV) This language may sound familiar because you have said it a few times yourself.

Maybe you feel that if you can find the right perspective or answer, the fear will stop. Yet God feels distant. This is a natural response. Asking “why” is not where the problem lies. In fact, it’s often the beginning of faith. The problem starts when the need for an answer becomes a condition of peace.

When that need for an absolute outcome outweighs your trust in God, certainty could be considered an idol. Unfortunately, certainty is often unattainable, as you want to take control of the uncontrollable. That might sound like a bit of a stretch, but when you break down the typical worry process, you see the striking similarities between the need for certainty and idol worship.

When you worry, you’re sacrificing your present peace for future certainty. You likely have rituals, much like the rituals in idol worship, that make you feel secure in the moment. You might rehearse the worst-case scenarios in your head, hoping not to be blindsided.

Scripture and psychology speak to certainty

Scripture and modern psychology hold similar insights when it comes to the human need for certainty. Both recognize that the mind is wired to seek predictability and control. This is particularly true in times of distress.

The difference is that Scripture frames this need as a matter of trust and ultimately, reliance on God. Psychology describes it in terms of cognitive patterns, nervous system responses, and coping strategies.

Where They Converge

The good news is that Scripture and psychology aren’t at odds with one another. When it comes to the need for certainty, they often work in tandem.

Therapists work with anxiety, obsessive thought patterns, and an intolerance of uncertainty. They examine how some people respond to the unknown with disproportionate distress. It isn’t the bad thing itself that is causing the most suffering, but the not knowing, the waiting, and the uncertainty.

Does this sound familiar? It’s the situation we see at the beginning of Habakkuk.

The goal in therapy isn’t to eliminate uncertainty because that’s impossible to do. But the goal is to help clients build a greater tolerance for that uncertainty. Through therapy, you can slowly train your mind and your nervous system to remain regulated even when the outcomes are unknown. This can be done through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and other methods that help your body feel safe even in moments of uncertainty.

Faith in God offers something remarkably similar. Scripture not only encourages you to tolerate the unknown but gives you an invitation to trust the One who holds your future. It gives you something to do with that anxiety while waiting.

God’s Perspective

It’s important to note that if you struggle with the need for certainty, God understands. He’s not standing on a distant planet, cross-armed, just waiting for you to have more faith. The same God who designed your nervous system understands why uncertainty feels threatening to it.

Psalms 103 says that He “knows how we are formed; He remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:14, NIV) That verse says that God understands your humanity.

Coming Back to Habakkuk

What makes Habakkuk’s story so powerful is that by chapter three, something has shifted. He hasn’t received all the answers he was looking for. The chaos around him hasn’t resolved, but his posture has changed.

He writes in chapter 3, “Through the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines… yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.” (Habakkuk 3:17-18, NIV)

Habakkuk is making a deliberate, hard-won choice to anchor his peace in something that uncertainty cannot touch. He moves from “How long, Lord?” to “Yet, I will.” As small as that shift might look on paper, it is a remarkable transformation from the need for certainty. It is a shift from holding that need for certainty as an idol to relying on God as the solution.

You can change too

That same transformation is available to you. That process of transitioning from “How long, Lord?” to “Yet, I will,” might just start with a phone call. Call one of the therapists on this site today to get started.

The post How to Stop Worrying: Is Certainty Your Idol? appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: How Online Bereavement Therapy Can Assist with the Grieving Process
item.description:
In a disconnected world, there is a new method for navigating grief therapy. Online bereavement has become a new avenue for individuals to navigate the process of losing a loved one. It is a hybrid of traditional mourning and the digital age. People who are grieving frequently face a paradox between needing a community and wanting to grieve alone.

The digital approach of online bereavement offers a lifeline that tailors support to those who have lost a close loved one. It is a place where faith can continue to guide hearts to hope and healing. This modern method acknowledges the evolving ways people can connect. It can also provide a space where emotional wounds can heal, even amid the chaos of loss and daily life.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

Understanding Online Bereavement

Online bereavement involves the grieving process being navigated on digital platforms such as virtual memorials or support groups. Modern life, busy schedules, and the pandemic have changed the way society as a whole grieves. There was a time when we gathered in person to commemorate the passing of loved ones. Now there is a way to share memories online.

Christian counselors can step in and help individuals process the shift to online bereavement so that no one feels as though they are alone in their pain. These counselors bring compassion through their expertise, fostering a sense of belonging in virtual spaces. This can be comforting and transformative for individuals who feel as though they are stranded in the middle of their grief and mourning.

Old grieving methods seem to be ill-fitting in today’s society. This is where online bereavement services adapt and offer forums or video calls for unique losses. This availability allows for grief to be processed so that it does not harden into despair. Though it may be unconventional, this process honors personal pathways and renders the rigid rules of grieving void. It will reveal the layers that accompany any death and meet people where they are with their grief.

Individuals are assured that the flexibility will allow them to express their sorrow at their own pace. Through written tributes or live discussions, a dynamic support network develops, allowing for a separation from traditional support systems.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction… – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, ESV

The Role of Grief Therapy

Grief therapy is transformed by online bereavement, extending its reach and using virtual sessions to connect those isolated by location or stigma. The cultural message pushes resilience, but online spaces allow raw emotion to surface. The clash between stoic expectations and inner turmoil is resolved, and trauma processing is tailored with care. Christian counselors integrate faith and offer spiritual anchors to those who have lost loved ones.

Professional Christian counselors can provide a steady hand that helps individuals find peace through prayer or scripture. These tools become vital when physical distance separates them from a traditional support system.

This approach breaks barriers and links individuals in rural areas to the support they need. Online bereavement fits into chaotic lives and eases the tension between work and morning. Christian counselors blend scripture with digital tools that prevent individuals from feeling lost in outdated practices.

Technology has enabled counselors to create accessible pathways for healing, ensuring that even the most isolated individuals can find a sense of community. This brings a sense of inclusion and hope, as well as an understanding that they may struggle uniquely, but they are not alone.

Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. – Isaiah 41:10, ESV

Benefits of Seeking Online Healing

The benefits of online bereavement and grief therapy lie in the flexibility of online sessions. Sessions can occur at any time and align with life’s demands. The cultural silence is countered, and vulnerability is allowed to breathe. Privacy draws those hesitant about face-to-face help and creates a haven for them to share their pain. Online groups are also readily available due to the lower costs. This bridges the gap for those who are far from traditional support.

Individuals are empowered through accessibility to seek help on their terms. This reduces the stigma that often comes with public mourning, and it opens doors to healing that may remain closed under traditional grief therapy. Knowing they are in a safe space, individuals who are grieving find freedom and express their emotions, whether positive or negative.

Each of these benefits addresses isolation, enabling people to connect through stories and reducing digital divides and loneliness. It can reduce overwhelming feelings with paced guidance that allows the individual to navigate the grieving process in a way that makes sense to them. Christian counselors use online prayer or Scripture discussions to integrate faith into the healing process. This blend helps individuals avoid feeling adrift.

Christian counselors understand this and can guide individuals through the process with compassion and understanding. The virtual presence of an online counselor offers a consistent source of encouragement. This is beneficial in building resilience over time, a vital component of long-term emotional recovery.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

Spiritual Integration

Faith can enhance the online bereavement role in grief therapy. Society often splits faith and mental health, creating a conflict in the individual. Scripture is full of hope, and this reframes loss through God’s lens. Online formats connect faith communities for prayer or to understand what Scripture says about grief and hope.

Christian counselors maintain a focus on identity in Christ, which facilitates healing with mercy. Spiritual connection is essential in providing a foundation of strength and resilience. This permits individuals to lean on divine support as a process, which is comforting in the anonymity of online spaces, particularly during their grief.

Journaling and group reflection are virtual tools that root this process in grace. Faith can help prevent isolation and build strength during times of unique loss. A resolution bridges the gap between despair and belief. Christian counselors emphasize the use of spiritual tools to empower individuals during the grief process. By integrating faith and community online, bereavement reminds the individual that they are not walking the path of grief alone.

These tools can encourage deeper exploration of personal faith. This fosters a sense of community and shared purpose that sustains individuals through the darkest moments of their grief journey.

So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. – 2 Corinthians 4:16, ESV

Learn about online grief therapy

Online bereavement assists grief therapy by bridging old and new and challenging the cultural silences of what is acceptable grieving. By transforming solitude into a shared experience, online bereavement challenges the notion that mourning a loss should be a private affair. Individuals emerge transformed in a way that honors the lost loved one.

A faith-based therapy provides enduring comfort and guidance toward a renewed purpose. This transforms grief into a hopeful experience, reminding individuals that even in the midst of loss, they can celebrate the goodness of God. This transformation is a testament to the power of community and faith, leaving a legacy of love that inspires even after the initial pain subsides.

If you would like more information about online bereavement, contact your local Christian counselor today to begin your pathway to healing and connection.

References:
https://www.verywellmind.com/grief-counseling-5217868
https://psychcentral.com/health/therapy-for-grief
https://www.verywellmind.com/what-is-bereavement-therapy-5115073
https://www.webmd.com/balance/grief-counseling
https://psychcentral.com/health/online-grief-support-groups
https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/groups?category=grief

“Online Therapy”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post How Online Bereavement Therapy Can Assist with the Grieving Process appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.

item.title: 5 Signs of Emotional Abuse in Marriage
item.description:
Emotional abuse is one of the more difficult forms of abuse to identify because it doesn’t leave any visible scars. For example, a person dating an emotionally abusive person can become so desensitized to abuse years into their relationship that they don’t recognize the abuse.

A person can go years without noticing that their mood is being impacted by and stemming from emotional abuse. A good relationship should feel like both parties are honored, cherished, and valued. If one party does not feel this way, it is an emotionally abusive marriage. People must see the warning signs of emotional abuse.

Some people ignore these signs, citing “psychobabble” or other ways of discounting the problem instead of looking more deeply into it. As a result, the victim of emotional abuse is being robbed of having a healthy relationship and healthy self-esteem. Here are five ways to identify emotional abuse in marriage.

Coercion or Control

The highly controlling person will check out your whereabouts, where you’ve been, what you’ve worn or eaten, etc. This person doesn’t honor you for who you are. They are insecure about who they are and desperate for someone to love them. They may deceive themselves into thinking that you don’t love them, and when they do, they control your every move.

Although not physical in nature, this type of abuse can place undeserved guilt and shame on someone who is just going about their business. People who control in this way want to avoid the pain of being left or the pain of being rejected. Anyone who is constantly questioned about where they are, what they’re doing, what they’re wearing, and having their location tracked could be subject to emotional abuse.

This behavior does not honor their relationship. The person will see themselves as feeling like that person loves and cares for them, but they only care about themselves. A way to get around coercion and control is simply not to share your whereabouts. Turn your location tracking off on your phone. Change the passwords on your e-mail and social media accounts.

Control has no place in a loving relationship. The person should not force you to tell them where you are. You are not at fault. There needs to be a certain level of trust in a healthy relationship. If there’s not, then it’s best to seek some help.

Manipulation

Manipulation occurs when someone gets you to believe something that is not true. A manipulative person will tell you that you did not see or hear what is taking place. For example, if you question their amount of control, they will deny that they are controlling and flip it so that you are to blame.

Manipulation is also when one states something one way, but the real reason is something else. The real reason is to meet an emotional need; they’re trying to get their needs met through you. A manipulative person is hard to spot because they’ve been manipulating you for a long time.

Giving in when a person pushes you to do something even after you’ve refused can give way to more manipulation. When you finally refuse them, it angers them; it may cause a fight or quarrel. Watch for the warning signs. If someone is manipulating you, refuse to be manipulated anymore.

Gaslighting

Gaslighting is defined as “a form of psychological abuse or manipulation in which the abuser attempts to sow self-doubt and confusion in their victim’s mind. Typically, gaslighters seek to gain power and control over the other person by distorting reality and forcing them to question their judgment and intuition.”

This behavior happens when someone denies or blames the behavior on the victim. This action also happens when someone does not take responsibility for their actions. This is a common manipulation tactic in which the other person flips the blame onto the other person.

This action makes the victim question whether their perception of events is true and their feelings are valid. However, gaslighters are good at convincing other people that the other person is at fault and not them.

Gaslighting is also difficult to pinpoint and change because the victims are normally in conflict with the gaslighter. A person who is good at manipulation can convince even professionals like counselors to see things from their perspective. Eventually, someone will discover the gaslighter’s behavior, but it often takes a long time to be noticed and recognized for what it is, creating shame and guilt.

A gaslighting victim should write down any situations in which they feel this is taking place. They should take careful notes on what happened, what was said, and how the person flipped it so the victim can take responsibility. They should then seek help from someone who can help them discern what is happening.

If the person is truly gaslighting, they need to be held responsible for their behavior. A witness or an advocate on the victim’s behalf will help bring clarity, provide relief that it is not only in their mind, and help the victim create and follow through with boundaries.

Degradation or Condemnation

This more than likely happens with words. Condemnation is when a person is constantly being put down, called names, and mocked because of their behavior, personality, or issues and is subject to emotional abuse. While we must continuously work to grow into greater Christlikeness, one party should honor the other by loving them exactly as they are.

The person should not feel degraded because they wear a particular outfit, eat something, or don’t do something up to the other party’s standard. If one party has such an issue with the other, it may be time to terminate the relationship. Degradation or mockery has no place in a healthy relationship. That person should not feel mocked because they hold a particular view contrary to the other person’s belief.

Refusal to Let Go

Another aspect of an unhealthy relationship is someone who refuses to let go of another person’s offense. This is where forgiveness is vital. Forgiveness is essential to a healthy relationship, whether the person is a believer or unbeliever. While forgiveness is possible, it does not mean reconciliation is always recommended or guaranteed.

Both parties must take responsibility for areas where they’ve done wrong. If they have hurt them, issue an apology to the other party. But if the other party still refuses to let it go or brings it up during every argument and treats the person as if they are still doing that behavior, it’s a form of emotional abuse.

Is restoration possible?

Giving an abuser the chance to change can be complicated. If a person continues their behavior and there is proof of continued sinful behavior, it is evident that they are unrepentant. This is where you would want to question it and bring it up in the hopes that that person will change.

If the person has repented and changed, and you see no evidence of that behavior taking place, healing and restoration are possible. God is faithful and forgives us as far as the East is from the West. He forgives all our sins and chooses to remember them no more. He does not hold these things against us because Jesus on the cross has already atoned for those sins.

Even when there is true repentance, however, a couple should seek Christian counseling to help the abuser change their behaviors long-term and learn healthy ways of communicating and relating to their spouse. Rebuilding trust and intimacy can take time and commitment. It is imperative not to ignore your emotions because faith is not ignoring your mind; it’s training it.

Emotional abuse is difficult to spot. But by taking the suggestions above, both parties can enjoy healthy relationships if they take responsibility, repent, and honor the other person. God can heal marriages.

If you have faced any of the above-mentioned issues, struggled with relationships, are facing a divorce, and/or are ready to commit to counseling and restoring your marriage after abuse, contact our office today to schedule an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our online directory.

Photo:
“Autumn Leaves”, Courtesy of Patti Black, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post 5 Signs of Emotional Abuse in Marriage appeared first on Orange County Christian Counseling.

Both parties must take responsibility for areas where they’ve done wrong. If they have hurt them, issue an apology to the other party. But if the other party still refuses to let it go or brings it up during every argument and treats the person as if they are still doing that behavior, it’s a form of emotional abuse.

Is restoration possible?

Giving an abuser the chance to change can be complicated. If a person continues their behavior and there is proof of continued sinful behavior, it is evident that they are unrepentant. This is where you would want to question it and bring it up in the hopes that that person will change.

If the person has repented and changed, and you see no evidence of that behavior taking place, healing and restoration are possible. God is faithful and forgives us as far as the East is from the West. He forgives all our sins and chooses to remember them no more. He does not hold these things against us because Jesus on the cross has already atoned for those sins.

Even when there is true repentance, however, a couple should seek Christian counseling to help the abuser change their behaviors long-term and learn healthy ways of communicating and relating to their spouse. Rebuilding trust and intimacy can take time and commitment. It is imperative not to ignore your emotions because faith is not ignoring your mind; it’s training it.

Emotional abuse is difficult to spot. But by taking the suggestions above, both parties can enjoy healthy relationships if they take responsibility, repent, and honor the other person. God can heal marriages.

If you have faced any of the above-mentioned issues, struggled with relationships, are facing a divorce, and/or are ready to commit to counseling and restoring your marriage after abuse, contact our office today to schedule an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our online directory.

The post 5 Signs of Emotional Abuse in Marriage appeared first on California Christian Counseling.

item.title: Long-Distance Relationship Tips for Couples Who Met Online
item.description:
Distance means very little to couples today. Since the pandemic, there has been an enormous spike in the popularity of online dating. It is estimated that one in ten couples met online in 2024, with people in their thirties and forties following the hordes of younger internet users looking for love online.

Although dating apps have become an ordinary way for couples to meet, virtually none of them provide long-distance relationship tips or even advice beyond generic safety warnings. Online dating not only provides opportunities for those looking to find love but also several obstacles, challenges, and risks.

There are a few important things you must consider if you find yourself pursuing a digital romance, particularly if you want your online relationship to work out. More than most, online relationships have an intense impact on our mental health. Communicating online with a love interest you have never met in person can be intense, exciting, and unusual. However, at some point, every digital couple must agree on what they want long-term.

Instant Connection with Online Dating

Online relationships tend to happen much faster than in-person dating. In a matter of clicks, you are in a private conversation getting to know someone in the safety of your own home while still being miles away from each other. The first stage of internet dating is often connecting like this in an app or on a platform, before choosing a more suitable chat app to use, preferably one with video calling capabilities.

One of the first long-distance relationship tips for online couples must be this: be wary of anyone unwilling to do a voice call or a video call.

People will give legitimate excuses for not wanting to do voice calls or video calls. They’re busy, or they’re in public. However, excuses like these only hold up one or two times. There is absolutely no future for the connection until you have seen or at least heard each other. This is especially true if your initial connection with someone on the internet feels promising and worth your time, and if they say they are interested too.

The Next Steps When Online Dating

Let’s say that you have matched with someone online, and sparks and butterflies are flying. Maybe you have spoken with them, seen them, and confirmed that they are who they say they are. What is next? This is a crucial stage for many online couples, because it determines the future of your connection.

You might have both stated what you are looking for on your profile on the app. That might be the main reason you swiped on each other in the first place. The second long-distance relationship tip for online couples is to establish what you are both looking for early in the relationship. Do this part on a video or voice call if possible.

Being online enables people to be selfish and flaky. It’s too easy to lead someone on, even after love-bombing them, only to disappear as soon as the connection leaves the flirting stage. You can save each other a lot of time and potential disappointment by establishing as early as possible what it is you are hoping for.

You don’t need to share your five-year plan, unless that’s something you both want to do. However, it is essential that you know if there is a possibility of meeting in person within the next few months, or else you will be investing in a potentially fruitless relationship.

There are many people who find themselves in intense, intimate, and even truly loving relationships in a matter of months after meeting online. Some people maintain these kinds of long-distance digital relationships for years. It sounds pointless and even torturous, but there is often a psychological reason for these kinds of connections.

These couples tell themselves that the reason they have never met and remained long-distance is due to logistics or practicalities. After more than a year, however, that excuse is merely a smokescreen. You can legitimately meet your future lover online, but the relationship cannot live unless you meet in person.

Similarly, a couple can be separated by distance for a season, but there is no future to it unless you have a mutual goal to be together again at some point. Too many couples who meet online settle for having a digital romance because it is safe and easy, and doesn’t require more than communication. Lasting relationships thrive on intentionality and planning. If you do not have a shared goal as a couple, you will not have a shared future.

The Best Long Distance Relationship Tips

You can say that you are in a long-distance relationship with someone you have met online if you have interacted over a voice or video call, established your shared hopes and intentions for the connection, and made a plan to at least meet in person within the next year. Even then, you might encounter some unpleasant surprises, but the same risk is true of relationships that begin any other way.

Once you share a common goal, there are some things you can do that will ensure the health of the relationship until you meet in person.

  • Don’t rely on texting alone: Schedule meaningful virtual dates regularly and have fun using other apps together. You can play regular one-on-one games online, watch movies and series together while you text each other, make and share music playlists, and take each other on video tours of places you visit. Long-distance relationships in the digital age should never feel static or dull.
  • Develop a rhythm with each other: A healthy connection with a long-distance loved one doesn’t come from constant communication. It comes from being consistent and intentional. You build trust with someone by showing up when you say you will and making them a priority in your life. Every relationship needs its little rhythms and rituals, like goodnight texts, video calls in the middle of the day, or weekly date nights online.
  • Continue to communicate your needs and thoughts: Life happens and tests even the strongest relationships. There will be nights when you can’t make the call you intended to, or even when you would rather process certain events alone. This is more than acceptable, provided you communicate your thoughts and feelings. Nothing affects a relationship more than overthinking and arriving at unhelpful conclusions.
  • Follow up on your individual and shared goals: In any relationship, you must be your partner’s biggest cheerleader and most constant truth-teller. If you have established a joint goal, keep each other accountable to it. As important, however, is encouraging each other towards personal goals. Long distance is no match for the couple who are united in their support for each other.

A Shared Future Together in Person

We live in a wonderful age where connection is possible despite distance and time zones. Digital dating is a solid stepping stone to a future you could only once dream of. When you find your person, do your best to connect with them in a better way than texting. Make it a goal and priority to overcome the obstacles keeping you apart, and be intentional and consistent until you do. One day, you will conquer the distance and enjoy the closeness you fostered while apart.

If you would like some personal support as you navigate the world of digital dating, or if you feel like you would benefit from more long-distance relationship tips, we recommend you find a counselor to talk to. You might find someone suitable from our online catalog of counselors, or our reception team can help. Either way, a counselor can help you navigate long-distance relationship tips and online dating.
