item.title: Understanding Seasonal Depression in Men Through Faith and Awareness
item.description:
Changing seasons often bring more than just shorter days and colder weather. For some, it brings changes in mood or depression. It’s not just women who can be affected by seasonal depression; men can also fall victim to this mental struggle. The shift from summer to fall and winter can carry an emotional weight that is difficult to name. Men may brush this off as stress from work or the holiday rush, but underneath, it’s something more persistent.

Depression in men does not always look like sadness. It can sometimes wear the mask of irritability, exhaustion, or a quiet retreat from everything that once mattered. Seasonal Affective Disorder affects men differently than women, and the symptoms often hide beneath the layers of what society tells men they should be.

The challenge for men is to recognize when the seasonal changes become something more concerning. The messages men receive throughout their lives about strength and pushing through difficulty without complaint create a framework where acknowledging depression feels like admitting defeat. But recognizing the symptom is not a weakness; it is the first step toward healing and wholeness in Christ.

Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in Your sight, Lord, my rock and my Redeemer. – Psalm 19:14, ESV

Increased Irritability and Anger

xWhen depression in men presents during the winter months, it rarely announces itself as sadness. It often appears as a shorter fuse, such as frustration that erupts over minor inconveniences. He may find himself snapping at his children over homework or getting agitated in traffic. These are not character flaws, but rather symptoms of a brain chemistry shift. It happens when sunlight decreases and melatonin increases during the darker months.

The cultural narrative says that anger in men is more acceptable than vulnerability. When seasonal depression settles in, irritability becomes the primary language. Rather than admit feeling lost or overwhelmed, men think it is easier to be angry.

The result is a painful cycle where relationships suffer, guilt increases, and depression deepens. Some men may recognize that they are acting differently and struggle to connect these outbursts to seasonal changes affecting their mental health.

The reality is that anger itself isn’t sinful or bad, but it is what we do with it that matters. Emotional regulation can be sidetracked by seasonal depression, making it harder to process anger in a healthy manner. Christian counselors understand the intersection between brain chemistry, seasonal changes, and spiritual well-being. This allows them to help men distinguish between righteous anger and the irritability connected to depression. This can also allow space for men to heal without shame.

Be angry, and yet do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger. – Ephesians 4:26, NASB

Physical Fatigue and Loss of Energy

Seasonal depression is accompanied by exhaustion that feels different from normal tiredness. This type of exhaustion is a heaviness that makes getting out of bed feel like moving through concrete. It makes simple tasks become monumental efforts that seem to deplete every ounce of energy.

A man may need multiple alarms to wake up and struggle to focus during meetings. Some may be completely drained by mid-afternoon, and it’s not laziness. It is a psychological response to reduced sunlight that affects serotonin production.

Men often interpret this fatigue as a personal failure. They push themselves harder, drink more coffee, and berate themselves for not keeping up. The result leads to a series of contradictions that become unbearable:

  • Be productive yet acknowledge limitations.
  • Be strong but admit exhaustion.
  • Be present yet barely functioning.

These opposing demands create a vicious cycle where stress compounds the depression. The body is signaling that it needs rest and intervention, and cultural expectations are demanding that they push through.

Scripture invites us to understand that we are not designed to carry everything alone. Seasonal depression drains energy reserves in ways that human willpower alone cannot overcome. When men recognize physical fatigue as a legitimate symptom rather than failure, it opens the door to seeking help.

Through light therapy, vitamin D supplementation, adjusting sleep schedules, and professional support, men can get help with addressing the biological components of seasonal exhaustion.

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

Social Withdrawal and Isolation

One of the most subtle symptoms of seasonal depression is the gradual pulling away from relationships. Men may start declining invitations to gatherings and respond to text messages less frequently. His excuse may be that he is too busy or he needs space. The result is deeper isolation as he spends more time alone. What may start as missing one church service leads to missing several, and what starts as skipping one small social event leads to avoiding all of them.

Society dictates that men should be independent and be able to solve their own problems without burdening others. Men feed on this message and heed an internal whisper that no one wants to hear about struggles or that real men handle things privately. The withdrawal will continue, and eventually, he will become less connected and more isolated. He will not notice the relationships that can provide support and perspective due to the lies of depression leading to isolation.

We were not designed to handle all the stress of this world alone. God’s word encourages us to bear one another’s burdens and love one another as we love ourselves. Seasonal depression convinces men that solitude is preferable to openness, yet we genuinely need one another during difficult times.

Christian counselors can help men recognize the withdrawal patterns and help them rebuild connections. They can emphasize that seeking support is not a sign of weakness but rather a display of wisdom.

Two are better than one because they have a good return for their labor, for if either of them falls, the one will lift up his companion. But woe to the one who falls when there is not another to lift him up! – Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, NASB

Changes in Sleep Patterns and Appetite

The natural rhythms of the body are disrupted by seasonal depression. Men might find themselves sleeping more than usual or spending ten or more hours in bed and still wake up unrefreshed. Some may experience the opposite, lying awake for hours, unable to find rest, while the mind races with worries.

Sleep is not the only thing affected by seasonal depression. Changes in appetite can also be a symptom. Some may lose interest in food, and others may have intense cravings. The symptoms are as unique as each man.

Men often rationalize these changes so that they do not disrupt the idea of men handling things by themselves. They may blame work stress for poor sleep or justify the late-night snacking as a bad habit. When these patterns emerge specifically during the fall and winter and disappear during the spring and summer, they point to seasonal depression. The body responds to decreased sunlight by altering sleep, wake cycles, and appetite regulation.

With seasonal depression, disrupted sleep and appetite can affect every area of life. This means it’s vital to understand and address. They are symptoms that require attention and not choices or bad habits. Concentration suffers, moods can worsen, relationships become strained, and spiritual vitality decreases. It is essential to address these symptoms through proper sleep hygiene, nutritional support, and professional guidance.

Some men can benefit from light therapy boxes that simulate their exposure to sunlight, and others can adjust meal timing or supplement with vitamin D. These strategies can help regulate circadian rhythms, boost mood, and support overall energy levels. Consistency in daily routines and incorporating outdoor activities when possible can further enhance these effects.

Support Is Available

Men experiencing seasonal depression need to look beyond societal expectations and recognize their symptoms. These can include irritability, exhaustion, withdrawal, and disrupted daily rhythms, and are responses to environmental changes affecting brain chemistry and hormone production. It’s crucial to name these symptoms and seek the right professional assistance.

Christian counselors offer both clinical expertise and spiritual insight, understanding that seasonal depression is a legitimate medical condition that can coexist with faith. Treatment options may include therapy, light exposure, medication, lifestyle changes, or a combination. The important step is to reach out for help rather than enduring in silence. Connect with a counselor on this site or near you to learn more.

item.title: Hope, Stewardship, and Therapy for Eating Disorders
item.description:
Sometimes our faith, which is meant to bring peace, gets tangled up with harmful eating habits. Spiritual devotion turns into rigid control over food, and we find ourselves trapped in a cycle where discipline becomes disordered eating. This struggle calls for spiritual wisdom and professional care so we can embrace the stewardship of the body God has given us.

Therapy for eating disorders is essential for those of us whose fake journey has been weighed down by restrictive eating and legalistic thinking. This struggle goes beyond the act of simply choosing food. It is created from cultural and religious messages linking spiritual maturity to denying physical means.

Many wrestle with the tension of wanting to honor God through discipline while feeling pressured to neglect our bodies’ needs to prove our faith. This conflict makes our faith feel like a burden and not a blessing. For many of us, the guilt of eating a simple meal can sometimes feel like a betrayal of faith. This is another lie that therapy can help us unravel as we seek to steward our bodies.

Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. – Matthew 4:4, ESV

When Faith Becomes Rules About Food

In our Christian communities, we celebrate virtues such as discipline, self-control, and sacrifice as achievements in spiritual growth. These truths are rooted in scriptures, but we have allowed them to become distorted as we apply them rigidly to our eating habits. We start with practices like fasting in an effort to grow closer to God, only to find ourselves becoming obsessed with controlling our food.

When we turn spiritual practices into a way to earn God’s approval through perfect eating, we run the risk of engaging in self-shame. Fasting is meant to deepen our reliance on God, not to create a pathway of self-punishment. Fasting should never make us feel exhausted or ashamed. This is a mindset based on a false gospel that says worth depends on dietary control, not God’s grace.

We are often caught in a false gospel, where our worth hinges on dietary control, such as our need to feel pure through starvation and avoiding entire food groups. These mindsets only leave us weak and ashamed, facing exhaustion and isolation. Through therapy, we learned to overcome this mindset and realize the way to draw closer to God is to trust His guidance in stewarding our bodies.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. – Colossians 2:16, ESV

Breaking Free from Rigid Rules

The similarities between eating disorders and legalistic faith can be striking. Both rely on earning acceptance through strict rule-following, which can create a cycle of striving, failing, and shame. This becomes an exhausting treadmill of always trying to be good enough, but never arriving, and eventually causes problems with mental well-being.

This cycle can be identified by behaviors, such as panic after eating a certain food or weeping because of a fear of failing God for eating a meal. These distorted thoughts reveal the burden that steals the peace of God and leaves us trapped in the false narrative of fasting.

When we pursue this constant effort, we find the peace that God intends for us slipping away. We feel as though we have become trapped, and we question our worth simply because we cannot meet the impossible standards for eating or spirituality. When we experience guilt due to breaking a rule, we tend to set stricter guidelines, creating a harsher cycle of striving and failing. We find ourselves slipping away from resting in grace and into exhaustion from self-punishment.

Christian counselors can offer therapy for eating disorders that will help with recognizing the distorted thoughts surrounding fasting and faith. These counselors help us understand how to build healthier relationships with food in our bodies and how faith can contribute positively. Therapy helps with healing from the struggles by replacing the rigid rules with grace-filled practices.

For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. – Ephesians 2:8-9, ESV

Healing Through Therapy

Choosing to seek therapy is a courageous step that aligns with biblical wisdom. God’s word encourages us to seek counsel and community. Obtaining Christian counseling does not mean there is a lack of trust in God. It can be seen as wisdom leading to the help we need to overcome eating disorders and strict faith rules.

Believers shouldn’t hesitate to seek therapy for fear of judgment. We should allow ourselves to feel freedom as we take a step that breaks down barriers, keeping us from healing through therapy.

Therapy for eating disorders can be complex because they affect thoughts, emotions, and physical health. The care required to treat eating disorders should address biological, psychological, and social factors. Therapy through Christian counselors can provide tools to identify the triggers, challenge harmful thoughts, and rebuild a healthy relationship with food.

Christian counseling provides a unique lens to address how faith can be misused to justify restriction. It also provides direction on how stewardship of the body can support recovery.

When we choose therapy to open doors or deeper spiritual growth, we can address eating disorders and find space to connect with God without shame. Christian counselors can help us reframe things. Biblical truths about stewardship encourage nurturing our bodies and not controlling them.

Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. – Proverbs 11:14, ESV

Reclaiming Body and Soul

Recovering from eating disorders means blending faith and therapy, not choosing one over the other. This recovery is about learning to honor our bodies as God’s temple through stewardship, not punishment. This process will challenge cultural ideas that tie spiritual strength to physical denial. It will require embracing biblical principles for caring for the body.

As we navigate this journey, we will let go of the false security that controlling food provides. It may result in grief over the loss, but true peace will be found in God’s unchanging love. Therapy will help us bridge the gap between knowing God’s grace and living a life surrounded by it. In this journey, we will encounter the unconditional love of God and realize that our actions do not have to earn it. Christian Counseling will help us align our hearts and actions with faith.

Christian counselors promote spiritual practices that support healing. These practices will include gratitude and rest while challenging the distorted use of faith. They will help individuals see their bodies as a gift rather than an enemy that must be conquered.

During the process, we will often realize that the food rules were about controlling our lives, and our restrictive eating may have stemmed from a need to feel worthy. Both of these realizations are ways that distorted thinking creates eating disorders, even when we think we’re being spiritual.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body. – 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, ESV

Finding Hope

In the struggle with eating disorders as believers, our freedom will come through seeking spiritual and professional support. We can find practical tools to heal in therapy, while our faith will provide an anchor of identity and worth. Together, these tools bring wholeness, physically, emotionally, and mentally.

As we move forward through the process, we will understand how to let go of false ideas that tie spiritual values to food restriction. We will be able to embrace stewardship, grace, and health as we find a community that supports our healing journey.

This journey is about finding God’s promise of healing as we seek it through every means He has provided. Call your local Christian counselor to start your journey of freedom from disordered eating to discover hope!

item.title: What to Do If You Encounter Signs of Infidelity in Your Spouse
item.description:
No one would like to think that it could happen to them, but any marriage can fall prey to infidelity. Infidelity is one of the main reasons why couples get divorced, and still, some couples experience infidelity and manage to work through it without arriving at divorce. There are many reasons why infidelity occurs. They can be more complex than the stereotypical image of an unhappy couple who turn outside the relationship to have their needs met.

There are some signs to look out for that can suggest that infidelity is either taking place or will happen soon. No one wants to be blindsided. Being aware of these possible signs will help you potentially nip the issue in the bud, or it may help you initiate a necessary conversation to address concerns.

When it comes to something as complex as human behavior and infidelity, one needs to be careful about how they read signs. Signs can be misinterpreted, or they may be pointing to something else entirely. While trusting your instincts if you feel something is wrong is not a bad way to go, proceeding with caution and being careful about making unfounded accusations is also a wise course of action.

Weigh the signs judiciously, and create room for a conversation with your spouse to explain their behavior. Below are a few of the signs to look out for that may point to infidelity.

Some Classic Signs of Infidelity

When a person is having an affair, whether that affair is an exclusively emotional one, a purely physical one, or one that is physical with real affections involved, it affects and changes them. Some of those changes may be subtle, while others are drastic and easy to spot. Human beings are creatures of habit, and we settle into patterns of behavior.

When new patterns of behavior emerge, and they don’t have a cause you can easily identify, that should raise some questions. Some patterns of behavior would suggest an attraction outside the primary relationship, and you should be aware of these. To ensure judicious wisdom when evaluating these signs, some alternative readings will be offered that may be worth thinking through to ensure that you’ve eliminated other, possibly innocent interpretations.

Sudden Interest in Their Appearance

If a person who hasn’t been very concerned about how they look suddenly begins to spend time grooming themselves, getting in shape, buying new clothes, cologne/perfume, and underwear, that should raise some concerns.

Of course, people can spark an interest in these things for a variety of reasons. Some benign reasons include starting a new job with different standards of dress and appearance, a midlife crisis, or experiencing a significant event that transforms their outlook on life, such as the death of a friend or a health scare.

You know what’s going on in your spouse’s life. If none of the alternatives resonate, their sudden interest in their appearance may be because of a third party. That doesn’t mean an affair is happening, but it might be pointing to your spouse having an attraction toward someone else and wanting to impress them.

Suspicious Financial Activity

Infidelity often has financial implications. Buying gifts, booking hotel rooms, and extra gas from driving farther than usual are a few extra expenses that may be evident. There is often a financial trail when infidelity is happening.

If you find unexplained purchases on your credit card, a larger phone or gas bill than the norm, and other financial oddities, it’s good to ask some questions. Keep in mind that with realities such as gambling addiction, shady financial practices from your spouse may stem from another source entirely, other than having an affair.

Increased Desire for Privacy, Secretive Behavior

In most healthy relationships, there is openness and a willingness to be held accountable. That doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be boundaries in a relationship, as boundaries can promote the health of a relationship and the people in it. However, changes in behavior can indicate a problem.

Hiding their phone from view when you’re near, no longer using the family computer to do their work, taking calls outside the room, changing their cloud storage settings so their devices don’t sync with the family account, and generally shutting off a part of themselves are a few indications that can point to something such as infidelity taking place. Other things like porn addiction could also explain this behavior, but that, too, requires a conversation.

Decreased Sexual Interest

Unexplained changes in sexual behavior in the marriage can also point to infidelity, inasmuch as those needs might be getting met elsewhere. Libido can change due to mental health challenges such as depression and certain medications. Pressures in life can also lower one’s libido. If these are excluded, and what’s left doesn’t quite add up, it may be a sign of infidelity.

Compensatory Behavior

Sometimes people will act nicer to make up for a guilty conscience or to cover up any suspicions of inappropriate behavior. Unexpected gifts that aren’t part of the norm or attached to significant events such as birthdays or anniversaries are often part of that compensatory behavior.

A partner may become more attentive, patient, sweet, generous, or compassionate. If such behavior is out of the norm for your spouse, and it isn’t attached to any significant events in their life (such as a new or renewed relationship with the Lord), some questions may be warranted.

Becoming Uninvolved

Infidelity requires energy, whether physical, mental, or emotional. With their energy being poured into the affair, you may find that they don’t have energy for their primary relationship. They may begin checking out of the relationship.

This happens in various ways, such as not fighting with you anymore and indicating they don’t seem to care one way or another, staying at work longer, unexplained absences and trips away from home, and other unusual things. They may not have the energy to play with the kids as much as before or be willing to help as much around the house.

There are other possibilities for these behaviors. This emotional and physical detachment may be the result of depression in men, for instance. Still, it may also signal that their energy is being used elsewhere.

Inadequate Responses When Questioned About Their Behavior

If you approach your spouse with concerns, consider their response. If you bring up things you’ve seen and heard that make you think infidelity is taking place, and their only response is anger, that can point to something they are trying to hide. Similarly, if they try to gaslight you, that too could point to the truth of the matter.

Consider the Signs Carefully

People aren’t necessarily formulaic about how they conduct affairs. The presence or absence of any one sign doesn’t mean it’s conclusive that an affair is happening. A bunch of signs taken together is certainly more suggestive of what’s going on.

Looking Beyond the Signs

Unless there is something conclusive, such as you walking in on your spouse having an affair or coming across a conversation or texts that show that an affair (emotional or physical) is taking place, one has to rely on signs and hints. Whether it’s your gut or a strange occurrence that has you on alert, it’s important to think about what comes next.

Talk through it Having a conversation about whether something might be going on can be difficult. Accusations can have repercussions for your relationship, but it’s important to bring up concerns and talk through them thoroughly.

It may turn out that there’s something else entirely that’s going on. If it is an affair, you may want to find out the details of the affair: who the affair is/was with, its duration, whether there is affection shared between them, and so on.

If there is no affair, if what raised your concerns was linked to any boundaries (for instance, privacy and what was perceived as secretive behavior), your spouse may need to consider that their boundary may be causing distress. Talk about changes you can make together.

Consider seeking help Express your concerns empathetically and clearly, indicating the various things you’ve seen that have brought you to this place, and talk through how to possibly remedy them. Affairs happen for a variety of reasons. Talking with your spouse about what may have led them to have an affair may bring up many emotions and questions about your relationship.

Having this conversation under the guidance of a trained and licensed marriage therapist can help you explore and unpack these questions and emotions in a constructive and safe space. Infidelity doesn’t mean the end of your relationship. It is possible to work through the issues and emerge stronger on the other side.

To connect with a counselor who can help, reach out to someone on this site.

Photo:
“Fighting”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post What to Do If You Encounter Signs of Infidelity in Your Spouse appeared first on Vancouver Christian Counseling.

item.title: 5 Techniques that May Aid Self-Care for Anxiety
item.description:
The term “self-care” has taken a winding path in recent years due to its popularity in wellness communities. But self-care for anxiety is different. Evidence shows that it employs specific skill-based techniques to help reduce anxiety levels in those who suffer from generalized social anxiety.

More than a bubble bath or pedicure, self-care for anxiety is based on proven research supported by clinical trials. For example, mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) has been tested alongside medication-based treatment, and its findings in one study show that it offers comparable results to a specific, commonly prescribed medication for generalized anxiety disorder.

While one study doesn’t negate the use of medicine to treat anxiety, it does show that there’s hope in a layered treatment plan that includes a wide range of self-care for anxiety treatment.

Why MBSR Works in Self-Care for Anxiety

Much of the literature that has recently been released points to the efficacy of mindfulness intervention because it uses small, doable techniques that are simple to apply in the midst of everyday life. As opposed to a long-awaited rest-filled vacation or a specific self-care day of the week, MBSR gives a person practical ways to fuel calm throughout their week.

Another reason MBSR is often successful is that it can integrate multiple emotional regulation interventions that are interchangeable. Other benefits are that it has a high patient satisfaction rating, high levels of compliance, and, in some studies, even though MBSR can be used to treat other diagnoses, patients reported decreased anxiety levels.

Five Self-Care for Anxiety Techniques

One thing to keep in mind with each of these techniques is that self-care for anxiety is not a one-and-done treatment plan. In fact, incorporating each of these techniques into your everyday life is what fuels the reduction in anxiety levels. Trying a few breathing exercises once or twice, for example, will only help you in that particular moment.

However, if you’re incorporating breathing exercises multiple days each week, you may find that the exercises help you pay attention to your body and emotions throughout the day – one of the goals of mindfulness practices as a whole. Treating something you don’t see coming is much more difficult than treating something you can name, recognize, and have experience with.

You gain confidence that these techniques will work when you apply them in your everyday life, whether at work, at home, or at school.

Breathing: Many people recognize the benefits of deep breathing, but it has been proven to decrease anxiety in peer-reviewed studies by several reputable research companies.

Some options for breathing exercises include diaphragmatic breathing, paced slow breathing, breathing with biofeedback, and alternate-nostril breathing (ANB).

Low-Intensity Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: LICBT is a form of therapy that involves meeting with a practitioner on a short-term basis. You’ll receive tools to help you learn about stress management and anxiety-reducing practices.

LICBT is a type of therapy that allows for a cost-effective way to treat anxiety, particularly when someone has low to moderate generalized anxiety. It’s a series of tools that can be offered with practitioners and some without, particularly internet-based CBT.

For patients with cost barriers, online CBT can provide tools to help you learn more about the causes and treatments for anxiety. These can be delivered in the form of educational materials; apps that help you track your feelings, mood, and behaviors related to anxiety; and journals that help you assess situational anxiety.

However, any therapy available through an app will likely treat generalized anxiety. If you suffer from a different form of anxiety or you want more personalized attention, seeing a licensed therapist is preferable. This way, you can work one-on-one in a safe setting where you’re able to get regular feedback from a trained counselor about the anxiety you’re learning how to process.

Emotional Regulation Flexibility: Regulating emotions is a key component of anxiety reduction because it helps a person distinguish between their present reality and what they feel about their present reality – two different things.

ER flexibility has been shown to impact people suffering from anxiety because it teaches them how to integrate multiple tools – switching between them – to help lower their anxiety in various situations. Some of these tools include reframing your thoughts (discussed below) and acceptance.

Acceptance requires allowing your emotions, recognizing their triggers, and then deciding which strategy is best to employ. Instead of trying to avoid your emotions or distract yourself from them, this tool can be helpful when an outcome is out of your hands.

Sometimes called ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy), this tool recognizes why you’re feeling anxious, helps you admit that you are feeling anxious about something that’s outside your control (such as a test result), and then gives you enough pause to choose another strategy – such as disengaging from your anxiety because you know the mental spiral you’re in will not change anything.

Reframing: Also known as reappraisal, this practice involves challenging fearful beliefs related to situations that cause anxiety and transitioning fixed mindset processes to growth-oriented thinking.

Reframing can be incorporated into cognitive therapy, and it can help people who suffer from anxiety because it integrates new thought processes into everyday life. Applied regularly, reframing can help someone avoid rumination or looping thoughts that don’t lead to the abatement of their stress. In fact, spiraling thoughts can exacerbate cognitive stalling.

An example of reframing is when someone is in a social situation and they fear others’ unspoken responses. If you’re giving a speech, for instance, and you see a room filled with blank faces staring back at you, the anxious thought may be that they’re all bored, and you start to panic and lose your place. However, reframing would involve telling yourself, “They’re likely just concentrating on what I’m saying.”

Another example is when faced with an unknown, you start to feel your heart racing and your temperature rise. Physical cues could trigger anxious thoughts that convince you you’re not going to escape the situation. A reframed thought might be, “This is just how my body responds to stress, and while unknowns are challenging, they are to be expected in life. It’s okay to feel this, and these feelings will pass soon.”

Exposure Therapy: Exposure therapy involves addressing fears based on a scale, from lowest to highest, without safety mechanisms to run to.

In the presence of a licensed therapist, exposure therapy can gradually help someone address what causes their anxiety, slowly making the stimuli no longer elicit stress responses and therefore lowering their overall anxiety level.

A practitioner helps you rate what causes your anxiety from the greatest anxiety to the least, and you gradually address the anxiety-causing stimuli over time. By the end, you come to disassociate the fearful stimuli that once caused anxiety from stress. Instead, you associate it with a safe environment.

Self-care for anxiety can involve a variety of self-imposed tools and therapeutic tools, depending on your budget, how severe your anxiety is, and whether you’re comfortable meeting with a licensed therapist. If you’ve been fearful of meeting with a counselor about your anxiety, call one of our offices.

A caring staff member will walk you through what to expect at your first session, and you’ll be matched with a counselor who specializes in anxiety disorders.

Anxiety isn’t anything to feel ashamed of or be embarrassed by, as many people suffer from it in various forms. In fact, learning how to manage it through self-care for anxiety techniques is often helpful for anyone – teaching emotional regulation skills, how to think about what you’re thinking, asking if your thoughts are true, and learning to recognize anxiety triggers.

Many people gain such powerful life skills from learning about anxiety and how it has shaped them that they’re able to grow in their ability to manage setbacks, disappointments, and unexpected life circumstances throughout their lifetime. Learning how to manage anxiety is a skill that benefits your family, too.

Family members struggling with anxiety may struggle to interact with family members or attend family events related to their anxiety. Sometimes after a person has met with a counselor to address their anxiety, it’s helpful to attend family counseling so that their family members can help them with things like reframing and emotional regulation flexibility.

Of course, this depends on the family and how much siblings and parents have been impacted. But it can give them tools and language to help you and others impacted by this mental health condition.

To meet with a counselor and learn more about these self-care techniques, contact our office today and speak to a representative.

item.title: Coping with Grief During the Holidays Years After Loss
item.description:
It’s expected that the first few years after losing someone, the holidays are a struggle. People often understand that declining invitations and tearing up during Christmas dinner is all part of grieving during the holidays. But what about when it’s five or 10 years later? It seems the world assumes you’ve moved on, that the heartache has healed, and that you’re ready to face the holidays with nothing but a smile.

The reality is that coping with grief during the holidays doesn’t follow a timeline, and the assumption that it should can make holidays more isolating. Life has gone on without them, and you have created new traditions, gained new family members, and found moments of genuine happiness. Yet, when December arrives, the absence resurfaces in ways that catch you off guard and make you question whether you are making progress in your healing.

It’s not a confusion about grief. It’s about the expectation that you should have had enough time to erase it. Coping with grief years after the loss means that learning to heal and ongoing loss are not opposites. They appear together during seasons, centered on memory and tradition.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NASB

When Grief Returns After Years of Feeling Fine

There was a time when you thought you had it figured out, and the daily reminders had softened. You felt as though you had learned to live around the space that was left. Then the holidays arrive, and now you find yourself crying in the grocery store because you passed their favorite cookies. Maybe you become overwhelmed during a church service for reasons you can’t quite articulate.

This recurrence of grief doesn’t mean you have regressed or that your healing has unraveled. It simply reflects that there are seasons that carry concentrated memories. The holidays are dense with moments that remind you of who’s missing.

Long-term holiday grief can be particularly disorienting because it often arrives without warning. You have managed through other Decembers well, so you assume that this year will be the same. Then, out of the blue, you hear a song or a memory mentioned, and the loss feels fresh again.

Christian counselors understand that this pattern is typical. Grief is not linear, and anniversaries have a way of awakening dormant emotions. There’s no indication of weakness just because you are coping with grief years after the loss. It reflects the depth of connection that continues even when the physical presence is gone.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, NASB

Navigating Traditions with People Who Never Knew Them

There’s no doubt that your family has changed since you lost someone. You may have remarried, and children have been born. There are people who will never remember the person except through stories. New relatives have joined holiday gatherings, bringing traditions and expectations. It’s a natural and healthy evolution, even though it creates a complicated emotional landscape.

Trying to honor someone’s memory when most of the people at the table have never met them can seem uncomfortable. You want to respect the desire for a joyful holiday season, yet you’re not able to erase them from the celebration.

The challenge of coping with grief in a family is finding a way to acknowledge the loss without making it the center of everyone’s experience. This may mean quietly setting a place for them in your heart rather than at the table, or sharing a story or incorporating something they loved into the celebration.

Christian counselors can help identify authenticity rather than obligation or performance. The goal isn’t to maintain comfort at the expense of reality, but it’s also not to force grief onto people who didn’t share the relationship with the person who is no longer present at the holiday gathering.

This balance requires permission to honor your own needs while simultaneously recognizing that others are building their own holiday experience and may not place the same emotional weight on it.

A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance. – Ecclesiastes 3:4, NASB

The Loneliness of Long-Term Grief

In the early days, support was abundant as people were checking in and bringing meals to acknowledge your heartbreak of losing your loved one. But as years passed, the support typically faded, and the culture around you operated on the assumption that grief had a reasonable expiration date.

If you’re still struggling years later, or you feel as if something must be wrong with you, it can result in a particular kind of isolation during the holidays. You want to be grateful and cheerful, yet you quietly manage waves of sadness that others no longer recognize.

Sometimes you feel as though you must carry your grief secretly because there is a lack of social permission to express it in an ongoing way, so you find yourself smiling through holiday parties and internally navigating between celebration and sorrow. You try to participate in traditions, only to notice who isn’t there.

Everyone around you has moved on, so you may start to question your own feelings, thinking that you should be over it by now. That thought process reflects the cultural message we all hear about grief. The natural reality is that some relationships leave permanent marks, and the holidays have a way of making those marks visible again.

Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. – Romans 12:15, NASB

The Fear of Forgetting and the Guilt of Moving Forward

Long-term grief comes with a unique struggle of holding on and letting go. You want to remember everything about them, from their voice to their mannerisms. Memory, however, isn’t static, and as years pass, some details will inevitably fade.

The fading of memories creates a low-level panic during the holidays when you’re surrounded by reminders that also highlight what you can no longer recall with precision. You have built a life that includes joy and new experiences, allowing you to laugh at holiday gatherings while creating new traditions. Sometimes change and happiness bring a sense of guilt.

Coping with grief years after the loss has occurred involves navigating this tricky balance of honoring the past and not being trapped in it. Moving forward without feeling like you’re leaving your loved one behind often comes with intense anxiety.

Christian counselors understand that these aren’t competing goals and that remembering and living aren’t mutually exclusive. The love you had for your person doesn’t mean you have to remain frozen in that moment of loss, and experiencing new joy doesn’t diminish what they meant to you.

It is possible to experience a holiday that holds both memory and a connection to the present moment. You can miss someone and appreciate the people who are currently at your table. There are times the guilt that accompanies this duality is a signal that you’re holding yourself to an impossible standard. Moving forward doesn’t mean you’re forgetting, and remembering doesn’t require your constant sorrow.

For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. – Romans 8:38-39, NASB

Living with Grief That Has Softened but Not Disappeared

Grief often changes shape years after a loss. It is no longer the breathtaking pain of early bereavement, but instead it is quieter and more integrated into the fabric of your life. This does not mean it is gone during the holidays, and you may be surprised at how present it still feels. This is not a representation of failure, but rather a reality: some losses become a part of who you are, rather than something to get over.

Scripture promises comfort during these times, but it’s not always the absence of pain. It sometimes looks like the strength to carry both grief and gratitude in the same moment. This is a reflection of wisdom: knowing that you can honor a person and their memory as you fully participate in your current life. Coping with grief during the holidays years after is not about resolution, but about rhythm and learning the patterns of when grief tends to surface.

Holidays are likely to carry a significant degree of bittersweetness. Yet, they can become something you move through with honesty and hope, knowing that the love that causes the ache is the same love that makes the present meaningful.

Navigating the holidays can be difficult. If you’re struggling with grief years after loss, a Christian counselor can help. Call a counselor to learn more today.

item.title: Relationship Depression: 11 Red Flags and How to Cope
item.description:
Relationship depression is a term used to describe depression that develops as a result of a problematic relationship. It is not a formal medical diagnosis.

Often cyclical in nature, it tends to create a loop in which the relationship problems that trigger the depression aggravate the depressed person’s symptoms. This increases the disconnect between them and their partner, creating frustration or resentment. It further damages their relationship dynamics through conflicts caused by a lack of communication and misunderstandings.

Relationships and Mental Health

Studies show that there is a close link between mental health and the quality of your relationships. Strong, supportive relationships, for instance, provide comfort, security, emotional support, and connection. This can give your mood a boost, help you maintain a positive outlook on life, and have a beneficial impact on your overall mental well-being.

Toxic or abusive relationships, on the other hand, can lead you to question your self-worth. They can also cause you to feel stressed, anxious, or depressed. Negative thinking patterns can arise that may contribute to or activate an underlying mental health struggle.

Because of this interconnectedness, any relationship can become strained by the symptoms of depression. It begins as the depressed person starts to withdraw from his or her partner and seems to lose interest in the things they used to enjoy doing together. Communication deteriorates, which can be misinterpreted as rejection and falling out of love. The depression is causing him or her to struggle to connect and making even simple interactions feel exhausting.

Possible Causes of Relationship Depression

There is no one definitive cause of relationship depression, but contributing factors can include a range of issues. Some possible examples include:

  • A spouse’s infidelity
  • Having your trust betrayed by your spouse
  • Physical or emotional abuse
  • Being consistently disappointed by the person you thought you could rely on
  • Communication breakdowns that cause you to feel misunderstood or emotionally disconnected
  • Unresolved conflicts that keep piling up
  • Financial stress
  • Mismatched expectations about roles and responsibilities in the relationship

Common Red Flags of Relationship Depression

Relationship depression tends to sink in gradually over time, and you may not notice the subtle changes in your thoughts and behavior patterns. If left unrecognized and unaddressed, however, it can impact every area of your life. It can interfere with your ability to interact with others in a healthy way and even impair your capacity to engage in your day-to-day responsibilities.

Common red flags that should not be ignored include:

Persistent sadness You may experience persistent sadness and frequent tears without knowing why.

Negative outlook You may feel helpless and hopeless, unable to see anything in a positive light, believe life isn’t worth living, and/or have thoughts of death or suicide.

Low self-esteem You may believe that you are a failure, worthless, unlovable, or a burden, and therefore pull away from the other person rather than express your needs or ask for help.

Emotional withdrawal You withdraw from the other person, stop sharing your thoughts and feelings with him or her, avoid eye contact, and are less responsive to his or her needs.

Irritability You may experience mood swings and increased irritability, becoming easily annoyed or frustrated, and snapping at seemingly small things.

Loss of intimacy You experience reduced feelings of affection toward your partner, a decline in physical intimacy, and avoidance of sexual contact.

Physical symptoms You may feel physically or mentally exhausted; experience changes in your sleeping and eating patterns, such as trouble sleeping or sleeping more than usual, or loss of appetite or binge eating; gastrointestinal problems; loss of sexual desire; and unexplained aches or pains.

Impaired communication You have trouble thinking clearly, struggle to articulate your feelings, feel disconnected from the other person, are reluctant to discuss important issues, and your relationship is full of conflict, misunderstandings, and arguments.

Dulling of your emotions You may feel emotionally numb; struggle to connect or express love and affection toward your partner; and feel indifferent to what he or she does or feels.

Loss of interest in things you used to do together Things you and the other person used to enjoy doing together may seem meaningless, and you may find yourself losing interest in doing them.

Distorted perceptions You may, for instance, mistakenly believe your relationship is the cause of your feelings of emptiness and depression, that it has lost its significance, and/or feel trapped or suffocated by it.

Practical Steps to Help You Cope with Relationship Depression

Journal Journaling about your feelings helps you identify and process them, get them out of your head and onto paper, and be able to identify your triggers.

Prioritize self-care Prioritize your health and well-being by getting enough sleep, eating balanced, nutritious meals, staying hydrated, getting some form of regular exercise, and setting healthy boundaries.

Stop listening to the negative Start talking to yourself instead of listening to your negative self-talk. Reject it and replace it with more realistic, positive statements that edify, encourage, and lift you up.

Communicate with your partner Even if you feel too tired to talk, ashamed, or undeserving of anything good, make an effort to have an open, honest conversation with your partner. Talk about your thoughts, feelings, and the symptoms and sensations you are experiencing, so he or she can understand what you are going through. This will help them know how to help and support you.

Avoid isolating Instead of pulling away and isolating, make an effort to connect with your partner, even if it’s just in simple ways such as taking a walk together.

Turn your focus onto God Take your eyes off your present circumstances and focus instead on the truths in God’s Word and on His steadfast, everlasting love for you.

Consider counseling Counseling provides a safe, nonjudgmental space where you can learn to identify and process your feelings and relationship concerns under the guidance of a trained mental health professional. They can also help you determine whether your depression really is being caused by your relationship, or by something else going on in your life.

How To Help and Support a Depressed Partner

Get informed Learning as much as you can about depression and its symptoms can help you better identify and understand what your partner is struggling with, identify the signs, and not take his or her behavior personally.

Talk about it Instead of ignoring the issue, talk to your partner about what you are seeing without being critical or judgmental. Ask what he or she is feeling, and offer encouragement and validation.

Be patient and empathetic Be patient and empathetic toward your partner and offer a listening ear. Let them know that you love and support them, and be a safe place to turn for validation and understanding. Make sure they know you won’t be dismissive of their feelings.

Work together as a team Ask your partner what you can do and what changes you can make to help him or her deal with his or her symptoms. Let them know that you are there for them and suggest working as a team to identify stressors and triggers together, and brainstorm ways they can cope with them when they arise.

Encourage professional help Encourage your partner to pursue counseling, and offer to go with them.

To learn more or address relationship depression in your life, counseling can help. If you would like to set up a risk-free appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors in our online directory, please call the office.

item.title: Navigating Depression and Relationships Through Biblical Hope
item.description:
Depression in a marriage can be particularly isolating. The person who knows you best feels like a stranger, and the relationship that once brought comfort now seems like another weight to carry.

Depression can impact relationships in ways that challenge everything you thought you understood about partnership. It is not simply sadness affecting two people, depression can reshape the connection, communication, and experience with each other’s presence.

Living with depression in a marriage extends beyond what most couples anticipate during their wedding vows. One spouse may feel like they’re watching helplessly from the shore as their partner feels as though they’re struggling to keep their head above water. The conversations that once flowed naturally now require tremendous effort.

Affection becomes complicated when one spouse barely feels anything. The distance created by these shifts has nothing to do with lost love, but rather an illness that doesn’t discriminate in people or marriages.

The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NIV

When Depression Changes How You See Each Other

Perception can become distorted by depression in ways that affect marital dynamics. The spouse experiencing depression often misreads the meaning behind comments and withdraws from conversations that may feel too demanding.

All the while, the other partner sees the distance as having done something wrong and as them no longer being enough. This misunderstanding eventually builds, creating a parallel experience of loneliness while being in the same house.

Recognizing that depression speaks through a filter of negativity and hopelessness is a challenge. It convinces the person experiencing depression that they are a burden and their spouse would be better without them, and that nothing will improve.

On the other side of the relationship, depression feels like a rejection when it is actually a symptom. Neither perspective presents the whole truth, and both feel entirely real to the person experiencing them.

Christian counselors address this gap between perception and reality by helping couples understand that depression is not a reflection of the marriage’s worth or the other person’s value. They create a faith-based plan to help both partners navigate the misconception that depression has placed in the relationship and navigate toward healing for both sides.

Unpredictability complicates the matter of depression even more. There are days when you glimpse the relationship you remember, only to return to a difficult day and feel like a failure.

The spouse without depression may rotate between compassion and frustration, guilt and resentment. These competing emotions do not make them a bad partner. It makes them human. Both people in the relationship must acknowledge depression; it affects both people, both people hurt, and both need support.

Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. – Colossians 3:13, NIV

The Weight of Unspoken Expectations

Marriage carries certain expectations regarding emotional availability, shared responsibilities, and support that go both ways. Depression doesn’t ask for permission before disrupting each of these areas. The person struggling with depression may not be able to complete the daily tasks or engage in activities they want to enjoy. This isn’t to say they are being neglectful. It is the nature of the illness that depletes the energy and motivation.

The spouse without depression may feel they are carrying the weight of two people and receiving little in return. The resentment that builds is not because they do not love their spouse, but because it is a response to the imbalance that feels unsustainable.

This leads to hesitation in expressing their own struggles for fear of worsening the condition of their partner. The result is a silence that creates a burden, leaving one person exhausted and the other unaware of the full impact that the illness is having on the relationship.

Christian counselors recognize that both people must address the unspoken expectations in honest conversation about capacity and need. They understand that depression doesn’t excuse behavior, but it requires a recalibration of what is realistic during hard times.

When couples insist on maintaining pre-depression standards, the relationship often ends up in a cycle of disappointment and self-blame. Grace is essential in the middle of a relationship where one partner struggles with depression.

So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. – Isaiah 41:10, NIV

Communicating When Words Feel Impossible

Communication can be affected subtly and profoundly by depression. The depressed spouse struggles to articulate their experience and defaults to “I’m fine” when they’re actually in the middle of their struggle.

On the other side, their spouse learns to read silence, body language, and changes in routine, trying to gauge the severity of the depression without asking. This unspoken dance can work for a time, but it can ultimately result in isolation for both people.

When depression convinces someone that sharing their thoughts will burden their spouse, or that no one can truly understand, they might withdraw not from lack of trust but from the false belief that silence protects the other person. No one can truly understand. The spouse may withdraw because of a false belief that silence protects the other person.

Meanwhile, the spouse without depression may avoid difficult topics for fear of bringing up concerns that will trigger a crisis or communicating criticism. Each of these forms of silence stems from care, and at the same time, contributes to the distance that has been created by depression.

Communicating through depression means accepting imperfect conversations. This means the spouse with depression chooses not to agree with the thought that they shouldn’t bother anyone, and the other spouse needs to express without guilt.

These conversations involve acknowledging that some days words won’t come easily, but presence matters more than a perfect dialogue. Depression and relationships aren’t healed through grand gestures, but by the small effort to remain connected, even when you want to retreat.

Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing. – 1 Thessalonians 5:11, NIV

Finding Hope Without Minimizing Pain

When depression threatens to undermine everything else, faith offers a foundation. It may not be a quick fix or guarantee of immediate relief, but when the couple facing depression in their marriage turns to Scripture, they find hope in God’s plan. This requires practical support, professional treatment, and a community that understands mental illness doesn’t reflect a weak faith.

A Christian counselor’s work within a faith-based framework helped a couple acknowledge the absolute need for Christ along with clinical intervention. Medication, therapy, and lifestyle changes aren’t signs of spiritual failure. They are tools that support healing in the process of navigating depression in relationships.

There needs to be spiritual, grounding, and practical resources. Prayer and Scripture offer comfort and peace that surpasses all understanding. Understanding the neuroscience of depression is also important.

In the context of depression and relationships, hope looks different than in other circumstances. It doesn’t involve returning to how things were before; it focuses on building something sustainable for the marriage now. It requires recognizing depression, which may be long-term, but a marriage can adapt without losing its meaning.

Navigating depression together can deepen their bond in unexpected ways and create empathy that would not have developed. Otherwise, this doesn’t minimize the pain. It acknowledges that suffering can coexist with growth.

And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast. – 1 Peter 5:10, NIV

Biblical Hope

Depression and relationships do not have a predictable path. Some couples find healing relatively quickly with the right support, while others face ongoing challenges that require continuous adjustment in the marriage. But what remains consistent is the need for both partners to receive care. Marriage wasn’t designed for us to navigate alone, and neither was depression.

The hope that sustains couples through depression is knowing that God’s presence remains constant when everything feels uncertain. It is about finding faith and strength to face another day, and the ability to forgive the limitations each of you carries. Depression may change how you relate to one another for a season, but it does not define whether the marriage survives.

With faith, commitment, and professional support, couples can navigate the darkest valleys together toward brighter mornings. Contact our office today to learn more and to schedule an appointment with one of the Christian counselors near you.

item.title: Anxiety and the Sabbath Reset
item.description:
Work, family life, carpools, commutes, after-school activities, and errands, oh my! Life sure can get busy when you’re working or trying to raise a family. This feels even more so when you’re trying to do both. Living a fruitful life can be a blessing, but when it’s too busy, it can cause anxiety, stress, and even affect your physical health.

Don’t have time for a vacation? Can’t eliminate anything from your to-do list? While the occasional extended period of rest is ideal for recuperating from a busy lifestyle, it’s not always practical. But even the busiest people can spare one day a week to focus on rest. In fact, God wants you to. He called it Sabbath.

You Need Rest

You may think that pushing yourself even when tired and overwhelmed is an admirable thing. Of course, it is to a certain extent. It’s good to have the willpower and tenacity to stick with a project, even when you’re feeling overwhelmed by it. And this is often praised in our modern society because it’s labeled as a good work ethic. But there comes a point where that perseverance goes from noble to harmful.

Taking a Sabbath

God instructs us to take a Sabbath. Even He rested on the seventh day of creation. Is God giving you that direct command just to see if you’re obedient? This, like all of God’s other directives, is for your own good, not just to force you into compliance.

Of course, God values a good work ethic. This can be seen in multiple verses across Scripture (Proverbs 14:23, Proverbs 12:24, Colossians 3:23). But He also recognizes our need for rest. Jesus acknowledges this in Mark 2: “Then he said to them, ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.’” (Mark 2:27, NIV)

This verse explains not only God’s law but also gives a glimpse of His heart. God’s commandment to “‘Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy,’” (Exodus 20:8, NIV) is an invitation to you to step out of your normal, frantic routine and to take a day of rest to reflect on the goodness of God.

Psychologists Agree

Most psychologists and psychiatrists would give you the same advice that Scripture commands. That’s because those who study the human brain and emotions know that it’s not designed to live in a constant state of chaos and busyness. Your brain needs intentional periods of rest to maintain cognitive function and emotional regulation.

In the clinical world, this is often referred to as cognitive offloading. Without downtime, your stress response remains constantly activated. This can lead to anxiety. Maybe you’re familiar with this anxiety because you feel it every Monday morning. This happens because, without a Sabbath, you end up carrying the burdens of last week’s stress directly into the new week.

A day of rest works like a circuit breaker because it allows your nervous system to reset. While you might feel like you don’t have time to take a break, research shows that taking time to relax actually increases long-term productivity.

How to Take a Sabbath

Knowing that you should take a Sabbath every week is more than half the battle, but you also have to know how to do it well. Here are some ideas to help you make the most of your weekly respite.

Place God at the center

The original intent of the Sabbath was to carve out an intentional day, in the midst of a busy life, to honor God. And this idea still holds true today. To fully enjoy your Sabbath, you should, as the Bible directs, keep it holy. That means don’t crowd your day with mundane things. Instead, make an intentional plan to worship your Heavenly Father, to learn about Him, and to invite Him into your life every Sabbath.

When you place God at the center of your free time, you’re giving Him a special gift. You’re showing God you trust Him and honoring Him by giving your precious free time to Him. And when you do, He will reciprocate. Because the Sabbath is actually a gift to you from a Heavenly Father who knows how exhausting life can be.

Choose your day

Your Sabbath doesn’t necessarily have to be on Sunday, though that’s perhaps the most commonly observed day of rest. Most churches meet on Sunday, and many businesses close early, so it might be easier for you to not only avoid the distractions of errands but to find deliberate time with God.

For some, it’s not always practical to take Sundays off. You have to choose the day that works best for your schedule.

Establish rules

It’s wise to establish rules or construct boundaries for your day of rest because it’s important to protect this precious time. Rules and boundaries help you to keep yourself accountable and help others know what you are and are not willing to do on that day.

Maybe you are willing to hang out with friends and family, or perhaps you would be better served to spend the day alone. Maybe you want to sleep in late on your day off and don’t want to be disturbed, or you would rather get up early to watch the sunrise. By creating a few simple rules for yourself and others to follow, you can protect the peace of your special day.

Work smarter, not harder

One of the best ways to ensure that you can take a Sabbath day without filling it with stray errands is to find the most efficient ways to complete your errands during the week. That might seem like obvious advice, but it often goes unheeded. It’s good to occasionally pause and take a look at how you complete tasks. You might find that you do things out of habit, and you might not realize that there are newer, more efficient ways of doing these things.

For example, maybe you’re in the habit of paying your electricity bill by check every month. But have you explored the option of going digital with automatic payments? Many companies offer this service and even give a discount to customers who pay this way.

Don’t have the time to run to the grocery store? Use online shopping services or multitask by going grocery shopping with a friend. That way, you can get your socializing in while still completing a necessary task.

Working smarter gives you the opportunity to take a much-needed break, even if your life feels overwhelmingly busy.

Be prepared

When possible, prepare yourself and your surroundings for your day of rest. Make sure that the house is clean before your Sabbath day approaches and that your errands are taken care of. It’s difficult to fully relax in the midst of a chaotic reminder of future chores.

Have some of your favorite activities ready and at your disposal. Prepare a praise and worship playlist for some solo worship. Keep your Bible accessible, along with some highlighters and a notebook for a study of God’s Word.

You might also find that passive rest is beneficial. Gather a stack of books you’ve been meaning to read, some new video games, or create a list of bingeable television shows you can watch. Use these activities to truly decompress, not just kill time. Even more beneficial, get outside. Walk, relax, feel the sun. Resting in the beauty of God’s creation is a wonderful way to recharge on the Sabbath.

Seeking Professional Help

While the Sabbath is a powerful tool to help you strike a balance in your life, it’s also important to acknowledge that chronic anxiety sometimes requires more than just a day of rest. A licensed therapist or counselor can provide you with specific clinical tools that can help you overcome some of your deeper emotional challenges.

If your anxiety feels unmanageable, even in a season of rest, make an appointment with one of our Christian therapists. Our mental health professionals can help you take the courageous next step toward finding peace.

Resources:
The Imperative of Rest: Enhancing Spirituality and Productivity in a Contemporary Society https://irasspublisher.com/assets/articles/1771568681.pdf

item.title: Recognizing Emotional Burnout in Church Ministry
item.description:
Faith communities hold the unspoken expectation that serving should always be fulfilling. This means that the moment you accept a role in children’s ministry, join the worship team, or volunteer for outreach, there is an assumption that joy and purpose will naturally follow. But when serving begins to feel heavy, it shifts to something different. What once felt life-giving becomes draining and uninteresting.

Emotional burnout doesn’t come with loud noises or big warning signs. It shows up quietly, disguised as a spiritual discipline of perseverance. Those of us who are deeply invested in our church recognize that it often feels like admitting failure in our faith.

The Pressure to Say Yes and Emotional Burnout

In the church culture, people who are always available are often celebrated. We have admiration for those who lead Bible studies, coordinate events, manage the tech booth, and still attend prayer meetings. The result is an environment where saying no feels like letting God down or abandoning the community. This can create a distorted message in which rest is viewed as selfishness and boundaries as a lack of commitment.

We impose expectations that conflict with what our bodies and minds can actually sustain, without realizing it. The result is a constant push to do more, even though everything in us is asking for less, leading to exhaustion that is not just physical.

Emotional burnout begins to permeate every area of life. Instead of feeling the joy of Sunday mornings, we are filled with dread as we set off to do our weekly service task. Our worship, which should be a source of renewal, has become a performance that we must maintain.

The emotional burnout in church ministry is accompanied by a layer of guilt that other forms of burnout don’t carry. It’s a spiritual component that questions whether or not fatigue is a sign of weak faith or insufficient trust in God. The resulting internal battle makes it hard to step back because that feels like we’re stepping away from God.

Christian counselors often see individuals who have been serving faithfully for years suddenly find themselves unable to be part of the very community they love. They have difficulty praying, attending services, and connecting with a community that should seek to nourish their faith. Instead, they feel separated from it.

Jesus didn’t instruct us to serve with complete disregard for our well-being. He was clear that we need breaks and times of rest:

The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all they had done and taught. Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” – Mark 6:30-31, NIV

When Serving Becomes Identity

We don’t realize how deeply the role in church can shape who we think we are until we try to imagine our lives without that service. When we are the person everyone depends on for sound equipment, or the one who always brings meals to new families, these roles become more than a task; they become our identity.

When an identity is tied to service, rest becomes a threat. It triggers a fear that if you stop serving, you’ll lose your place in the community or your value in God’s eyes. The result is a fear that drives people to continue beyond the point of healthy and sustainable service.

When there is a shift from serving out of love to serving out of obligation, it happens gradually. Serving begins as a privilege, and over time, it becomes a requirement externally or internally. The joy has faded, but the routine remains the same. People often continue because they don’t know how to stop without creating disappointment or disruption. It is in these moments that emotional burnout becomes particularly damaging.

Someone can still be present in the role, but completely absent in their heart. They go through the motions and fulfill expectations, leaving them feeling disconnected from the purpose that once motivated them. The life they are living no longer reflects their beliefs or needs. God calls us to use our gifts with faithful stewardship. Serving with little regard for that stewardship is not how He wants us to use our gifts.

Each of you should use whatever gift you have received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God’s grace in its various forms. – 1 Peter 4:10, NIV

The Physical Symptoms that Signal Deeper Struggles

The manifestation of emotional burnout can extend far beyond feeling tired. There’s a change in sleep patterns, and appetite often shifts. Each of these symptoms can create irritability and affect concentration. Along with these, there’s a persistent sense of being overwhelmed, and decision-making seems challenging.

Physical symptoms, such as headaches, gastrointestinal symptoms, and muscle tension, are also common manifestations of emotional burnout. These are the ways our bodies let us know that something has to change and that it’s time to stop ignoring it. People deeply embedded in church service often dismiss these signals as temporary stress or spiritual warfare instead of the legitimate burnout that is looming within.

The complication arises when Church environments frequently emphasize pushing through hardship as an act of faith. We read Scriptures about perseverance, running the race, and enduring to the end, and these truths are essential. However, without discernment, they can also prevent us from acknowledging when we’ve reached our breaking point. It’s a narrative that becomes about enduring hardship instead of addressing the root issue.

Christian counselors can help us recognize that burnout is not a form of spiritual failure. They provide ways to understand that awareness can enable healing. They provide strategies to identify bodily signals so that we can facilitate recovery rather than cause further harm.

Creating Space for Healing Without Abandoning Faith

Recovering from emotional burnout in church ministry is a process that requires more than just taking a break. It will require examining the beliefs that led to the burnout in the first place. There are difficult questions that must be answered to identify a pathway to genuine recovery. Healing isn’t about abandoning service. It’s about relearning what healthy service looks like.

Professional support is invaluable in recovering from emotional burnout. Christian counselors are trained to help us separate our identity from our roles and establish boundaries that honor our calling and our limitations. We can learn to rebuild relationships within the church community in a way that does not deplete us.

Recovery entails redefining rest as a spiritual practice rather than a personal weakness. When we acknowledge that withdrawal is not rejection and that saying no is an act of wisdom, we can protect our well-being as we serve from a place of genuine love rather than obligation. Our goal isn’t to walk away from serving. It is to learn how to serve from wholeness instead of emptiness. It is prioritizing our hope in God instead of ourselves. And this is when we soar.

But those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not be faint. – Isaiah 40:31, NIV

Don’t Keep Suffering with Emotional Burnout in Church Ministry

Recognizing emotional burnout in church ministry acknowledges our humanity. It doesn’t mean we aren’t good enough in our faith or service. When we care deeply, give generously, and feel the weight of responsibility, it is easy to experience emotional burnout. Our exhaustion doesn’t mean we lack love for God or our community. It is a reality that even in our most devoted moments, we have limits.

Churches will always need people who are willing to serve. That doesn’t mean it’s ok for these people to become worn out and weary. Rest and boundaries are what enable long-term ministry. When we understand this, we find that our commitment is not diminished, but instead protected.

If you struggle with emotional burnout related to church ministry, counseling can help. A Christian counselor can help you identify the struggle and create new ways of moving forward. Contact a counselor at this office to get started.
